The FPAA recharacterized all \$47,612,000 in priority profit allocations as ordinary income and asserted the 20% accuracy-related penalty under IRC § 6662. Quillen Decl. ¶ 39; Ex. 14.

236	
237	32\. The government\'s motion for summary judgment is supported by the Declaration of Special Agent Teresa Quillen with Exhibits 1 through 14, filed concurrently herewith, and the Expert Declaration of Professor Leah Ashford of Whitman University School of Law, also filed concurrently.
238	
239	**[III. LEGAL STANDARD FOR SUMMARY JUDGMENT]{.underline}**
240	
241	Summary judgment is appropriate where \"there is no genuine dispute as to any material fact and the movant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law.\" Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(a). The Supreme Court has explained that the purpose of the summary judgment procedure is to \"pierce the pleadings and to assess the proof in order to see whether there is a genuine need for trial.\" *Matsushita Elec. Indus. Co. v. Zenith Radio Corp.*, 475 U.S. 574, 587 (1986).
242	
243	The moving party bears the initial burden of demonstrating the absence of a genuine dispute of material fact. *Celotex Corp. v. Catrett*, 477 U.S. 317, 322 (1986). This burden may be satisfied by \"pointing out to the district court . . . that there is an absence of evidence to support the nonmoving party\'s case.\" *Id.* at 325. Once the moving party has met this initial burden, the burden shifts to the non-moving party, which \"must do more than simply show that there is some metaphysical doubt as to the material facts.\" *Matsushita*, 475 U.S. at 586. Rather, the non-moving party must \"set forth specific facts showing that there is a genuine issue for trial.\" *Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc.*, 477 U.S. 242, 248 (1986) (quoting Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(e)).
244	
245	A dispute is \"genuine\" only if \"the evidence is such that a reasonable jury could return a verdict for the nonmoving party.\" *Anderson*, 477 U.S. at 248. A fact is \"material\" only if it \"might affect the outcome of the suit under the governing law.\" *Id.* In evaluating a motion for summary judgment, the court must view the evidence in the light most favorable to the non-moving party and draw all reasonable inferences in its favor. *Id.* at 255. However, \"the mere existence of a scintilla of evidence\" in support of the non-moving party\'s position is insufficient to defeat summary judgment. *Id.* at 252.
246	
247	In federal tax cases, including partnership-level proceedings, it is well established that the taxpayer bears the burden of proving that the Commissioner\'s determination --- here, the adjustments set forth in the FPAA --- is incorrect. *See* Welch v. Helvering, 290 U.S. 111, 115 (1933). The FPAA carries a presumption of correctness, and HCP bears the burden of overcoming that presumption unless it can satisfy the requirements for burden-shifting under IRC § 7491(a), which requires, *inter alia*, that the taxpayer introduce credible evidence with respect to any factual issue and comply with all substantiation and record-keeping requirements. There is no indication in the record that HCP has satisfied these requirements.
248	
249	The government respectfully submits that this case is well suited for resolution on summary judgment. The underlying facts are not in genuine dispute: the execution of the waiver elections, the dollar amounts waived, the mechanics of the priority profit allocations, the Carry-Forward Provision, and HCP\'s tax reporting are all documented in the record and are not contested. The sole question presented is one of legal characterization --- whether the priority profit allocations constitute long-term capital gains, as HCP reported, or ordinary income, as the FPAA determined. This is a question of law, not of fact, and it is therefore appropriate for summary judgment. *See Anderson*, 477 U.S. at 250 (\"The judge\'s inquiry . . . unavoidably asks whether reasonable jurors could find by a preponderance of the evidence that the plaintiff is entitled to a verdict.\").
250	
251	**[IV. ARGUMENT]{.underline}**
252	
253	**A. The Management Fee Waiver Allocations Are Disguised Payments for Services Under IRC § 707(a)(2)(A)**
254	
255	The management fee waiver allocations at issue are, in both form and substance, disguised payments for services within the meaning of IRC § 707(a)(2)(A). The statute, the implementing regulations, and the governing case law compel this conclusion.
256	
257	**1. Statutory Framework**
258	
259	Section 707(a)(2)(A) of the Internal Revenue Code provides:
260	
261	> If ---
262	>
263	> \(A\) a partner performs services for any partnership or transfers property to a partnership,
264	>
265	> \(B\) there is a related direct or indirect allocation and distribution to such partner, and
266	>
267	> \(C\) the performance of such services (or such transfer) and the allocation and distribution, when viewed together, are properly characterized as a transaction occurring between the partnership and a partner acting other than in his capacity as a member of the partnership,
268	>
269	> then such allocation and distribution shall be treated as a transaction described in \[section 707(a)(1)\].
270	
271	IRC § 707(a)(2)(A). When an allocation and distribution are recharacterized under this provision, the payment is treated as compensation for services rendered to the partnership by a non-partner --- that is, as ordinary income. The legislative history of the Tax Reform Act of 1984 confirms that Congress enacted § 707(a)(2)(A) to prevent the use of partnership allocations as a vehicle for converting what is, in economic substance, ordinary service income into preferentially taxed partnership distributive shares. *See* H.R. Rep. No. 98-861, at 861 (1984) (Conference Report).
272	
273	Here, there is no dispute that HCP performed services for the Funds --- specifically, investment management, portfolio monitoring, and administrative services identical to those for which HCP charged management fees. There is no dispute that HCP received related allocations (the priority profit allocations) and distributions from the Funds. The determinative question is whether, under the third element, the performance of services and the allocation and distribution, \"when viewed together, are properly characterized as a transaction occurring between the partnership and a partner acting other than in his capacity as a member of the partnership.\" IRC § 707(a)(2)(A)(iii).
274	
275	**2. The Six-Factor Test of Treasury Regulation § 1.707-2(c)**
276	
277	The Treasury Regulations provide a six-factor test for determining whether an allocation and distribution constitute a disguised payment for services. Treas. Reg. § 1.707-2(c). The government submits that each applicable factor weighs decisively in favor of recharacterization.
278	
279	**\*Factor (1): Whether the payment is subject to an appreciable risk that it will not be made.**\* Treasury Regulation § 1.707-2(c)(1) directs inquiry into whether the payment to the partner is \"subject to appreciable risk\" --- that is, whether there is a genuine possibility that the partner will not receive the economic benefit of the allocation. Here, the priority profit allocations were subject to negligible risk. The Carry-Forward Provision ensured that if a Fund did not generate sufficient realized long-term capital gains in the year of the waiver, the unfulfilled amount would carry forward to subsequent years \"until fully allocated,\" with no expiration date and with a compounding return at the applicable federal rate. Quillen Decl. ¶ 13; Ex. 4.
280	
281	The only circumstance under which HCP would fail to receive the full priority allocation was if a Fund suffered a total and permanent loss of all invested capital --- a catastrophic scenario that, while theoretically possible, is extraordinarily remote for diversified private equity funds with billions of dollars in committed capital and broad portfolio diversification. The Carry-Forward Provision effectively guaranteed that HCP would receive the full dollar amount of the waived management fees, thereby negating any appreciable risk. *See Pinnacle Partners v. Commissioner*, T.C. Memo 2019-88, at \*12 (finding that a substantially identical carry-forward mechanism eliminated meaningful risk). Professor Ashford confirms that the Carry-Forward Provision \"rendered the risk of non-payment de minimis.\" Ashford Decl. ¶ 22. This factor weighs heavily in favor of recharacterization.
282	
283	**\*Factor (2): Whether the partner providing services also receives a guaranteed payment or a preferred return.**\* Treasury Regulation § 1.707-2(c)(2) considers whether the service-providing partner receives additional fixed or preferential compensation from the partnership. While HCP did not receive a separately denominated \"guaranteed payment\" under IRC § 707(c) from the Funds, the priority profit allocations themselves functioned as the economic equivalent of a preferred return. The allocations were satisfied from the \"first dollars\" of realized long-term capital gains --- that is, HCP\'s priority claim was senior to the allocations of all other partners, including limited partners. Quillen Decl. ¶ 12; Ex. 4.
284	
285	Moreover, the Carry-Forward Provision with its compounding return at the applicable federal rate further underscored the preferential nature of the allocation. HCP was not merely a passive participant in the Funds\' investment returns; it occupied a creditor-like position in the allocation waterfall. This factor supports recharacterization.
286	
287	**\*Factor (3): Whether the allocation and distribution have the effect of converting what would be ordinary income to capital gain.**\* Treasury Regulation § 1.707-2(c)(3) examines whether the arrangement has the practical effect of income character conversion. This factor is dispositive in the present case. The entire purpose and effect of the Fee Waiver Program was to convert ordinary management fee income into long-term capital gains. HCP\'s management fees were, by their nature, ordinary income --- compensation for services rendered. By waiving those fees and receiving in their place priority profit allocations from realized long-term capital gains, HCP effectuated a dollar-for-dollar conversion of income character without altering the economic substance of the compensation arrangement.
288	
289	This is not a case where the income conversion was incidental or secondary. It was the primary --- indeed, the sole --- objective. Quillen Decl. ¶ 44; Ashford Decl. ¶ 18. As the Tax Court recognized in *Pinnacle Partners*, \"when the effect of an allocation is to convert what would otherwise be ordinary income into capital gain, this factor weighs heavily in favor of characterizing the allocation as a disguised payment for services.\" T.C. Memo 2019-88, at \*13. This factor weighs overwhelmingly in favor of recharacterization.
290	
291	**\*The Priority Allocations Constitute Transitory Allocations Lacking Substantial Economic Effect.**\* In addition to the foregoing factors, the priority profit allocations must be evaluated under the principles governing transitory allocations set forth in Treasury Regulation § 1.704-1(b)(2)(iii).\^9 Under this regulation, an allocation is \"transitory\" where it is made with a strong likelihood that it will be largely offset by one or more subsequent allocations, such that the net economic effect on the partners\' capital accounts is minimal. Treas. Reg. § 1.704-1(b)(2)(iii)(b) and (c).
292	
293	\^9 *See* Treas. Reg. § 1.704-1(b)(2)(iii) (defining transitory allocations and providing that such allocations will not be respected for purposes of the substantial economic effect safe harbor).
294	
295	Here, the priority profit allocations to HCP were transitory in nature because they were offset by corresponding reductions in HCP\'s management fee entitlements. The net economic impact on the Funds and their limited partners was zero: the Funds avoided paying a management fee and instead made a priority allocation of identical amount. The net economic impact on HCP was likewise zero: HCP received the same dollar amount it would have received as management fees, albeit labeled as a partnership allocation. The allocation did not alter the economic bargain between HCP and the Funds in any meaningful respect. It merely relabeled the compensation and changed its tax character. Such transitory allocations lack substantial economic effect and should not be respected for federal tax purposes. This analysis further supports the conclusion that the priority allocations were disguised payments for services.
296

297:**\*Factor (5): Whether the amount of the allocation is relatively fixed in relation to the services rendered.**\* Treasury Regulation § 1.707-2(c)(5) asks whether the amount allocated bears a fixed or determinable relationship to the services provided. Here, the relationship was not merely fixed --- it was dollar-for-dollar identical. The amount of each priority profit allocation was precisely equal to the management fee that HCP waived. There was no variability, no negotiation, and no market-based adjustment. The amount was set in advance by the waiver election documents, which specified the exact dollar amounts to be waived for each Fund. Quillen Decl. ¶ 12; Ex. 6. This mechanical substitution of character --- same amount, same timing, different label --- is the hallmark of a disguised payment. This factor strongly supports recharacterization.
**\*Factor (5): Whether the amount of the allocation is relatively fixed in relation to the services rendered.**\* Treasury Regulation § 1.707-2(c)(5) asks whether the amount allocated bears a fixed or determinable relationship to the services provided. Here, the relationship was not merely fixed --- it was dollar-for-dollar identical. The amount of each priority profit allocation was precisely equal to the management fee that HCP waived. There was no variability, no negotiation, and no market-based adjustment. The amount was set in advance by the waiver election documents, which specified the exact dollar amounts to be waived for each Fund. Quillen Decl. ¶ 12; Ex. 6. This mechanical substitution of character --- same amount, same timing, different label --- is the hallmark of a disguised payment. This factor strongly supports recharacterization.

**\*Factor (6): Whether the allocation is subject to a ceiling.**\* Treasury Regulation § 1.707-2(c)(6) considers whether the partner\'s right to the allocation is capped. While the priority allocations were nominally limited to the amount of realized long-term capital gains in a given year, the Carry-Forward Provision effectively eliminated any practical ceiling. Unfulfilled allocations were carried forward indefinitely and accrued a compounding return. Quillen Decl. ¶ 13; Ex. 4. The absence of any meaningful ceiling on the allocation reinforces the conclusion that HCP\'s right to compensation was not contingent on the Funds\' investment performance in any meaningful sense. This factor weighs in favor of recharacterization.

**3. \*Pinnacle Partners\* Confirms That Fee Waiver Arrangements Are Disguised Payments**

The government\'s position is directly supported by the Tax Court\'s decision in *Pinnacle Partners v. Commissioner*, T.C. Memo 2019-88. In *Pinnacle Partners*, the Tax Court examined a management fee waiver arrangement that was substantially identical to HCP\'s Fee Waiver Program. The fund manager in *Pinnacle* waived management fees and received priority profit allocations payable from realized long-term capital gains, with a carry-forward provision ensuring eventual satisfaction of the full waived amount. The Tax Court held that the arrangement was a disguised payment for services under IRC § 707(a)(2)(A).\^10

\^10 In *Pinnacle Partners*, the Tax Court held that a substantially identical fee waiver arrangement lacked economic substance because the priority allocation carried no genuine risk of non-payment. T.C. Memo 2019-88, at \*12-14.

The Tax Court\'s analysis in *Pinnacle* is instructive. The court focused on the absence of genuine entrepreneurial risk, noting that the carry-forward provision \"ensured that the manager would ultimately receive the full amount of the waived fees, regardless of the fund\'s performance in any particular year.\" *Pinnacle Partners*, T.C. Memo 2019-88, at *13. The court further observed that the fee waiver \"did not alter the economic relationship between the manager and the fund\'s investors\" and was \"a re-labeling exercise designed to achieve a tax result.\"* Id. *at* 14.

The same analysis applies with equal force here. Like the arrangement in *Pinnacle*, HCP\'s Fee Waiver Program involved: (a) a dollar-for-dollar substitution of priority allocations for management fees; (b) a carry-forward provision eliminating meaningful risk of non-payment; (c) no change in the economic substance of the compensation arrangement; and (d) a sole purpose of converting ordinary income to capital gains. *Pinnacle Partners* categorically establishes that management fee waivers of this type fail to shift meaningful entrepreneurial risk to the fund manager and are properly recharacterized as disguised payments for services.

**4. Revenue Procedure 93-27 Further Supports the Government\'s Position**

The IRS has long recognized that profits interests received for services carry significant tax implications. Indeed, the IRS has long recognized that profits interests received in exchange for services are taxed at the time of receipt if they have a determinable value. *See* Rev. Proc. 93-27, 1993-2 C.B. 343.\^11 While HCP may argue that the priority allocations were merely allocations of partnership income to a partner in its capacity as a partner, the economic reality is that these allocations were compensation for management services that HCP had already agreed to provide. The fact that the allocations were denominated as profits interests does not insulate them from recharacterization under § 707(a)(2)(A).

\^11 Rev. Proc. 93-27, 1993-2 C.B. 343.

**5. Conclusion on Disguised Payment Analysis**

Every applicable factor under Treasury Regulation § 1.707-2(c) weighs in favor of treating HCP\'s priority profit allocations as disguised payments for services under IRC § 707(a)(2)(A). The allocations bore negligible risk of non-payment, functioned as the economic equivalent of a preferred return, had the express purpose and effect of converting ordinary income to capital gains, were fixed in amount relative to the services rendered, and were not subject to any meaningful ceiling. The fee waiver arrangement was a transaction between the Funds and HCP acting other than in its capacity as a partner, and the resulting allocations must be recharacterized as ordinary income.

**B. The Management Fee Waiver Allocations Are Economically Indistinguishable from Carried Interest**

The government further contends that HCP\'s priority profit allocations are economically indistinguishable from carried interest --- that is, a profits interest in the Fund that provides the general partner or fund manager with a share of the fund\'s investment gains in compensation for services rendered. The priority allocations are economically indistinguishable from carried interest. In both cases, the fund manager receives a share of the fund\'s long-term capital gains in compensation for services rendered. The only structural difference is the mechanism by which the allocation arises: in a traditional carried interest arrangement, the general partner is entitled to a specified percentage of the fund\'s profits (typically 20%) above a preferred return; in HCP\'s fee waiver arrangement, the manager is entitled to a specified dollar amount of the fund\'s long-term capital gains, determined by the amount of management fees waived.

This distinction is one of form, not substance. The economic reality is identical: in both cases, the fund manager receives a portion of the fund\'s long-term capital gains as compensation for the management and advisory services it provides. The fee waiver arrangement is, in essence, a \"synthetic\" carried interest --- manufactured by waiving management fees and receiving in their place an allocation of capital gains equal to the waived amount.

Congress has recognized the tension between the taxation of carried interest at capital gains rates and the reality that such compensation is derived from services. In 2017, Congress enacted IRC § 1061, which imposes a three-year holding period requirement on certain carried interest gains, reflecting the legislative determination that carried interest gains should be subject to heightened scrutiny and, in some cases, recharacterized as short-term capital gains (taxable at ordinary income rates) where the underlying assets are held for three years or less. While § 1061 does not directly apply to fee waiver arrangements, its enactment reflects a broader Congressional policy judgment that gains derived from fund management activities should not automatically receive preferential capital gains treatment.

HCP\'s fee waiver arrangement is even more aggressive than a traditional carried interest. In a traditional carried interest arrangement, the general partner\'s allocation is genuinely contingent on the fund\'s profitability --- the general partner receives nothing unless and until the fund generates returns in excess of the preferred return hurdle. By contrast, HCP\'s priority profit allocations were payable from the \"first dollars\" of realized long-term capital gains, without regard to any preferred return or hurdle rate, and carried forward indefinitely with a compounding return. This arrangement eliminated the very risk that provides the theoretical justification for capital gains treatment of carried interest --- namely, that the fund manager\'s compensation is at risk because it depends on the fund\'s investment performance.

The investment performance of the Funds underscores this point. Fund III, the earliest fund in the Hargrove platform, realized net gains of only \$298 million on \$820 million in committed capital --- a net multiple of approximately 0.36x, well below median performance for its vintage year.\^12 Yet HCP received the full \$11,850,000 in priority allocations attributable to Fund III (\$7,200,000 in TY 2018 and \$4,650,000 in TY 2019). If HCP\'s compensation had been structured as a genuine carried interest --- contingent on fund performance above a hurdle --- it is doubtful that Fund III would have generated sufficient returns to trigger any carried interest payment at all. The fact that HCP received full compensation from Fund III, notwithstanding the fund\'s below-median performance, further demonstrates that the fee waiver arrangement was not a genuine entrepreneurial bet but rather a compensation mechanism dressed in the garments of partnership allocation.

\^12 The Court may take judicial notice of industry-standard benchmarking data regarding private equity fund performance by vintage year. *See* Preqin, *Global Private Equity Report 2021*, at 34-37; McKinsey & Company, *Private Markets Annual Review 2020*, at 18-22.

Moreover, HCP\'s decision to extend the fee waiver program to Fund V in its very first year of operation --- before the fund had completed its initial capital deployment, let alone generated any realized investment returns --- further evidences the disconnect between the fee waiver arrangement and genuine entrepreneurial risk. Fund V deployed only \$380 million of its \$1.75 billion in committed capital during 2020, and yet HCP purportedly received a \$6,000,000 priority allocation from Fund V. The inclusion of a newly formed fund in the fee waiver program, at a stage when the fund\'s investment track record was nonexistent, confirms that the program was designed to convert management fee income rather than to align the interests of the fund manager with those of the fund\'s investors.

The government recognizes that the current tax treatment of carried interest remains a matter of ongoing legislative debate. But regardless of how one resolves the policy question of carried interest taxation, HCP\'s fee waiver arrangement represents an attempt to manufacture the favorable tax treatment of carried interest without accepting the genuine economic risk that carried interest entails. This synthetic structure should not be respected for federal tax purposes.

**C. The Fee Waiver Arrangement Lacks Economic Substance**

Independent of the disguised payment analysis, the government contends that HCP\'s fee waiver arrangement lacks economic substance and must be disregarded under the economic substance doctrine, as codified by IRC § 7701(o).

**1. The Economic Substance Doctrine**

The economic substance doctrine is a longstanding judicial doctrine, now codified by statute, that disallows tax benefits arising from transactions that lack genuine economic substance apart from their tax consequences. IRC § 7701(o), enacted as part of the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010, provides:

> In the case of any transaction to which the economic substance doctrine is relevant, such transaction shall be treated as having economic substance only if ---
>
> \(A\) the transaction changes in a meaningful way (apart from Federal income tax effects) the taxpayer\'s economic position, and
>
> \(B\) the taxpayer has a substantial purpose (apart from Federal income tax effects) for entering into such transaction.

IRC § 7701(o)(1). The doctrine has deep roots in the tax law, tracing its origins to *Gregory v. Helvering*, 293 U.S. 465 (1935), and has been consistently applied to disallow tax benefits arising from transactions that lack genuine business purpose or meaningful economic consequences. *See ASA Investerings Partnership v. Commissioner*, 201 F.3d 505, 512-13 (D.C. Cir. 2000) (applying economic substance doctrine to disallow losses from partnership transaction lacking genuine economic consequences); *Frank Lyon Co. v. United States*, 435 U.S. 561, 573 (1978) (noting that the form of a transaction will be respected for tax purposes where it is \"imbued with tax-independent considerations\").

**2. The Fee Waiver Arrangement Lacks a Genuine Business Purpose**

The fee waiver arrangement lacks economic substance because HCP had no legitimate, non-tax business purpose for implementing the waiver program. The sole motivation was to convert ordinary management fee income into preferentially taxed long-term capital gains. The evidence on this point is overwhelming and uncontroverted.

First, HCP has never articulated any business justification for the fee waiver arrangement other than tax savings. During the IRS examination, HCP was asked to identify any non-tax business reasons for the fee waiver program. HCP\'s responses, as documented in Special Agent Quillen\'s declaration, cited only \"alignment of interests\" between HCP and the Funds\' limited partners --- a generic justification that is belied by the mechanics of the arrangement. Quillen Decl. ¶ 44. The \"alignment of interests\" rationale presupposes that the fund manager is assuming genuine investment risk by tying its compensation to the fund\'s performance. But here, the Carry-Forward Provision eliminated virtually all investment risk. HCP\'s compensation was not genuinely at risk; it was merely deferred. The \"alignment of interests\" rationale is pretextual.

Second, the timing and execution of the waiver elections demonstrate that the fee waiver program was a paper exercise divorced from genuine business considerations. For Tax Years 2018 and 2019, the elections were executed in late November or December of the preceding year --- after HCP had full visibility into the Funds\' portfolio performance and could predict with substantial confidence whether sufficient realized long-term capital gains would be generated in the coming year. This retrospective knowledge undermined any suggestion that HCP was making a genuine prospective business decision to accept investment risk in lieu of certain management fee income.

The TY 2020 elections are even more telling. The TY 2020 elections for both Fund IV and Fund V were executed after the commencement of the fiscal year, demonstrating that the waivers were retroactive adjustments rather than genuine prospective business decisions.\^13 The Fund V election was signed on January 28, 2020, twenty-eight days after the start of the fiscal year. This retroactive timing is inconsistent with a genuine pre-commitment to accept investment risk and is instead consistent with a post hoc adjustment designed to ensure favorable tax treatment.

\^13 *See* Quillen Decl. ¶ 22; Ex. 6. The retroactive nature of the TY 2020 elections is particularly significant because a genuine fee waiver --- one that reflects a true prospective business decision to accept investment risk in lieu of certain fee income --- must be made before the period to which it relates. *See* Treas. Reg. § 1.707-2(c)(1).

Third, the background and sophistication of HCP\'s managing partners confirm the tax motivation. Elliot R. Hargrove is a former tax attorney who practiced at Thornfield & Locke LLP, where he specialized in partnership taxation and private fund structuring for approximately eight years before founding HCP.\^14 Hargrove possessed the precise expertise needed to design and implement a fee waiver arrangement optimized for tax benefits. His professional background strongly suggests that the fee waiver program was the product of deliberate tax planning rather than genuine business necessity.

\^14 *See* Quillen Decl. ¶ 9; Ex. 5.

Fourth, all three Funds generated substantial capital gains during the relevant tax years, providing the foundation for the priority allocations. The existence of realized gains at the Fund level was a necessary precondition for the fee waiver program to function as designed. HCP\'s decision to participate in the waiver program only when the Funds had sufficient realized gains --- and to calibrate the waiver amounts to match available gains --- further evidences the tax-driven nature of the arrangement. Quillen Decl. ¶ 34.

**3. Application to HCP\'s Fee Waiver Program**

Under the economic substance doctrine, HCP\'s fee waiver arrangement must be disregarded because it served no purpose other than the generation of tax benefits. The arrangement did not change the services HCP provided, did not change the amount of compensation HCP received, and did not change the economic relationship between HCP and the Funds. The only thing that changed was the tax character of HCP\'s compensation --- from ordinary income to long-term capital gains. This is precisely the type of transaction that the economic substance doctrine is designed to address.

As the D.C. Circuit explained in *ASA Investerings*, the economic substance doctrine operates to \"prevent taxpayers from subverting the legislative purpose of the tax code by engaging in transactions that are fictitious or lack economic reality.\" 201 F.3d at 512. HCP\'s fee waiver arrangement subverts the legislative purpose of IRC § 707(a)(2)(A), which was enacted to prevent the very type of income conversion that HCP effectuated. Allowing the fee waiver arrangement to stand would render § 707(a)(2)(A) a nullity --- any fund manager could avoid the statute\'s reach simply by \"waiving\" management fees and receiving \"priority allocations\" of capital gains in their place.

The Supreme Court\'s admonition in *Frank Lyon* is equally pertinent. While the Court in *Frank Lyon* recognized that a transaction\'s form will be respected where it is \"compelled or encouraged by business or regulatory realities, is imbued with tax-independent considerations, and is not shaped solely by tax-avoidance features,\" 435 U.S. at 583-84, HCP\'s fee waiver arrangement satisfies none of these conditions. The arrangement was not compelled by any business necessity, was not imbued with tax-independent considerations, and was shaped solely by tax-avoidance objectives. The economic substance doctrine therefore requires that it be disregarded.

**D. The Priority Allocations Do Not Satisfy IRC § 702(b) Character Requirements**

The government further submits that the priority profit allocations do not properly qualify as long-term capital gains at the Fund level under IRC § 702(b) and the implementing regulations.

Section 702(b) of the Internal Revenue Code provides that \"\[t\]he character of any item of income, gain, loss, deduction, or credit included in a partner\'s distributive share . . . shall be determined as if such item were realized directly from the source from which realized by the partnership, or incurred in the same manner as incurred by the partnership.\" IRC § 702(b). The implementing regulations at Treasury Regulation § 1.702-1(b) confirm that the character of partnership income is determined at the partnership (here, the Fund) level and passes through to the partners.

HCP\'s claimed tax treatment depends on the proposition that the priority profit allocations derive their character from the realized long-term capital gains generated by the Funds\' investment activities. The government does not dispute that the Funds\' investment gains, standing alone, constitute long-term capital gains. The government\'s contention is that when an allocation of partnership income is, in substance, compensation for services, the character of the allocation must be determined by reference to the nature of the underlying transaction --- *i.e.*, the provision of management services --- rather than by reference to the character of the fund-level income from which the allocation is drawn.

To hold otherwise would permit fund managers to cherry-pick the character of their compensation by directing that their fees be paid from the most tax-advantaged pool of fund income. A fund manager could waive management fees and receive \"priority allocations\" drawn exclusively from long-term capital gains, dividend income, or tax-exempt interest, while ordinary income generated by the fund\'s operations flows exclusively to the limited partners. This selective allocation of character is precisely the type of manipulation that § 707(a)(2)(A) was enacted to prevent.

The \"priority\" nature of HCP\'s allocation --- the fact that HCP received the \"first dollars\" of realized long-term capital gains --- is itself a mechanism designed to cherry-pick character. In a genuine partnership allocation, the character of income allocated to a partner reflects the character of the partnership\'s overall income. The priority allocation, by contrast, is specifically structured to ensure that HCP receives only long-term capital gains character, even if the Fund generates substantial ordinary income. This character cherry-picking is not consistent with the principles of IRC § 702(b) when the underlying allocation is, as the government has demonstrated, a disguised payment for services.

Accordingly, because the priority profit allocations are in substance compensation for services, they must be characterized as ordinary income under IRC § 707(a)(2)(A), regardless of the character of the fund-level income from which they are drawn. IRC § 702(b) does not override § 707(a)(2)(A); rather, § 707(a)(2)(A) operates as a recharacterization rule that determines the nature of the transaction before § 702(b) character rules apply.

**E. The Step Transaction Doctrine Supports Recharacterization**

As an alternative and supplementary basis for recharacterization, the government invokes the step transaction doctrine. Under this well-established judicial doctrine, a series of formally separate transactions may be collapsed into a single integrated transaction when the individual steps are so interdependent that the legal relations created by one step would be meaningless without completion of the subsequent steps. *See Gregory v. Helvering*, 293 U.S. 465, 469-70 (1935); *Klamath Strategic Investment Fund v. United States*, 568 F.3d 537, 544 (5th Cir. 2009).

The step transaction doctrine applies under any of its three recognized tests: the \"binding commitment\" test, the \"mutual interdependence\" test, and the \"end result\" test. Under the mutual interdependence test, a series of steps will be collapsed where \"the steps are so interdependent that the legal relations created by one transaction would have been fruitless without a completion of the series.\" *Klamath*, 568 F.3d at 544.

Here, HCP\'s fee waiver arrangement involves a multi-step process: (1) HCP elects to waive management fees otherwise payable by a Fund; (2) the Fund does not pay the management fee; (3) the Fund instead makes a priority profit allocation to HCP in an amount equal to the waived fee; and (4) the Fund distributes cash to HCP in satisfaction of the priority allocation. These steps are mutually interdependent --- no step has independent business significance without the others. The waiver election is meaningless without the corresponding priority allocation. The priority allocation is meaningless without the corresponding distribution. And the distribution is economically identical to the management fee payment that would have been made absent the waiver.

When collapsed under the step transaction doctrine, the multi-step arrangement reduces to a single transaction: the payment of ordinary management fee income by the Fund to HCP in exchange for management services. The intermediate steps --- the waiver, the priority allocation, and the recharacterization as long-term capital gains --- are transitory formalities that serve no purpose other than tax avoidance. The step transaction doctrine therefore provides an independent basis for treating the \$47,612,000 in priority allocations as ordinary income.

The \"end result\" test further supports this conclusion. Under the end result test, \"purportedly separate transactions will be amalgamated into a single transaction when it appears that they were really component parts of a single transaction intended from the outset to be taken for the purpose of reaching the ultimate result.\" *Klamath*, 568 F.3d at 544. The ultimate result here is clear: HCP received \$47,612,000 in compensation for management services. The intermediate steps were designed solely to alter the tax character of that compensation.

**[V. THE APPROPRIATE REMEDY AND PENALTIES]{.underline}**

**A. All \$47,612,000 Should Be Recharacterized as Ordinary Income**

Based on the foregoing analysis, the proper remedy is the recharacterization of all \$47,612,000 in priority profit allocations received by HCP during Tax Years 2018, 2019, and 2020 as ordinary income. This recharacterization should be applied as follows:

  -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Tax Year**   **Fund III**       **Fund IV**        **Fund V**        **Total**
  -------------- ------------------ ------------------ ----------------- ------------------
  2018           \$7,200,000        \$5,200,000        ---               \$12,400,000

  2019           \$4,650,000        \$14,200,000       ---               \$18,850,000

  2020           ---                \$10,362,000       \$6,000,000       \$16,362,000

  **Total**      **\$11,850,000**   **\$29,762,000**   **\$6,000,000**   **\$47,612,000**
  -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The recharacterization of the priority allocations as ordinary income flows through to HCP\'s partners under IRC § 702(a). The individual partner impacts are as follows:

> • **Elliot R. Hargrove** (42% profits interest): \$19,997,040 recharacterized from long-term capital gains to ordinary income.
>
> • **Diane K. Sato** (38% profits interest): \$18,092,560 recharacterized from long-term capital gains to ordinary income.
>
> • **Remaining partners** (20% collective profits interest): \$9,522,400 recharacterized from long-term capital gains to ordinary income.

The priority allocations are, in substance, guaranteed payments within the meaning of IRC § 707(c).\^15 They were determined without regard to the partnership\'s income and were payable for services --- management services --- rendered by HCP to the Funds. The dollar amounts were fixed in advance by the waiver election documents, and the Carry-Forward Provision ensured that HCP would receive the full amounts regardless of the Funds\' income in any particular year. Under IRC § 707(c), guaranteed payments are treated as ordinary income to the recipient partner, and the partnership is entitled to a deduction for such payments. Recharacterization of the priority allocations as guaranteed payments is therefore the appropriate remedy.

\^15 IRC § 707(c) provides: \"To the extent determined without regard to the income of the partnership, payments to a partner for services or the use of capital shall be considered as made to one who is not a member of the partnership, but only for the purposes of section 61(a) (relating to gross income) and, subject to section 263, for purposes of section 162(a) (relating to trade or business expenses).\"

The resulting aggregate federal tax benefit to HCP\'s partners was \$9,530,400, representing the 17% differential between the ordinary income rate of 37% and the long-term capital gain rate of 20% applied to \$47,612,000 in recharacterized income. This tax benefit inured solely to Hargrove, Sato, and HCP\'s other partners, and constituted a windfall derived from an arrangement that lacked economic substance and violated the disguised payment rules of IRC § 707(a)(2)(A).

The FPAA\'s determination that the priority allocations should be recharacterized as ordinary income for Tax Years 2018, 2019, and 2020 is supported by each of the independent legal theories set forth in this Memorandum and should be sustained.

**B. HCP Is Liable for the 20% Accuracy-Related Penalty Under IRC § 6662**

In addition to the recharacterization of the \$47,612,000 in priority allocations, the FPAA asserted the 20% accuracy-related penalty under IRC § 6662(a) and (b). The government respectfully submits that this penalty should be sustained.

**1. The Statutory Standard**

Section 6662(a) of the Internal Revenue Code imposes a penalty equal to 20% of the portion of an underpayment of tax \"attributable to\" any of the grounds specified in § 6662(b). Relevant here are two independent grounds:

> \(1\) **Negligence or disregard of rules or regulations.** IRC § 6662(b)(1). Negligence includes \"any failure to make a reasonable attempt to comply with the provisions of this title.\" IRC § 6662(c).
>
> \(2\) **Substantial understatement of income tax.** IRC § 6662(b)(2). An understatement is \"substantial\" if it exceeds the greater of 10% of the tax required to be shown on the return or \$5,000. IRC § 6662(d)(1)(A).

**2. HCP\'s Understatement Is Substantial**

The recharacterization of \$47,612,000 from long-term capital gains to ordinary income results in a substantial understatement of income tax attributable to each tax year at issue. The tax deficiency attributable to the character conversion vastly exceeds both the 10% threshold and the \$5,000 floor. The understatement is therefore \"substantial\" within the meaning of IRC § 6662(d)(1)(A), and the 20% penalty applies.

**3. HCP\'s Position Lacks Substantial Authority**

Under IRC § 6662(d)(2)(B), a taxpayer may reduce the amount of a substantial understatement by the amount attributable to items for which there was \"substantial authority\" for the tax treatment claimed. The government submits that HCP\'s claimed tax treatment of the management fee waivers lacked substantial authority. No reasonable taxpayer could have concluded that the conversion of \$47,612,000 in management fee income to long-term capital gains would be sustained.\^16

\^16 *See* IRC § 6662(d)(2)(B).

The statutory text of IRC § 707(a)(2)(A), the implementing regulations at Treas. Reg. § 1.707-2, and the relevant case law --- including *Pinnacle Partners v. Commissioner*, T.C. Memo 2019-88 --- collectively establish that management fee waiver arrangements of the type employed by HCP are subject to recharacterization as disguised payments for services. The weight of authority is overwhelmingly against the position adopted by HCP, and HCP\'s claimed tax treatment therefore does not meet the \"substantial authority\" standard.

Furthermore, the application of the economic substance doctrine, as codified at IRC § 7701(o), independently supports the penalty. Section 7701(o)(5)(A) provides that \"\[n\]o penalty shall be imposed under \[§ 6662\] with respect to any portion of an underpayment which is attributable to one or more non-economic substance transactions if --- (i) the relevant facts affecting the tax treatment of such transaction are adequately disclosed in the return or in a statement attached to the return, and (ii) there is a reasonable basis for the tax treatment.\" HCP did not adequately disclose the fee waiver arrangement on its returns, and, as demonstrated above, there is no reasonable basis for its claimed tax treatment.

**4. HCP Was Negligent**

In the alternative, HCP\'s claimed tax treatment reflects negligence within the meaning of IRC § 6662(b)(1). Given the clear statutory authority under § 707(a)(2)(A), the express guidance in the Treasury Regulations, and the Tax Court\'s holding in *Pinnacle Partners*, HCP\'s failure to report the priority allocations as ordinary income constitutes a failure to make a \"reasonable attempt to comply with the provisions of\" the Code. IRC § 6662(c). This is particularly so given that Hargrove --- HCP\'s co-founder and 42% owner --- was a former tax attorney who practiced partnership taxation at a prominent New York law firm. HCP possessed the sophistication and expertise to recognize that its fee waiver arrangement was subject to recharacterization, and its failure to report accordingly was negligent.

The 20% accuracy-related penalty under IRC § 6662 should therefore be sustained for Tax Years 2018, 2019, and 2020.

**[VI. CONCLUSION]{.underline}**

For the foregoing reasons, the undisputed material facts establish that Hargrove Capital Partners LLC\'s management fee waiver program was a disguised payment for services under IRC § 707(a)(2)(A), lacked economic substance under IRC § 7701(o), improperly invoked the character provisions of IRC § 702(b) to claim long-term capital gain treatment, and may independently be collapsed under the step transaction doctrine. Through this arrangement, HCP converted \$47,612,000 in ordinary management fee income into long-term capital gains for Tax Years 2018, 2019, and 2020, generating tax savings of \$9,530,400 that inured solely to the benefit of HCP\'s partners --- principally Elliot R. Hargrove and Diane K. Sato, who together control 80% of HCP\'s profits interests.

No genuine dispute of material fact exists. The waiver elections, the allocation mechanics, the amounts involved, and HCP\'s tax reporting are all established by the undisputed documentary record. The sole question is one of legal characterization, which this Court may resolve as a matter of law.

The United States of America respectfully requests that this Court:

1\. Grant the government\'s Motion for Summary Judgment;

2\. Sustain the Notice of Final Partnership Administrative Adjustment dated June 15, 2022, recharacterizing \$47,612,000 in priority profit allocations as ordinary income for Tax Years 2018, 2019, and 2020; and

3\. Impose the 20% accuracy-related penalty under IRC § 6662 for each tax year at issue.

Respectfully submitted,

Dated: April 3, 2024

MARCUS D. FELTON Senior Litigation Counsel Tax Division U.S. Department of Justice 950 Pennsylvania Avenue NW Washington, DC 20530 Telephone: (202) 514-3361 Facsimile: (202) 514-6770

Email: marcus.d.felton@usdoj.gov

Attorney for Plaintiff United States of America

I hereby certify that on April 3, 2024, a true and correct copy of the foregoing Memorandum of Law in Support of Plaintiff\'s Motion for Summary Judgment, together with all exhibits and declarations filed concurrently therewith, was served via the Court\'s Electronic Case Filing (ECF) system on all counsel of record, including:

UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT SOUTHERN DISTRICT OF NEW YORK

  **UNITED STATES OF AMERICA,**

  v\.

  HARGROVE CAPITAL PARTNERS LLC,

> • - -

**DECLARATION OF SPECIAL AGENT TERESA QUILLEN IN SUPPORT OF PLAINTIFF\'S MOTION FOR SUMMARY JUDGMENT**

> • - -

Filed: April 3, 2024

I, Teresa Quillen, pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1746, do hereby declare under penalty of perjury as follows:

**[I. INTRODUCTION AND QUALIFICATIONS]{.underline}**

1\. I am a Special Agent employed by the Internal Revenue Service (\"IRS\"), assigned to the Large Business & International Division (\"LB&I\"). I am currently stationed in the LB&I\'s Northeast Compliance Practice Area, with my duty station in New York, New York. I submit this declaration based on my personal knowledge, my review of the books, records, tax returns, and other documents of Hargrove Capital Partners LLC and its affiliated entities, and the documents attached hereto or referenced herein as Exhibits 1 through 14. I am competent to testify to the matters set forth in this declaration if called as a witness at trial.

2\. I have been employed by the IRS for approximately seventeen years. During the first five years of my tenure, I served as a Revenue Agent in the Small Business/Self-Employed Division, where I conducted examinations of individual and small business returns. For the past twelve years, I have been assigned to the Large Business & International Division, where my work has focused specifically on the examination of partnership returns and pass-through entities, including private equity fund structures, hedge fund managers, and other alternative investment vehicles. In that capacity, I have conducted or supervised examinations of more than forty partnerships and pass-through entities with combined assets exceeding \$15 billion.

3\. I hold a Bachelor of Science degree in Accounting from Millbrook University and a Master of Science degree in Taxation from Fordham University Graduate School of Business. I am a Certified Public Accountant licensed in the State of New York. I am the examining agent assigned to the examination of Hargrove Capital Partners LLC (\"HCP\"), Employer Identification Number 82-4539176, for the federal income tax years ending December 31, 2018, December 31, 2019, and December 31, 2020 (respectively, \"TY 2018,\" \"TY 2019,\" and \"TY 2020\").

4\. The facts set forth in this declaration are based on my personal knowledge acquired through my examination of HCP and its affiliated funds, my review of HCP\'s books and records, the partnership tax returns (Forms 1065 and associated Schedules K-1) filed by HCP for the tax years at issue, fund-level financial documents and capital account records, and correspondence exchanged with HCP\'s representatives during the examination and administrative proceedings. In addition, this declaration is based on my review of the documents attached hereto as Exhibits 1 through 14, or referenced herein and incorporated by reference.

5\. I have reviewed each of the exhibits referenced in this declaration and can attest to their origin, authenticity, and relevance to the matters described herein. The documents attached as exhibits were either maintained in the ordinary course of the IRS\'s examination files, obtained from HCP or its representatives during the examination through formal Information Document Requests, or produced by HCP during the discovery phase of this litigation pursuant to the Court\'s scheduling order.

6\. If called as a witness, I am competent to testify to the matters set forth in this declaration. My testimony would be consistent with the statements made herein, and I would be able to explain the basis for each factual assertion by reference to the underlying documents and records that I reviewed during the course of the examination.

7\. This declaration is submitted in support of the Motion for Summary Judgment filed by the United States of America (\"the Government\") in the above-captioned action. The purpose of this declaration is to set forth the undisputed material facts supporting the Government\'s motion and to identify and authenticate the documentary evidence upon which the Government relies.

8\. Specifically, this declaration addresses: (a) the organizational structure of HCP and the affiliated Hargrove Capital Funds; (b) the management fee waiver elections implemented by HCP and their mechanics; (c) the tax reporting of income arising from or in connection with the management fee waiver program; (d) the IRS examination and administrative proceedings relating to HCP\'s tax years 2018, 2019, and 2020; and (e) the documents and records supporting the Government\'s position that the management fee waivers constituted disguised payments for services under Internal Revenue Code § 707(a)(2)(A) and should be recharacterized as ordinary income.

**[II. ORGANIZATIONAL STRUCTURE OF HCP AND THE HARGROVE CAPITAL FUNDS]{.underline}**

9\. Hargrove Capital Partners LLC is a Delaware limited liability company formed on March 12, 2014, pursuant to a Certificate of Formation filed with the Delaware Secretary of State. HCP\'s principal office is located at 600 Lexington Avenue, 31st Floor, New York, New York 10022. HCP has elected to be, and is, treated as a partnership for federal income tax purposes. At all times relevant to this declaration, HCP has not elected to be treated as a corporation under Treasury Regulation § 301.7701-3.

10\. HCP serves as the management company for a family of private equity funds known collectively as the Hargrove Capital Funds. In its capacity as management company, HCP provides investment advisory, portfolio management, and administrative services to the Hargrove Capital Funds in exchange for management fees, as further described below. The managing partners of HCP are Elliot R. Hargrove and Diane K. Sato. Mr. Hargrove holds a 42% profits interest in HCP, and Ms. Sato holds a 38% profits interest. The remaining 20% profits interest is held collectively by four junior partners, whose individual allocations are reflected in the partnership\'s operating agreement and Schedules K-1.

11\. Diane K. Sato has served as the Tax Matters Partner of HCP since the entity\'s formation in 2014. In that capacity, Ms. Sato has been the primary point of contact between HCP and the IRS for purposes of partnership-level proceedings, and she has authorized the engagement of outside counsel and tax advisors to represent HCP in examination and litigation matters.

12\. Exhibit 7, attached hereto and described more fully below, is a true and correct copy of pages 1 and 5 of HCP\'s Form 1065, U.S. Return of Partnership Income, for TY 2018. The Form 1065 reflects HCP\'s entity information, including its name, address, Employer Identification Number, and the tax year ending December 31, 2018. The return was filed on September 15, 2019, pursuant to an extension of time to file. The Form 1065 also includes the designation of a Partnership Representative, as required under the Bipartisan Budget Act of 2015 for tax years beginning after December 31, 2017.

13\. During the tax years at issue, HCP served as the management company for three private equity funds within the Hargrove Capital Fund family. The first of these is Hargrove Capital Fund III, LP (\"Fund III\"), a Delaware limited partnership formed on June 1, 2015, pursuant to a Certificate of Limited Partnership filed with the Delaware Secretary of State. Fund III\'s general partner is Hargrove GP III LLC, a Delaware limited liability company wholly owned by HCP. Fund III raised committed capital of approximately \$820 million from institutional and accredited individual investors. The investment period for Fund III commenced on June 1, 2015, and ended on June 1, 2019. By the close of the examination period, Fund III had substantially completed its investment cycle and had realized net gains of approximately \$298 million on its \$820 million of committed capital. Fund III\'s vintage was characterized by industry participants as \"difficult,\" reflecting challenging market conditions during its deployment years and underperformance relative to its target returns.

14\. The second fund is Hargrove Capital Fund IV, LP (\"Fund IV\"), a Delaware limited partnership formed on September 15, 2017, pursuant to a Certificate of Limited Partnership filed with the Delaware Secretary of State. Fund IV\'s general partner is Hargrove GP IV LLC, a Delaware limited liability company wholly owned by HCP. Fund IV raised committed capital of approximately \$1.35 billion from institutional and accredited individual investors. The investment period for Fund IV commenced on September 15, 2017, and ended on September 15, 2021. As of TY 2020, Fund IV had realized net gains of approximately \$742 million on its \$1.35 billion of committed capital; however, the fund\'s portfolio was still partially unrealized at the time of the examination, with several portfolio companies remaining in the fund\'s portfolio and subject to future disposition.

15\. The third fund is Hargrove Capital Fund V, LP (\"Fund V\"), a Delaware limited partnership formed on February 1, 2020, pursuant to a Certificate of Limited Partnership filed with the Delaware Secretary of State. Fund V\'s general partner is Hargrove GP V LLC, a Delaware limited liability company wholly owned by HCP. Fund V raised committed capital of approximately \$1.75 billion. The investment period for Fund V was still active at the time of the examination and remained active through the date of this declaration. Fund V\'s formation and initial capital deployment occurred during calendar year 2020, and its performance during TY 2020 is discussed in Section IV below.

16\. Exhibit 1, attached hereto, consists of certified copies of the Delaware Certificates of Limited Partnership for Hargrove Capital Fund III, LP; Hargrove Capital Fund IV, LP; and Hargrove Capital Fund V, LP. Exhibit 2, attached hereto, consists of excerpts from the Limited Partnership Agreements (\"LPAs\") of Funds III, IV, and V, including the provisions governing management fees and priority allocations. Exhibit 3, attached hereto, is an organizational chart depicting the relationships among HCP, the general partner entities (Hargrove GP III LLC, Hargrove GP IV LLC, and Hargrove GP V LLC), and the Hargrove Capital Funds.

17\. Under each fund\'s Limited Partnership Agreement, HCP is engaged to provide investment advisory, portfolio management, and administrative services to the respective fund. These services include, without limitation, sourcing and evaluating potential investments, negotiating and structuring acquisitions and dispositions, monitoring portfolio company performance, arranging financing and capital calls, preparing and distributing investor communications and capital account statements, and coordinating the fund\'s annual audit and tax reporting. The scope of HCP\'s management services is substantially identical across all three funds, as reflected in the relevant LPA provisions included in Exhibit 2.

18\. In exchange for the management services described above, HCP receives an annual management fee from each fund. The management fee is calculated as a percentage of the fund\'s committed capital during the investment period and as a percentage of the fund\'s invested capital (i.e., the cost basis of unrealized investments) after the expiration of the investment period. For each of Funds III, IV, and V, the standard management fee rate is 2.0% per annum during the investment period and 1.5% per annum thereafter. These rates are consistent with customary market terms for private equity funds of comparable size and strategy during the relevant time period.

19\. The management fees payable to HCP constitute compensation for services rendered and are treated by HCP and the funds as ordinary course payments. Absent the fee waiver elections described in Section III below, these fees would be recognized by HCP as ordinary income and reported on its Form 1065 as gross receipts from services.

20\. At no time during the tax years at issue did HCP provide services to any entity other than the Hargrove Capital Funds and their affiliated general partner entities. HCP\'s sole source of revenue was the management fees (and, following implementation of the waiver program, priority profit allocations) received from the Hargrove Capital Funds.

**[III. THE MANAGEMENT FEE WAIVER PROGRAM]{.underline}**

21\. Beginning in late 2016, HCP implemented a management fee waiver program (the \"Waiver Program\") pursuant to which HCP\'s managing partners could elect, prior to the start of each fiscal year, to waive a specified dollar amount of the management fees otherwise payable to HCP by one or more of the affiliated Hargrove Capital Funds. The Waiver Program was designed and structured with the assistance of Ridgeline Advisors LLP, HCP\'s outside tax advisor, and was authorized by amendments to the LPAs of the participating funds.

22\. The mechanics of the Waiver Program operated as follows. For each dollar of management fees that HCP elected to waive with respect to a particular fund, HCP was entitled to receive a corresponding \"priority profit allocation\" from that fund. The priority profit allocation was equal in dollar amount to the management fees waived, but was payable exclusively from the fund\'s realized long-term capital gains. That is, the priority allocation could only be satisfied if, and to the extent that, the relevant fund generated realized long-term capital gains during the fiscal year for which the waiver was in effect.

23\. If a fund\'s realized long-term capital gains during a particular fiscal year were insufficient to satisfy the full amount of the priority profit allocation, the unfulfilled portion would carry forward to subsequent fiscal years and would be satisfied from realized long-term capital gains of the fund in those subsequent years. This carry-forward mechanism continued \"until fully allocated,\" meaning that the obligation to satisfy the priority allocation persisted across multiple fiscal years until the total waived amount had been fully allocated from realized gains. I characterize this feature as a \"make-whole\" or \"carry-forward\" provision, because it effectively ensured that HCP would eventually receive the economic equivalent of the waived management fees, albeit from a different source (capital gains rather than fee income) and potentially on a delayed basis.

24\. Exhibit 5, attached hereto, consists of the template Management Fee Waiver Election Form utilized by HCP in connection with the Waiver Program, along with the individual executed election forms for each fund and tax year at issue (designated as Exhibits 5-A through 5-F). Exhibit 6, attached hereto, consists of the amendments to the Limited Partnership Agreements of Funds III, IV, and V authorizing the priority profit allocations in connection with the Waiver Program. The LPA amendments were executed contemporaneously with the first waiver elections applicable to each fund and provide for the priority allocation mechanism described above.

25\. For TY 2018, HCP executed two management fee waiver elections. The first election pertained to Hargrove Capital Fund III, LP and provided for the waiver of \$7,200,000 in management fees otherwise payable by Fund III to HCP during the fiscal year ending December 31, 2018. This election was executed by Elliot R. Hargrove on behalf of HCP on December 15, 2017. A true and correct copy of this executed election form is attached hereto as Exhibit 5-A.

26\. The second TY 2018 election pertained to Hargrove Capital Fund IV, LP and provided for the waiver of \$5,200,000 in management fees otherwise payable by Fund IV to HCP during the fiscal year ending December 31, 2018. This election was executed by Elliot R. Hargrove on behalf of HCP on December 18, 2017. A true and correct copy of this executed election form is attached hereto as Exhibit 5-B.

27\. Both TY 2018 waiver elections were executed prior to the commencement of the fiscal year for which the waivers were to apply (i.e., prior to January 1, 2018). The total management fees waived for TY 2018 was \$12,400,000 (\$7,200,000 from Fund III and \$5,200,000 from Fund IV).

28\. I confirmed through my review of HCP\'s books and records, as well as the fund-level accounting records, that the waived management fees for TY 2018 were not invoiced by HCP to the respective funds, and that the corresponding priority profit allocations of \$12,400,000 were reflected on the funds\' capital account statements and allocation schedules for TY 2018.

29\. For TY 2019, HCP executed two management fee waiver elections. The first election pertained to Hargrove Capital Fund III, LP and provided for the waiver of \$4,650,000 in management fees otherwise payable by Fund III to HCP during the fiscal year ending December 31, 2019. This election was executed by Elliot R. Hargrove on behalf of HCP on November 28, 2018. A true and correct copy of this executed election form is attached hereto as Exhibit 5-C.

30\. The second TY 2019 election pertained to Hargrove Capital Fund IV, LP and provided for the waiver of \$14,200,000 in management fees otherwise payable by Fund IV to HCP during the fiscal year ending December 31, 2019. This election was also executed by Elliot R. Hargrove on behalf of HCP on November 28, 2018. A true and correct copy of this executed election form is attached hereto as Exhibit 5-D.

31\. Both TY 2019 waiver elections were executed prior to the commencement of the fiscal year for which the waivers were to apply (i.e., prior to January 1, 2019). The total management fees waived for TY 2019 was \$18,850,000 (\$4,650,000 from Fund III and \$14,200,000 from Fund IV).

32\. For TY 2020, HCP executed two management fee waiver elections. The first election pertained to Hargrove Capital Fund IV, LP and provided for the waiver of \$10,362,000 in management fees otherwise payable by Fund IV to HCP during the fiscal year ending December 31, 2020. A true and correct copy of this executed election form is attached hereto as Exhibit 5-E.

33\. The second TY 2020 election pertained to Hargrove Capital Fund V, LP and provided for the waiver of \$6,000,000 in management fees otherwise payable by Fund V to HCP during the fiscal year ending December 31, 2020. This election was executed by Elliot R. Hargrove on behalf of HCP on January 28, 2020. A true and correct copy of this executed election form is attached hereto as Exhibit 5-F.

34\. With respect to the Fund V election for TY 2020 (Exhibit 5-F), I note that this election was executed on January 28, 2020, which was twenty-eight days after the commencement of the fiscal year for which the waiver was to apply (January 1, 2020). This stands in contrast to the TY 2018 and TY 2019 elections, all of which were executed prior to the start of the respective fiscal years.

35\. The total management fees waived for TY 2020 was \$16,362,000 (\$10,362,000 from Fund IV and \$6,000,000 from Fund V). The details of each TY 2020 election, including the dates of execution, are set forth in the election forms themselves, copies of which are attached as Exhibits 5-E and 5-F respectively.

36\. The Fund V waiver election for TY 2020 was executed after the commencement of the taxable year for which the waiver was to apply, raising questions about whether the election was prospective in nature. A prospective election made before the start of the relevant taxable year may be treated differently from a retroactive election made after the year has already begun, because the retroactive nature of such an election may suggest that the election was made with the benefit of hindsight regarding the fund\'s anticipated investment activity and income.

37\. In total, across all three tax years at issue, HCP elected to waive an aggregate of \$47,612,000 in management fees through the Waiver Program. This aggregate figure is derived from the following annual totals: \$12,400,000 for TY 2018; \$18,850,000 for TY 2019; and \$16,362,000 for TY 2020. The sum of these three annual totals is \$47,612,000.

38\. The effect of the Waiver Program was to convert \$47,612,000 that would otherwise have been reported by HCP as ordinary management fee income into long-term capital gain income, which was allocable to HCP\'s partners in proportion to their respective profits interests. Based on the profits interests of HCP\'s partners, the allocations were as follows: Elliot R. Hargrove received \$19,997,040 in priority profit allocations (reflecting his 42% profits interest); Diane K. Sato received \$18,092,560 (reflecting her 38% profits interest); and the remaining junior partners received \$9,522,400 in the aggregate (reflecting the remaining 20% profits interest). These amounts were reported on the respective partners\' Schedules K-1 as long-term capital gain, as further discussed in Section V below.

**[IV. FUND V DEPLOYMENT AND PERFORMANCE DATA]{.underline}**

39\. As part of the examination, I obtained and reviewed the capital account statements and investment activity reports for Hargrove Capital Fund V, LP for TY 2020. These documents are maintained in the ordinary course of business by Fund V\'s administrator and were produced by HCP in response to Information Document Request No. 7, issued on October 14, 2021. A true and correct copy of the Fund V Capital Account Statements and Investment Activity Reports for TY 2020 is attached hereto as Exhibit 4.

40\. My review of Exhibit 4 revealed the following information regarding Fund V\'s investment activity and performance during TY 2020. Fund V had total capital commitments of \$1,750,000,000 from its limited partners. As of December 31, 2020, Fund V had called and deployed capital of approximately \$380,000,000, representing approximately 21.7% of total commitments. The remaining unfunded commitments as of that date were approximately \$1,370,000,000. Fund V had not realized any capital gains, whether short-term or long-term, during TY 2020. Fund V had likewise not realized any capital losses during TY 2020. The fund\'s portfolio as of December 31, 2020, consisted entirely of unrealized positions in portfolio companies acquired during the fund\'s initial deployment period. Fund V\'s portfolio showed unrealized appreciation of approximately \$41,000,000 as of December 31, 2020, based on the fund administrator\'s fair market value estimates. However, this unrealized appreciation was subsequently marked down in Q2 2021 following portfolio company revaluations that reflected revised financial projections and market conditions.

41\. The fact that Fund V had zero realized gains during TY 2020 is significant to the matters at issue in this case. Because the priority profit allocation mechanism under the Waiver Program required that the allocation be satisfied from realized long-term capital gains, and because Fund V generated no such gains during TY 2020, the \$6,000,000 priority allocation that HCP claimed from Fund V for TY 2020 could not have been satisfied from realized gains. According to the fund\'s records, this allocation was carried forward under the make-whole provision of the LPA amendment to subsequent fiscal years, pending the realization of long-term capital gains by Fund V. The capital account statements in Exhibit 4 reflect this carry-forward.

42\. By contrast, Fund III\'s priority allocations to HCP during the tax years at issue were funded from actual realized long-term capital gains of the fund. Fund III realized net gains of approximately \$298 million on its \$820 million of committed capital. Although this represented underperformance relative to the fund\'s target returns, it generated sufficient realized long-term capital gains to satisfy the priority profit allocations designated for HCP in TY 2018 (\$7,200,000) and TY 2019 (\$4,650,000). My review of Fund III\'s capital account statements and allocation schedules confirmed that the priority allocations in both years were allocated from realized long-term capital gains.

43\. Similarly, Fund IV\'s priority allocations to HCP were funded from actual realized long-term capital gains. Fund IV realized net gains of approximately \$742 million on its \$1.35 billion of committed capital during its operational period through the date of the examination. While Fund IV\'s portfolio was still partially unrealized at the time of the examination, the fund had generated realized long-term capital gains well in excess of the total priority allocations designated for HCP across TY 2018 (\$5,200,000), TY 2019 (\$14,200,000), and TY 2020 (\$10,362,000). My review of Fund IV\'s capital account statements and allocation schedules confirmed that these priority allocations were each satisfied from realized long-term capital gains.

44\. In summary, the priority allocations from Fund III and Fund IV were satisfied from realized long-term capital gains of the respective funds, whereas the Fund V allocation for TY 2020 remained unsatisfied and carried forward due to the absence of any realized gains in Fund V during that year.

**[V. TAX REPORTING]{.underline}**

45\. As part of the examination, I reviewed the federal income tax returns (Forms 1065, U.S. Return of Partnership Income) filed by HCP for TY 2018, TY 2019, and TY 2020, as well as the associated Schedules K-1 issued to HCP\'s partners for each of those tax years. I also reviewed the individual income tax returns (Forms 1040) of the managing partners, Elliot R. Hargrove and Diane K. Sato, for the corresponding tax years.

46\. HCP\'s Form 1065 for TY 2018 was filed on September 15, 2019, pursuant to an extension of time to file. The return reported \$12,400,000 in long-term capital gains attributable to the priority profit allocations received from Fund III (\$7,200,000) and Fund IV (\$5,200,000) under the Waiver Program. The return reported \$0 in management fee income with respect to the waived amounts. The management fee income reported on the TY 2018 return reflected only fees that were not subject to waiver elections.

47\. Exhibit 7, attached hereto, is a true and correct copy of pages from HCP\'s Form 1065 for TY 2018, including the signature page and the Partnership Representative designation. Page 1 of the return reflects HCP\'s entity name, Employer Identification Number (82-4539176), principal business address (600 Lexington Avenue, 31st Floor, New York, NY 10022), and the tax year ending December 31, 2018. Page 5 of the return includes the Partnership Representative designation section, which identifies the individual designated by HCP to serve as Partnership Representative for purposes of the centralized partnership audit regime enacted by the Bipartisan Budget Act of 2015.

48\. HCP\'s Form 1065 for TY 2019 was filed on extension and reported \$18,850,000 in long-term capital gains attributable to the priority profit allocations received from Fund III (\$4,650,000) and Fund IV (\$14,200,000) under the Waiver Program. HCP\'s Form 1065 for TY 2020 was also filed on extension and reported \$16,362,000 in long-term capital gains attributable to the priority profit allocations receiv
