The TY 2020 return reported the \$6,000,000 priority allocation from Fund V as long-term capital gain notwithstanding that, as set forth in Section IV above, Fund V had not realized any capital gains during TY 2020.

49\. The Schedules K-1 (Partner\'s Share of Income, Deductions, Credits, etc.) issued by HCP to its partners for TY 2018, TY 2019, and TY 2020 reflected the long-term capital gain character of the priority profit allocations. Each partner\'s Schedule K-1 allocated the partner\'s distributive share of the priority profit allocations in accordance with the partner\'s profits interest in HCP.

50\. The allocations reflected on the Schedules K-1 were consistent with the profits interests described in paragraph 10 above. Specifically, for the aggregate priority profit allocations of \$47,612,000 across the three tax years, the Schedules K-1 reflected allocations of \$19,997,040 to Elliot R. Hargrove (42%), \$18,092,560 to Diane K. Sato (38%), and \$9,522,400 in the aggregate to the remaining junior partners (20%). These figures are consistent with the year-by-year allocations reflected in the individual Schedules K-1 for each partner.

51\. Exhibit 8, attached hereto, consists of sample Schedules K-1 for TY 2018, TY 2019, and TY 2020 issued to Elliot R. Hargrove and Diane K. Sato. I have reviewed these Schedules K-1 and confirmed that the amounts reported thereon are consistent with the priority profit allocations described in Section III and the profits interest percentages described in paragraph 10.

52\. I also reviewed the individual income tax returns (Forms 1040) of Elliot R. Hargrove and Diane K. Sato for TY 2018, TY 2019, and TY 2020. My review confirmed that both Mr. Hargrove and Ms. Sato reported the K-1 amounts attributable to the priority profit allocations on their respective individual returns, treating the income as long-term capital gains. The long-term capital gain amounts were reported on Schedule D (Capital Gains and Losses) and Form 8949 (Sales and Other Dispositions of Capital Assets) of each partner\'s individual return.

53\. The long-term capital gain treatment reported on the individual returns resulted in the priority profit allocation income being taxed at the preferential long-term capital gain rate of 20% (plus the 3.8% net investment income tax under IRC § 1411, where applicable), rather than at the ordinary income tax rates that would have applied had the income been reported as management fee income. The reporting of this income as long-term capital gains rather than ordinary income is the central issue in this case.

54\. I note that HCP\'s reporting of the priority profit allocations as long-term capital gains was consistent across all three tax years and across all partners. At no point during the tax years at issue did HCP report any portion of the waived management fees as ordinary income, nor did any partner of HCP report the K-1 amounts attributable to the priority allocations as ordinary income on his or her individual return.

**[VI. IRS EXAMINATION AND ADMINISTRATIVE HISTORY]{.underline}**

55\. In March 2021, the IRS Large Business & International Division opened an examination of HCP\'s Form 1065 for TY 2018. I was assigned as the examining agent for this case on March 15, 2021. The examination was initiated based on a referral from LB&I\'s compliance campaign focused on management fee waiver arrangements employed by private equity fund managers, which had been identified as a compliance priority.

56\. During the initial phase of the examination, I issued a series of Information Document Requests (\"IDRs\") to HCP and its representatives seeking, among other things, copies of HCP\'s partnership agreements, the management fee waiver election forms, the LPA amendments authorizing the priority profit allocations, the capital account statements and allocation schedules for each fund, internal communications regarding the Waiver Program, and the tax opinion letter obtained from Ridgeline Advisors LLP. HCP, through its counsel at Thornfield & Locke LLP, responded to these IDRs and produced the requested documents over the course of several months.

57\. In August 2021, following my review of HCP\'s TY 2019 and TY 2020 Forms 1065 and the documents produced in response to the initial IDRs, I recommended that the examination be expanded to include TY 2019 and TY 2020. This recommendation was approved by my group manager, and HCP was notified of the expansion of the examination by letter dated August 23, 2021. The expansion was based on my identification of the same fee waiver pattern in TY 2019 and TY 2020 as in TY 2018, indicating that the Waiver Program was a recurring practice rather than a single-year transaction.

58\. Throughout the examination, I communicated with HCP\'s representatives, including attorneys at Thornfield & Locke LLP and tax professionals at Ridgeline Advisors LLP. The correspondence included written exchanges regarding the legal characterization of the priority profit allocations, the application of IRC § 707(a)(2)(A) and the Treasury Regulations thereunder, and the relevance of various judicial decisions, including the Tax Court\'s decision in *Pinnacle Partners v. Commissioner*, T.C. Memo 2019-88.

59\. All examination correspondence and formal notices were directed to HCP and its authorized representatives. In accordance with the examination procedures, all notices, including the Notice of Final Partnership Administrative Adjustment described below, were served upon Ms. Sato in her capacity as Tax Matters Partner of HCP. HCP\'s responses to such notices were submitted through Thornfield & Locke LLP, which had been designated as HCP\'s authorized representative pursuant to a Power of Attorney (Form 2848) filed with the IRS.

60\. On February 7, 2022, the IRS issued a 30-day letter to HCP proposing adjustments to HCP\'s partnership returns for TY 2018, TY 2019, and TY 2020. The proposed adjustments recharacterized the priority profit allocations from long-term capital gains to ordinary income (management fees) in the amounts of \$12,400,000 for TY 2018, \$18,850,000 for TY 2019, and \$16,362,000 for TY 2020. HCP timely submitted a written protest to the 30-day letter on March 9, 2022, and the case was referred to the IRS Office of Appeals. The matter was not resolved during the Appeals process. In its protest letter, HCP cited the Ridgeline Advisors opinion letter (Exhibit 9) as support for the taxpayer\'s position and argued that the priority allocations were genuine allocations of partnership income subject to entrepreneurial risk.

61\. On June 15, 2022, the IRS issued a Notice of Final Partnership Administrative Adjustment (\"FPAA\") for TY 2018, TY 2019, and TY 2020. The FPAA recharacterized all \$47,612,000 in priority profit allocations reported by HCP as long-term capital gains, treating such amounts instead as ordinary income constituting management fees for services rendered by HCP to the affiliated Hargrove Capital Funds. The recharacterization was based on the IRS\'s determination that the fee waiver arrangement constituted a disguised payment for services under IRC § 707(a)(2)(A) and that the arrangement lacked economic substance.

62\. The FPAA also asserted a 20% accuracy-related penalty under IRC § 6662 with respect to the proposed adjustments for each of the three tax years. The penalty was asserted on the basis that HCP\'s reporting of the priority profit allocations as long-term capital gains constituted a substantial understatement of income tax and/or negligence or disregard of rules or regulations.

63\. On September 8, 2022, HCP filed a petition in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York challenging the FPAA. The case was assigned Case No. 1:22-cv-07841-LTS and was assigned to the Honorable Laura T. Sievert. This action remains pending.

**[VII. RIDGELINE ADVISORS OPINION LETTER]{.underline}**

64\. During the examination, HCP produced a tax opinion letter prepared by Ridgeline Advisors LLP, HCP\'s outside tax advisor. The opinion letter is dated November 1, 2017, and was prepared by Nathan S. Moreau, CPA, the lead engagement partner at Ridgeline Advisors responsible for HCP\'s tax advisory and compliance work. The opinion letter is addressed to Elliot R. Hargrove and Diane K. Sato at Hargrove Capital Partners LLC. A true and correct copy of the Ridgeline Advisors opinion letter is attached hereto as Exhibit 9.

65\. The Ridgeline Opinion was obtained by HCP prior to the execution of any management fee waiver elections under the Waiver Program. As noted in paragraphs 25 and 26 above, the earliest waiver elections (for TY 2018) were executed on December 15, 2017 (Fund III) and December 18, 2017 (Fund IV). The Ridgeline Opinion, dated November 1, 2017, preceded these elections by approximately six to seven weeks.

66\. Based on my review of the Ridgeline Opinion, the letter analyzes the federal income tax treatment of the proposed management fee waiver structure and reaches the following principal conclusion: \"Based on our analysis of the applicable provisions of the Internal Revenue Code, Treasury Regulations, and relevant judicial authority, it is our opinion that the management fee waiver structure described herein will more likely than not be sustained on its merits for federal income tax purposes.\" The opinion analyzes the following legal authorities and doctrines: (a) IRC § 707(a)(2)(A) and Treasury Regulation § 1.707-2, which address disguised payments for services; (b) the economic substance doctrine, including its application to partnership allocation arrangements; (c) the entrepreneurial risk inherent in tying the priority allocations to realized long-term capital gains of the funds; and (d) the carry-forward provision, which the opinion characterizes as creating meaningful investment risk because the allocation is contingent upon the fund\'s future performance. The opinion specifically notes that the priority allocations are subject to genuine investment risk because they are payable only from realized gains, and there is no guarantee that any particular fund will generate sufficient realized long-term capital gains to satisfy the priority allocation in any given year or at all.

67\. I make the following factual observations regarding the Ridgeline Opinion. First, the opinion was issued before any management fee waiver elections were executed by HCP, indicating that HCP sought professional tax advice regarding the proposed structure before implementing it.

68\. Second, the Ridgeline Opinion was prepared by the same firm---Ridgeline Advisors LLP---that designed the fee waiver structure and prepared HCP\'s partnership tax returns for the tax years at issue. Nathan S. Moreau, the author of the opinion, was also the engagement partner responsible for the preparation of HCP\'s Forms 1065 and the associated Schedules K-1 for TY 2018, TY 2019, and TY 2020.

69\. Third, the opinion addresses the tax treatment of the priority allocations and concludes that they qualify as distributive shares of partnership income under IRC § 704(b), rather than disguised payments for services under IRC § 707(a)(2)(A). The opinion\'s analysis includes a discussion of the factors set forth in Treasury Regulation § 1.707-2(c) for determining whether a payment constitutes a disguised payment for services, including whether the allocation is subject to significant entrepreneurial risk.

70\. HCP cited the Ridgeline Opinion in its protest letter to IRS Appeals, which was submitted on March 9, 2022, in response to the 30-day letter described in paragraph 60 above. In its protest, HCP argued that its reliance on the Ridgeline Opinion constituted reasonable cause and good faith under IRC § 6664(c)(1), thereby precluding the imposition of the accuracy-related penalty asserted by the IRS under IRC § 6662. I note these facts without expressing any legal opinion as to whether the Ridgeline Opinion in fact establishes reasonable cause for purposes of the penalty defense.

**[VIII. THE \*PINNACLE PARTNERS\* PRECEDENT]{.underline}**

71\. During the course of the examination and the subsequent administrative proceedings, both the IRS and HCP referenced the Tax Court\'s decision in *Pinnacle Partners v. Commissioner*, T.C. Memo 2019-88, as relevant authority bearing on the proper tax treatment of management fee waiver arrangements. The *Pinnacle Partners* case was decided by the United States Tax Court on June 14, 2019.

72\. The *Pinnacle Partners* case involved a private equity fund management company that implemented a management fee waiver arrangement similar in general structure to the Waiver Program employed by HCP. In that case, the fund manager waived a portion of its management fees in exchange for priority profit allocations from the affiliated fund, which were characterized as long-term capital gains on the fund manager\'s tax returns.

73\. Exhibit 12, attached hereto, consists of excerpts from the Tax Court\'s opinion in *Pinnacle Partners v. Commissioner*, T.C. Memo 2019-88. I have reviewed these excerpts and set forth below a summary of the key factual findings and legal conclusions contained therein.

74\. The Tax Court in *Pinnacle Partners* held that the management fee waiver arrangement employed by the taxpayer lacked economic substance and constituted a disguised payment for services under IRC § 707(a)(2)(A). The court determined that the priority profit allocation was not subject to genuine entrepreneurial risk, as required for the allocation to be respected as a distributive share of partnership income under the Treasury Regulations.

75\. In reaching its conclusion, the Tax Court emphasized a specific feature of the Pinnacle Partners arrangement. The court stated: \"Unlike a typical profits interest, the priority allocation at issue here was backed by a deficit restoration obligation under the partnership agreement, which effectively guaranteed that Pinnacle Partners would receive the full amount of the waived fees regardless of the fund\'s investment performance. This deficit restoration obligation eliminated any meaningful downside risk.\" The court found that the deficit restoration obligation was a critical fact supporting its determination that the priority allocation lacked genuine entrepreneurial risk.

76\. The court further stated: \"The court emphasizes that its holding is based on the specific facts before it, including the presence of the deficit restoration obligation and the absence of any meaningful economic risk to the taxpayer.\" This language appears in the concluding section of the opinion and is included in the excerpts attached as Exhibit 12.

77\. The factual findings and legal conclusions of the *Pinnacle Partners* decision, as reflected in the excerpts attached as Exhibit 12, were discussed at length during the IRS examination and in HCP\'s protest letter to IRS Appeals. Both parties cited *Pinnacle Partners* in their correspondence, though with differing interpretations of the case\'s applicability to HCP\'s Waiver Program.

**[IX. ADDITIONAL EXHIBITS AND SUPPORTING DOCUMENTS]{.underline}**

78\. Exhibit 13, attached hereto, consists of excerpts from the subscription credit facility agreements between Hargrove Capital Fund IV, LP, as borrower, and Greystone National Bank, as lender. The subscription credit facility is a revolving credit line secured by the unfunded capital commitments of Fund IV\'s limited partners. The credit facility was originally entered into on December 1, 2017, and was subsequently amended on June 15, 2019, and January 10, 2020.

79\. These documents are relevant to the matters at issue because the credit facility agreements include borrowing base certificates that disclose the existence of the management fee waiver arrangements between HCP and Fund IV. Specifically, the borrowing base certificate dated January 15, 2020, references the fee waiver elections for TY 2019 and TY 2020 and discloses the resulting priority profit allocation obligations of Fund IV to HCP. The disclosure of the fee waiver arrangements in the subscription credit facility documents indicates that the arrangements were integrated into Fund IV\'s broader financial operations and were known to the fund\'s lender.

80\. I obtained Exhibit 13 from documents produced by HCP in response to Information Document Request No. 12, issued on January 19, 2022. The documents were produced by HCP\'s counsel at Thornfield & Locke LLP on February 16, 2022.

81\. Exhibit 10, attached hereto, consists of internal emails between Elliot R. Hargrove and Diane K. Sato regarding the management fee waiver program. These emails were produced by HCP during the discovery phase of this litigation, pursuant to the Court\'s discovery order entered on March 15, 2023. The emails span the period from September 2017 through December 2019 and discuss various aspects of the Waiver Program, including the timing and amounts of proposed waiver elections, the expected tax treatment of the priority profit allocations, and the coordination of the waiver elections with the fund-level financial planning.

82\. My review of the internal emails in Exhibit 10 revealed that the communications between Mr. Hargrove and Ms. Sato discuss the \"tax efficiency\" of the waiver structure, including references to the preferential capital gains rates applicable to long-term capital gains as compared to ordinary income rates. In one email chain dated October 12, 2017, Ms. Sato forwarded to Mr. Hargrove a memorandum from Nathan S. Moreau of Ridgeline Advisors summarizing the anticipated tax benefits of the proposed Waiver Program, and Mr. Hargrove responded with comments regarding the proposed waiver amounts for TY 2018.

83\. Exhibit 11, attached hereto, consists of minutes from HCP\'s annual partner meetings for 2017, 2018, and 2019. The meeting minutes were maintained in the ordinary course of HCP\'s business and were produced during the examination in response to Information Document Request No. 9. The minutes reflect that the Waiver Program was discussed at each of the three annual partner meetings. The 2017 meeting minutes, in particular, reflect a presentation by Nathan S. Moreau of Ridgeline Advisors regarding the \"benefits\" of the fee waiver program and the anticipated tax treatment of the priority profit allocations.

84\. The 2018 and 2019 meeting minutes reflect discussions regarding the performance of the waiver elections, including the amounts waived, the priority allocations received, and the character of income reported on HCP\'s tax returns. These meeting minutes were produced by HCP pursuant to the Court\'s discovery order and are maintained in the IRS\'s examination files for this case.

85\. Exhibit 14, attached hereto, consists of my examination workpapers, which I prepared during the course of the examination of HCP for TY 2018, TY 2019, and TY 2020. The workpapers summarize the management fee waiver amounts, the priority profit allocation calculations, and the character of income reported by HCP on its partnership returns for each of the three tax years at issue.

86\. The figures reflected in my examination workpapers are consistent with the amounts set forth throughout this declaration: \$12,400,000 in waived management fees (and corresponding priority profit allocations) for TY 2018; \$18,850,000 for TY 2019; \$16,362,000 for TY 2020; and an aggregate of \$47,612,000 across all three tax years. The workpapers also reflect the allocation of these amounts to HCP\'s individual partners in accordance with their respective profits interests, as described in paragraph 38 above.

87\. I attest that the documents referenced and attached hereto as Exhibits 1 through 14 are true and correct copies of documents maintained in the IRS\'s examination files for Hargrove Capital Partners LLC, Case No. 1:22-cv-07841-LTS, or of documents produced by HCP or its representatives during the examination and the subsequent discovery phase of this litigation.

88\. I have personal knowledge of the origin, custody, and authenticity of each document. Each exhibit was obtained through the formal examination or discovery processes described in this declaration, and I have maintained custody of each document (or a true and correct copy thereof) since its receipt.

UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT SOUTHERN DISTRICT OF NEW YORK

**UNITED STATES OF AMERICA,**

Plaintiff,

v\.

**HARGROVE CAPITAL PARTNERS LLC,**

Defendant.

Case No. 1:22-cv-07841-LTS

Hon. Laura Taylor Swain

**DECLARATION OF PROFESSOR LEAH ASHFORD IN SUPPORT OF PLAINTIFF\'S MOTION FOR SUMMARY JUDGMENT**

Filed: April 3, 2024

I, Leah Ashford, hereby declare as follows pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1746:

**[I. Qualifications and Background]{.underline}**

**A. Identity and Academic Position**

1\. My name is Leah Ashford. I am a tenured professor of tax law at Whitman University School of Law in Whitman, Connecticut, a position I have held for approximately eighteen years. I joined the Whitman faculty in 2006 after practicing tax law for seven years at a major national law firm, where I focused on partnership taxation and fund formation.

2\. My areas of academic specialization include partnership taxation, pass-through entity taxation, and tax policy relating to investment fund structures, with particular emphasis on the taxation of private equity and hedge fund managers, carried interest arrangements, management fee structures, and the application of the economic substance doctrine to investment fund transactions.

3\. I have published extensively in legal and tax academic journals on topics directly relevant to the matters at issue in this case. My principal publications include:

> \(a\) \"The Taxation of Profits Interests After *Diamond*: A Reassessment,\" 72 Whitman Law Review 1403 (2010);
>
> \(b\) \"Fee Waiver Structures in Private Equity: Substance Over Form,\" 46 Tax Law Review 289 (2014);
>
> \(c\) \"Disguised Payments for Services and the Limits of Partnership Allocations,\" 68 National Tax Journal 721 (2015);
>
> \(d\) \"Carried Interest, Management Fees, and the Character of Fund Manager Compensation,\" 91 Southern California Law Review 855 (2018); and
>
> \(e\) \"The Economic Substance Doctrine in the Investment Management Context: A Framework for Analysis,\" 127 Yale Law Journal Forum 45 (2021).

4\. In addition to my academic publications, I have presented at numerous tax law conferences, including the American Bar Association Tax Section Annual Meeting, the New York University Tax Institute, and the Tax Policy Center\'s Annual Conference on Pass-Through Entity Taxation. I hold a J.D. from Columbia Law School, where I graduated *magna cum laude* and served as an editor of the Columbia Law Review, and an LL.M. in Taxation from New York University School of Law.

**B. Prior Expert Engagements**

5\. I have been retained as an expert witness in seven prior federal tax cases. Four of those engagements involved proceedings before the United States Tax Court, and three involved proceedings before United States District Courts. I have been qualified as an expert witness under Federal Rule of Evidence 702 in all seven of those cases. My prior engagements have included matters involving partnership taxation, disguised payment recharacterization, and the application of anti-abuse doctrines to investment fund structures.

6\. I have testified on behalf of both the government and taxpayers. My prior engagements include, among others: *Ridgemont Holdings LLC v. Commissioner*, T.C. Dkt. No. 15782-18 (retained by taxpayer; testified at trial regarding characterization of management company allocations); *United States v. Clearwater Fund Advisors LP*, No. 1:19-cv-03221 (S.D.N.Y.) (retained by the government; submitted expert declaration regarding fee waiver arrangements); and *Stonebridge Capital Partners v. Commissioner*, T.C. Dkt. No. 22915-20 (retained by taxpayer; testified at trial regarding the economic substance of partnership profit-sharing arrangements). In each instance, I offered opinions based on my independent analysis of the facts and applicable legal authorities.

**C. Retention and Compensation**

7\. I have been retained in this matter by the Tax Division of the United States Department of Justice through Senior Litigation Counsel Marcus D. Felton. I am being compensated at a rate of \$750 per hour for my work in connection with this engagement. My total fees to date are approximately \$67,500, reflecting approximately ninety hours of work reviewing materials, conducting research, and preparing this declaration. My compensation is not contingent on the outcome of this case, the content of my testimony, or the substance of the opinions expressed herein.

**D. Materials Reviewed**

8\. In forming the opinions set forth in this declaration, I have reviewed the following materials:

> \(a\) The partnership agreements governing Hargrove Capital Partners LLC, including the operating agreements for Funds III, IV, and V, together with all amendments thereto through the date of this declaration;
>
> \(b\) The management fee waiver election forms executed by the managing partners of Hargrove Capital Partners LLC for Tax Years 2018, 2019, and 2020, including the form of the annual election letter and the carry-forward provisions contained therein;
>
> \(c\) Hargrove Capital Partners LLC\'s Forms 1065, U.S. Return of Partnership Income, for Tax Years 2018, 2019, and 2020, together with all Schedules K-1 issued to the partners of HCP for those tax years;
>
> \(d\) The limited partnership agreements for Hargrove Capital Fund III, LP (formed June 1, 2015, with \$820 million in committed capital from limited partners), Hargrove Capital Fund IV, LP (formed September 15, 2017, with \$1.35 billion in committed capital from limited partners), and Hargrove Capital Fund V, LP (formed February 1, 2020, with \$1.75 billion in committed capital from limited partners);
>
> \(e\) The Declaration of Special Agent Teresa Quillen, sworn on February 15, 2024, together with all exhibits attached thereto;
>
> \(f\) The opinion letter prepared by Nathan S. Moreau, CPA, of Ridgeline Advisors LLP, dated November 1, 2017, addressed to Hargrove Capital Partners LLC, concerning the tax treatment of the management fee waiver program;
>
> \(g\) Subscription credit facility documents between Hargrove Capital Fund IV, LP and Greystone National Bank, including the credit agreement dated October 1, 2017, and all amendments thereto;
>
> \(h\) Fund performance data for Hargrove Capital Funds III, IV, and V, including quarterly reports reflecting realized and unrealized gains and losses for each fund through December 31, 2020; and
>
> \(i\) Various legal authorities, including Internal Revenue Code Sections 707(a)(2)(A), 707(c), 702(b), and 704(b); Treasury Regulation Section 1.707-2; Revenue Procedure 93-27; and relevant case law as cited herein.

**E. Summary of Opinions**

9\. Based on my review of the materials described above and my expertise in the areas of partnership taxation and investment fund structures, I have formed four principal opinions, each of which I hold to a reasonable degree of professional certainty:

> \(1\) The management fee waiver structure employed by Hargrove Capital Partners LLC lacks economic substance independent of its tax benefits;
>
> \(2\) The priority profit allocations received by HCP in exchange for waived management fees are, in substance, guaranteed payments for services within the meaning of IRC § 707(c) and should be taxed as ordinary income to HCP and its partners;
>
> \(3\) Revenue Procedure 93-27 does not shelter the fee waiver arrangement from taxation; rather, it supports the conclusion that the profits interests received in exchange for waived fees should be taxed upon receipt; and
>
> \(4\) The fee waiver structure is a paradigmatic example of a disguised payment for services within the meaning of IRC § 707(a)(2)(A), and the priority profit allocations should be recharacterized as ordinary income payments to a non-partner for services rendered.

10\. I elaborate on each of these opinions below, following a description of the relevant background facts.

**[II. Background: The Management Fee Waiver Structure]{.underline}**

**A. Overview of HCP\'s Business and Fund Family**

11\. Hargrove Capital Partners LLC (\"HCP\") is a Delaware limited liability company formed on March 12, 2014. Its Employer Identification Number is 82-4539176, and its principal office is located at 600 Lexington Avenue, 31st Floor, New York, New York 10022. HCP is classified as a partnership for federal income tax purposes and files a Form 1065 annually.

12\. HCP\'s managing partners are Elliot R. Hargrove, who holds a 42% profits interest in HCP, and Diane K. Sato, who holds a 38% profits interest. The remaining 20% profits interest is held by other junior partners and employees of the firm. HCP serves as the management company for the Hargrove Capital Fund family, which during the relevant period consisted of three active private equity funds: Hargrove Capital Fund III, LP (\"Fund III\"), Hargrove Capital Fund IV, LP (\"Fund IV\"), and Hargrove Capital Fund V, LP (\"Fund V\"). The general partners of these funds are, respectively, Hargrove GP III LLC, Hargrove GP IV LLC, and Hargrove GP V LLC, each of which is a separate Delaware limited liability company controlled by Messrs. Hargrove and Sato.

13\. HCP provides investment management services to each of the Hargrove Capital Funds pursuant to management agreements between HCP and the general partner of each fund. Under these management agreements, HCP is entitled to receive an annual management fee, generally calculated as a percentage of each fund\'s committed or invested capital, in exchange for its investment advisory, portfolio management, and administrative services.

**B. Mechanics of the Fee Waiver Program**

14\. Beginning in 2016, HCP implemented a management fee waiver program (the \"Fee Waiver Program\" or the \"Program\"). Under the Program, HCP\'s managing partners could elect, prior to the start of each fiscal year, to waive a portion of the management fees otherwise payable to HCP by the affiliated funds. The election was memorialized in a written fee waiver election form executed by the managing partners and delivered to the general partner of each applicable fund.

15\. In exchange for each dollar of management fees waived by HCP, the applicable fund would grant HCP a \"priority profit allocation\" --- that is, a priority claim on profits of the fund --- equal in dollar amount to the waived management fees. Under the terms of the waiver election forms and the applicable fund partnership agreements, priority profit allocations were payable exclusively from realized long-term capital gains of the fund. The intended and actual effect of this arrangement was to convert what would otherwise have been ordinary management fee income --- taxable at ordinary income tax rates --- into long-term capital gains income, taxable at the preferential capital gains rate.

16\. Critically, the waiver election forms contained a \"carry-forward\" or \"make-whole\" provision. Under this provision, if the applicable fund did not generate sufficient realized long-term capital gains in the year of the waiver to satisfy the full amount of the priority profit allocation, the unfulfilled amount would carry forward to subsequent fiscal years and would be satisfied from realized long-term capital gains generated by the fund in those future years \"until fully allocated.\" The carry-forward provision had no stated expiration date. The practical effect of this mechanism was that HCP\'s entitlement to receive the full economic value of the waived management fees was not extinguished by a shortfall in any given year; rather, the entitlement persisted indefinitely until the fund generated sufficient gains to fulfill the allocation in its entirety.

**C. Waiver Amounts and Tax Years at Issue**

17\. The following table summarizes the management fee waiver amounts for the Tax Years at issue:

  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Tax Year**    **Fund III**       **Fund IV**        **Fund V**        **Total**
  --------------- ------------------ ------------------ ----------------- ------------------
  2018            \$7,200,000        \$5,200,000        ---               \$12,400,000

  2019            \$4,650,000        \$14,200,000       ---               \$18,850,000

  2020            ---                \$10,362,000       \$6,000,000       \$16,362,000

  **Aggregate**   **\$11,850,000**   **\$29,762,000**   **\$6,000,000**   **\$47,612,000**
  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

18\. All \$47,612,000 in priority profit allocations were reported as long-term capital gains on HCP\'s Forms 1065 for Tax Years 2018 through 2020. The character of these allocations flowed through to HCP\'s partners on their respective Schedules K-1. As a result, Elliot R. Hargrove received \$19,997,040 in long-term capital gains attributable to the priority allocations (reflecting his 42% profits interest), and Diane K. Sato received \$18,092,560 (reflecting her 38% profits interest). Had these amounts been properly reported as ordinary income, they would have been subject to federal income tax at the top marginal rate of 37%, rather than the preferential long-term capital gains rate of 20%, producing a rate differential of 17 percentage points. The aggregate federal tax benefit attributable to the mischaracterization was therefore approximately \$8,094,040.

**D. Fund Investment Performance**

19\. The investment performance of each fund is relevant context for evaluating the economic substance of the fee waiver arrangement and the degree of entrepreneurial risk borne by HCP.

20\. Fund III had committed capital of \$820 million. As of the close of its investment period on June 1, 2019, it had generated realized net gains of approximately \$298 million, representing a net multiple of approximately 0.36x on committed capital. Fund III underperformed relative to its vintage year peer group and represented a below-market return for HCP\'s limited partners.

21\. Fund IV had committed capital of \$1.35 billion. As of December 31, 2020, it had generated realized net gains of approximately \$742 million, representing a net multiple of approximately 0.55x on committed capital at that time. Fund IV\'s investment period ended on September 15, 2021, and the fund remained partially unrealized at the close of the period at issue.

22\. Fund V had committed capital of \$1.75 billion. By year-end 2020, it had deployed only approximately \$380 million in capital --- less than 22% of total commitments --- and had generated no realized gains whatsoever. The fund\'s portfolio consisted entirely of unrealized positions, and certain of those positions reflected unrealized appreciation that was subsequently marked down in 2021.

23\. Fund V\'s lack of realized gains as of Tax Year 2020 is particularly significant. Despite the absence of any realized gains, HCP nonetheless received a \$6,000,000 priority profit allocation from Fund V in TY 2020. This allocation could not have been funded by realized capital gains from Fund V because no such gains existed. The allocation was presumably carried forward under the make-whole provision, yet HCP reported it as long-term capital gain on its TY 2020 return.

**[III. Opinion 1: The Fee Waiver Structure Lacks Economic Substance]{.underline}**

**A. Framework --- The Economic Substance Doctrine**

24\. The economic substance doctrine is a longstanding judicial doctrine that provides that a transaction will not be respected for federal income tax purposes unless it has meaningful economic effects apart from the creation of tax benefits. The doctrine reflects the fundamental principle that the tax law looks through formal arrangements to the substance of the underlying economic activity, and that transactions designed solely to generate tax benefits --- without any genuine change in the taxpayer\'s economic position --- will be disregarded.

25\. As codified by Congress in IRC § 7701(o), a transaction is treated as having economic substance only if it meets a conjunctive two-prong test: the transaction must (1) meaningfully change the taxpayer\'s economic position apart from federal income tax effects, and (2) the taxpayer must have a substantial non-tax business purpose for entering into the transaction. The central inquiry is whether the fee waiver arrangement served any legitimate non-tax business purpose or was motivated solely by the desire to convert ordinary income into capital gains.

26\. In the context of investment fund structures, the economic substance doctrine has particular salience. Private equity fund managers occupy a unique position in which they both manage the fund and participate in the fund\'s economics as partners. This dual role creates opportunities for managers to restructure their compensation in ways that alter the tax character of their income without changing the underlying economic substance of the arrangement. Courts have consistently scrutinized such restructuring arrangements under the economic substance doctrine, asking whether the manager\'s business purpose for adopting a particular compensation structure was motivated by genuine business considerations or was instead driven exclusively by tax avoidance.

27\. In applying the economic substance doctrine to HCP\'s fee waiver arrangement, I focus primarily on whether HCP had a substantial non-tax business purpose for implementing and maintaining the Fee Waiver Program. This inquiry requires an examination of whether the waiver arrangement altered the nature, scope, or quality of the services provided by HCP; whether it changed the economic relationship between HCP and its affiliated funds or their limited partners; and whether it served any identifiable business objective other than reducing HCP\'s effective tax rate by converting ordinary income into long-term capital gains.

**B. Application --- No Non-Tax Business Purpose**

28\. In my opinion, the fee waiver arrangement implemented by HCP had no meaningful non-tax business purpose. I base this conclusion on the following observations.

29\. First, HCP\'s management services to the funds did not change in nature, scope, or quality regardless of whether fees were waived or collected directly. The waiver election forms did not condition the waiver on any change in HCP\'s services, any increase in the scope of management activities, or any alteration in the fee structure that would reflect a genuine renegotiation of the management relationship. HCP provided the same portfolio management, deal sourcing, due diligence, monitoring, and administrative services to each fund irrespective of whether the management fee was collected as a fee or waived in exchange for a priority allocation. The managing partners of HCP continued to perform their duties in the same manner and with the same level of effort.

30\. Second, the funds\' limited partners received the same management services regardless of whether HCP elected to waive fees. The waiver did not result in any reduction in management fee burdens borne by the limited partners, any change in fund economics, or any alteration in the carried interest waterfall. The limited partners were economically indifferent to the waiver election because it affected only the tax character of HCP\'s compensation, not its amount or the net returns available to the limited partners.

31\. Third, the only discernible effect of the waiver was to reclassify income from ordinary to capital gain character. The dollar-for-dollar matching between waived fees and priority allocations underscores this conclusion: for every dollar of management fee waived, HCP received a priority allocation of exactly one dollar. There was no premium, no discount, and no adjustment for risk. The one-for-one substitution strongly suggests that the arrangement was designed not to alter the economics of HCP\'s compensation but solely to change its tax label.

32\. Fourth, the carry-forward provision ensured that HCP would eventually receive the full economic value of the waived management fees, regardless of fund performance in any particular year. Any purported \"risk\" that the priority allocations might not be funded was, in practice, a timing issue rather than a genuine risk of economic loss. The carry-forward had no stated expiration and operated to accumulate unfulfilled allocations until the fund generated sufficient gains to satisfy them.

33\. Fifth, while Fund III\'s underperformance --- \$298 million in realized gains on \$820 million in committed capital --- might initially appear to demonstrate meaningful risk, in fact all of HCP\'s priority allocations attributable to Fund III were ultimately satisfied. The aggregate amount waived from Fund III across Tax Years 2018 and 2019 was \$11,850,000, a figure far below Fund III\'s \$298 million in realized gains. The apparent risk was never a real risk.

**C. The Fee Waiver as \"Alchemical\" Income Conversion**

34\. The management fee waiver arrangement employed by HCP is a textbook example of what tax commentators have described as \"tax alchemy\" --- the conversion of income from one character to another without any corresponding change in the underlying economic reality. HCP\'s managing partners performed the same services, in the same capacity, for the same funds, and received the same dollar amounts; only the tax character of their compensation changed from ordinary income to long-term capital gains.

35\. The arrangement is, in its economic effects, functionally indistinguishable from carried interest. In the standard private equity fund structure, the fund manager receives a \"carried interest\" --- a profits interest in the fund that entitles the manager to a share of the fund\'s investment gains. The priority profit allocations received by HCP in exchange for waived management fees are, in economic substance, indistinguishable from carried interest --- they represent a share of fund profits allocated to the manager in connection with the provision of investment management services. The fee waiver arrangement effectively created a second carried interest layer on top of HCP\'s existing promote, funded dollar-for-dollar by the waived management fees. The only distinction between the priority profit allocations and HCP\'s existing carried interest was that the priority allocations were not subject to the same hurdle rate and clawback provisions applicable to the fund\'s general carried interest waterfall, making them, if anything, less entrepreneurial and more fee-like in character.

36\. The distinction between a genuine carried interest and a fee waiver arrangement is critical. A genuine carried interest reflects an allocation of partnership profits that is contingent on the fund\'s success; it is a return to the manager for its role as an equity participant. The priority profit allocations at issue here served a different function: they were a mechanism for delivering management fee compensation through an alternative channel that afforded preferential tax treatment.

**[IV. Opinion 2: The Priority Allocations Are, In Substance, Guaranteed Payments Under IRC § 707(c)]{.underline}**

**A. Legal Framework --- IRC § 707(c)**

37\. Under IRC § 707(c), payments to a partner for services rendered to the partnership that are \"determined without regard to the income of the partnership\" are treated as \"guaranteed payments.\" Guaranteed payments are taxed as ordinary income to the recipient partner, regardless of the character of the underlying partnership income from which they are paid. The purpose of Section 707(c) is to ensure that when a partner receives compensation for services that is economically equivalent to a salary or fee --- that is, when the amount of the payment does not vary meaningfully with the partnership\'s income --- the payment is taxed as ordinary income rather than taking on the c

content.content:
ith the partnership\'s income --- the payment is taxed as ordinary income rather than taking on the character of the partnership\'s income.

38\. The determination of whether a payment to a partner is \"determined without regard to the income of the partnership\" is made based on economic reality, not on the formal labels or structures employed by the parties. As the Tax Court has recognized, the relevant inquiry is whether the partner\'s right to receive the payment is, in practical effect, substantially independent of the partnership\'s actual economic performance. Where a partner\'s compensation is structured to be contingent on partnership income but is, in substance, assured by contractual mechanisms that eliminate the practical risk of non-payment, the payment is properly treated as a guaranteed payment under Section 707(c).

**B. Application --- The Carry-Forward Provision Eliminates Risk**

39\. In my opinion, the priority profit allocations received by HCP in exchange for waived management fees are, in substance, guaranteed payments within the meaning of IRC § 707(c). My conclusion rests primarily on the operation of the carry-forward or \"make-whole\" provision contained in the waiver election forms.

40\. Under the carry-forward provision, if a fund did not generate sufficient realized long-term capital gains in the year of the waiver to satisfy the full amount of HCP\'s priority allocation, the unfulfilled balance would carry forward to subsequent fiscal years and be satisfied from realized long-term capital gains generated by the fund in those future years \"until fully allocated.\" The carry-forward provision had no stated expiration date and no cap on the number of years over which the unfulfilled allocation could be carried forward.

41\. The carry-forward mechanism effectively guarantees that HCP will receive compensation equal to the waived management fees, rendering the allocation a guaranteed payment within the meaning of IRC § 707(c). Although the priority allocations are nominally contingent on the fund\'s generation of realized long-term capital gains, the carry-forward provision strips this contingency of practical significance. The contingency is not a genuine condition that exposes HCP to a meaningful risk of non-payment; it is merely a timing mechanism that defers payment until the fund generates gains, while preserving HCP\'s right to the full amount indefinitely.

42\. I acknowledge that, in a purely formal sense, the priority allocations are tied to the fund\'s realization of long-term capital gains and therefore appear to be \"determined with regard to the income of the partnership.\" However, this formal contingency is illusory in practice for three independent reasons.

43\. First, Fund IV --- which was the primary source of waived fees, accounting for \$29,762,000 of the total \$47,612,000 in waivers --- generated \$742 million in realized gains on \$1.35 billion in committed capital during the relevant period and thereafter. The aggregate priority allocations attributable to Fund IV (\$29,762,000) represented less than 4.1% of Fund IV\'s realized gains. There was no realistic prospect that Fund IV would fail to generate sufficient gains to satisfy HCP\'s priority allocations.

44\. Second, the carry-forward provision means that even if a fund experienced a temporary shortfall in realized gains in any given year, the unfulfilled allocation was not lost. It accumulated and would be satisfied from gains realized in future years. This mechanism transformed what might otherwise be a genuine contingency into a mere timing difference.

45\. Third, Fund III, despite its relative underperformance, generated \$298 million in realized gains --- an amount that far exceeded the \$11,850,000 in aggregate priority allocations attributed to Fund III. Even a fund that underperformed its vintage peer group and delivered below-market returns to its limited partners generated realized gains more than twenty-five times the amount of the waived fees. The suggestion that HCP bore meaningful risk of non-payment is not supported by the actual fund economics.

46\. In light of these facts, I conclude that the priority profit allocations received by HCP were, in substance, determined without regard to the income of the partnership and should be treated as guaranteed payments under IRC § 707(c), taxable as ordinary income to HCP and its partners.

**C. Fund V\'s Priority Allocation as Exemplar**

47\. The \$6,000,000 priority allocation from Fund V in Tax Year 2020 is a particularly compelling illustration of the guaranteed nature of the arrangements. As of December 31, 2020, Fund V had deployed only approximately \$380 million of its \$1.75 billion in committed capital and had generated no realized gains whatsoever. The fund\'s portfolio consisted entirely of unrealized positions, and certain of those positions reflected unrealized appreciation that was subsequently marked down in 2021.

48\. Despite the complete absence of realized gains, HCP reported a \$6,000,000 priority allocation from Fund V as long-term capital gains on its TY 2020 return. This allocation could not have been sourced from realized capital gains because no such gains existed. The allocation was evidently carried forward under the make-whole provision with the expectation that future gains would eventually fund it. This demonstrates that HCP treated the priority allocation as a right to receive a fixed amount of compensation regardless of Fund V\'s actual performance --- the hallmark of a guaranteed payment. HCP\'s expectation that it would eventually receive the full \$6,000,000, regardless of whether Fund V generated realized gains in 2020 or in any particular subsequent year, confirms that the arrangement operated as a compensation mechanism rather than a genuine entrepreneurial allocation.

**[V. Opinion 3: Revenue Procedure 93-27 Does Not Protect the Fee Waiver Arrangement]{.underline}**

**A. Background on Revenue Procedure 93-27**

49\. Revenue Procedure 93-27 addresses the federal income tax treatment of the receipt of a partnership profits interest in exchange for services rendered to or for the benefit of a partnership. The Revenue Procedure was issued in 1993 against the backdrop of considerable uncertainty in the law regarding whether, and to what extent, a service provider must recognize income upon receiving a profits interest in a partnership.

50\. Revenue Procedure 93-27 establishes that profits interests received in exchange for services are taxed at the time of receipt if they have a determinable value. The Revenue Procedure contemplates that where a profits interest can be valued at the time of grant --- as where the interest represents a substantially certain and predictable income stream --- the recipient must recognize ordinary income equal to the fair market value of the interest at the time it is received. In this respect, the Revenue Procedure draws a distinction between profits interests that are genuinely speculative and uncertain in value, on the one hand, and profits interests that have ascertainable and determinable values at the time of grant, on the other.

51\. The Revenue Procedure identifies certain conditions under which a profits interest will be deemed to have a determinable value such that taxation at receipt is appropriate. Among these conditions, the Revenue Procedure specifically identifies profits interests that relate to a \"substantially certain and predictable stream of income from partnership assets.\" Where a profits interest is associated with such a stream of income, the Revenue Procedure contemplates that the interest can be valued at the time of grant and should accordingly be taxed at that time. This condition is directly relevant to HCP\'s priority profit allocations, which --- as I explain below --- represent a substantially certain and predictable income stream funded by the carry-forward provision.

52\. The distinction drawn by Revenue Procedure 93-27 between interests with determinable values and those without is a critical element of the tax framework governing profits interests. The Revenue Procedure does not exempt all profits interests from taxation at receipt; rather, it confines favorable treatment to those interests that are genuinely uncertain in value and that expose the service provider to meaningful entrepreneurial risk. Where the value of a profits interest is determinable --- as where it is contractually linked to a fixed dollar amount of waived management fees and is backstopped by a make-whole provision --- the Revenue Procedure\'s recognition requirement applies.

**B. Application to HCP\'s Fee Waiver Structure**

53\. The priority profit allocations received by HCP in exchange for waived management fees are \"profits interests received in exchange for services\" within the meaning of Revenue Procedure 93-27. HCP received these allocations in direct exchange for the investment management services it provided to the Hargrove Capital Funds. The allocations represented a right to share in future fund profits, allocated in priority to other profit-sharing arrangements, and were granted in lieu of cash management fees.

54\. In my opinion, these priority profit allocations fall squarely within the category of profits interests that Revenue Procedure 93-27 requires to be taxed at the time of receipt. Each priority allocation has a readily ascertainable value equal to the management fee waived, and therefore falls squarely within the ambit of Revenue Procedure 93-27\'s recognition requirement. The dollar-for-dollar correspondence between the waived management fee and the priority allocation eliminates any uncertainty regarding the value of the allocation at the time of grant. HCP knew, at the time of each waiver election, the precise dollar amount of the priority allocation it would receive.

55\. Moreover, the carry-forward provision in the waiver election forms makes the income stream \"substantially certain and predictable\" within the meaning of the Revenue Procedure. The carry-forward mechanism ensures that unfulfilled priority allocations are not forfeited but are instead accumulated and satisfied from future gains, creating a contractual right to a fixed dollar amount of future partnership income. This contractual right constitutes a substantially certain and predictable income stream that, under Revenue Procedure 93-27, triggers recognition at the time of receipt. The priority allocations therefore do not qualify for any deferral or safe harbor treatment under the Revenue Procedure; rather, they should be taxed as ordinary income at the time HCP received them.

**C. Comparison to \*Pinnacle Partners\***

56\. The conclusion that Revenue Procedure 93-27 does not protect HCP\'s fee waiver arrangement is consistent with the Tax Court\'s analysis in *Pinnacle Partners v. Commissioner*, T.C. Memo 2019-88. In *Pinnacle Partners*, the Tax Court addressed a private equity fund manager\'s use of a fee waiver structure that was materially similar to the one at issue here. The Tax Court concluded that the fee waiver arrangement failed to shift meaningful entrepreneurial risk to the fund manager and that the priority allocations received by the manager in exchange for waived fees were properly treated as compensation for services rather than genuine profit-sharing allocations.

57\. The *Pinnacle Partners* decision reinforces the principle that the form of a profits interest cannot override the economic substance of the arrangement. Where a profits interest is structured as a dollar-for-dollar substitute for a management fee, with contractual protections that minimize the risk of non-payment, the interest is not a genuine entrepreneurial allocation entitled to capital gain treatment. The same principle applies with equal force to HCP\'s priority profit allocations.

**[VI. Opinion 4: The Structure Constitutes a Disguised Payment for Services Under IRC § 707(a)(2)(A)]{.underline}**

**A. Legal Framework --- IRC § 707(a)(2)(A) and Treasury Regulation § 1.707-2**

58\. IRC § 707(a)(2)(A) provides that if a partner performs services for the partnership and receives a related allocation and distribution, and the transaction, when viewed as a whole, is properly characterized as one occurring between the partnership and a person acting in a capacity other than as a partner, then the transaction shall be treated as a payment to a non-partner for services. The purpose of this provision is to prevent the use of partnership allocation and distribution mechanisms to disguise what is, in substance, a payment for services --- thereby avoiding the ordinary income characterization that would apply if the payment were made directly.

59\. Treasury Regulation § 1.707-2 provides guidance for applying Section 707(a)(2)(A). The regulation sets forth a general framework under which an allocation and distribution to a partner will be treated as a disguised payment for services if, based on all the facts and circumstances, the allocation and distribution are properly characterized as a transaction between the partnership and a non-partner. The regulation identifies a central consideration in this analysis: whether the allocation and distribution are subject to significant entrepreneurial risk. Where an allocation and distribution are structured to minimize or eliminate entrepreneurial risk --- as where the amount of the allocation is predetermined, the allocation is funded by a carry-forward mechanism, and the allocation bears a direct dollar-for-dollar relationship to the value of services provided --- the allocation is properly treated as a disguised payment for services.

60\. The regulation contemplates that the disguised payment analysis requires an evaluation of the totality of the circumstances, including the relationship between the allocation and the services performed, the timing of the allocation relative to the services, and the degree to which the allocation exposes the service-providing partner to the same types and magnitudes of risk borne by the other partners. Where these factors indicate that the allocation is, in substance, a payment for services rather than a return on partnership capital or a genuine sharing of partnership profits, recharacterization under Section 707(a)(2)(A) is warranted.

**B. Application --- HCP\'s Allocations Are Disguised Payments**

61\. In my opinion, the priority profit allocations received by HCP in exchange for waived management fees are disguised payments for services within the meaning of IRC § 707(a)(2)(A). I base this conclusion on the following analysis.

62\. First, HCP performed management services for Hargrove Capital Funds III, IV, and V that would have entitled it to management fees under the management agreements governing each fund. These services included investment advisory services, portfolio monitoring, deal sourcing, due diligence, and fund administration. The services were rendered on an ongoing basis throughout each fiscal year and were the same services that HCP would have provided regardless of whether the fee waiver was in effect.

63\. Second, HCP waived a portion of its management fees and received, in their place, priority profit allocations from the funds. The waiver and the receipt of the priority allocations were directly linked: the allocations were granted in exchange for the waiver, and the dollar amount of each allocation precisely matched the dollar amount of the waived fee. The allocations were not independent of the fee waiver; they were the consideration for it.

64\. Third, the dollar-for-dollar correspondence between the waived fees and the priority allocations demonstrates that the allocations were predetermined compensation rather than genuine entrepreneurial returns. A true profit-sharing allocation reflects the partner\'s share of the partnership\'s economic returns and varies with the partnership\'s performance. Here, the amount of the priority allocation did not vary with fund performance; it was fixed at the outset of each fiscal year in an amount equal to the waived management fee.

65\. Fourth, the carry-forward provision substantially eliminated any meaningful entrepreneurial risk associated with the priority allocations. Even if a fund did not generate sufficient realized long-term capital gains in a given year to satisfy the full allocation, the unfulfilled balance was carried forward indefinitely. HCP was not exposed to a genuine risk that it would fail to receive compensation for its services; it faced, at most, a risk that the timing of payment would be delayed.

66\. In my opinion, the priority profit allocations received by HCP are, within the meaning of IRC § 707(a)(2)(A), disguised payments for services that should be recharacterized as ordinary income. The arrangement was structured to give the appearance of a genuine profit-sharing allocation while delivering predetermined service compensation through an alternative channel. The substance of the transaction, rather than its form, must control.

**[VII. Rebuttal of Anticipated Defenses]{.underline}**

**A. The \"Entrepreneurial Risk\" Defense**

67\. I anticipate that HCP will argue that the priority profit allocations bore meaningful entrepreneurial risk because they were contingent on the funds generating realized long-term capital gains. This argument is unpersuasive for several reasons.

68\. First, as I have discussed, the carry-forward provision virtually eliminated the risk of non-payment. Even if a fund failed to generate sufficient gains in the waiver year, the unfulfilled amount was accumulated and carried forward to future years until fully allocated. This mechanism ensured that HCP\'s right to receive the full economic value of the waived management fees was preserved indefinitely.

69\. Second, Funds III and IV had extensive realized gains that far exceeded the aggregate waiver amounts attributed to them. Fund III generated \$298 million in realized gains, while only \$11,850,000 in fees were waived from Fund III. Fund IV generated \$742 million in realized gains, while \$29,762,000 in fees were waived from Fund IV. In neither case was there a realistic risk that the priority allocations would go unfulfilled.

70\. Third, even Fund V\'s shortfall --- no realized gains as of TY 2020 --- would be addressed by the carry-forward mechanism. The \$6,000,000 priority allocation from Fund V was not forfeited; it was carried forward with the expectation that future gains would satisfy it. The presence of the carry-forward provision meant that the temporal gap between the waiver election and the eventual payment of the allocation was a timing issue, not a genuine economic risk.

71\. Fourth, the dollar-for-dollar matching of waived fees to priority allocations is itself indicative of predetermined compensation rather than an entrepreneurial return. A genuine entrepreneurial allocation would bear some relationship to the fund\'s overall performance and would not be mathematically identical to the fee that was waived. The lockstep correspondence between waived fees and priority allocations demonstrates that the allocations were substitutes for management fees, not returns on an at-risk investment.

**B. The \"Advance Election\" Defense**

72\. I also anticipate that HCP will argue that because the waiver elections were made before the start of each fiscal year, they reflect genuine prospective risk-bearing --- that is, that by electing to waive fees before the relevant performance period began, HCP was accepting a genuine risk that the fund would not generate sufficient gains to satisfy the priority allocation.

73\. While the timing of the election is a relevant consideration, it is a necessary but not sufficient condition for respecting the arrangement as a genuine entrepreneurial allocation. The form of an advance election cannot transform what is in substance a predetermined payment into a genuine entrepreneurial allocation. The relevant inquiry is not merely whether the election was made in advance, but whether the arrangement as a whole --- including the carry-forward provision, the dollar-for-dollar matching, and the historical and projected fund performance --- exposed HCP to meaningful economic risk.

74\. Moreover, the waiver elections were routine and repeated annually. HCP elected to waive fees in every year from 2016 through the tax years at issue, following the same pattern and using substantially the same election forms. This regularity suggests that HCP\'s managing partners viewed the fee waiver as a standard element of their compensation structure rather than a genuine annual risk assessment requiring independent evaluation of each fund\'s investment prospects. The elections were not the product of careful deliberation regarding the likelihood of fund performance in any given year; they were a standing practice designed to ensure that HCP\'s compensation was received in long-term capital gain form.

**[VIII. Conclusion and Certification]{.underline}**

**A. Summary of Opinions**

75\. Based on my review of the materials described in Section I.D above, my expertise in partnership taxation and investment fund structures, and my analysis of the applicable legal authorities, I hold the following opinions to a reasonable degree of professional certainty:

> \(1\) The management fee waiver structure employed by HCP lacks economic substance independent of its tax benefits. The arrangement served no non-tax business purpose and did not meaningfully alter HCP\'s economic position apart from the conversion of ordinary income into long-term capital gains.
>
> \(2\) The priority profit allocations received by HCP in exchange for waived management fees are, in substance, guaranteed payments for services within the meaning of IRC § 707(c) and should be taxed as ordinary income to HCP and its partners.
>
> \(3\) Revenue Procedure 93-27 does not shelter the fee waiver arrangement from taxation. To the contrary, because the priority profit allocations have determinable values equal to the dollar amounts of the waived management fees and are associated with a substantially certain and predictable income stream backstopped by the carry-forward provision, the Revenue Procedure supports the conclusion that the profits interests should be taxed at the time of receipt.
>
> \(4\) The fee waiver structure constitutes a disguised payment for services within the meaning of IRC § 707(a)(2)(A), and the priority profit allocations should be recharacterized as ordinary income.

76\. These opinions are based on my independent review and analysis of the materials and authorities described herein. I have not been asked by counsel to reach any particular conclusion, and my opinions would be the same regardless of which party retained me.

**B. Certification Under 28 U.S.C. § 1746**

77\. I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the United States of America that the foregoing is true and correct to the best of my knowledge, information, and belief.

Executed on April 1, 2024, at Whitman, Connecticut.
