**RIDGELINE ADVISORS LLP** Tax Advisory \| Accounting \| Consulting 200 Park Avenue South, Suite 1400 New York, NY 10003 Telephone: (212) 555-0187 \| Facsimile: (212) 555-0188 www.ridgelineadvisors.com

November 1, 2017

Mr. Elliot R. Hargrove Managing Partner Ms. Diane K. Sato Managing Partner Hargrove Capital Partners LLC 600 Lexington Avenue, 31st Floor New York, NY 10022

Dear Mr. Hargrove and Ms. Sato:

**[I. Purpose and Scope of Opinion]{.underline}**

Ridgeline Advisors LLP (\"Ridgeline\" or \"we\") has been engaged by Hargrove Capital Partners LLC (\"HCP\"), a Delaware limited liability company (EIN: 82-4539176) formed on March 12, 2014, to provide a written tax opinion regarding the federal income tax treatment of HCP\'s proposed management fee waiver program (the \"Fee Waiver Program\" or the \"Structure\"). This engagement was initiated at the request of HCP\'s counsel, Thornfield & Locke LLP, and has been conducted in accordance with applicable professional standards, including Circular 230 and the AICPA Statements on Standards for Tax Services.

This opinion addresses the following specific questions:

First, whether the priority profit allocations received by HCP in exchange for waived management fees will be properly characterized as allocations of partnership income --- specifically, long-term capital gains --- under Subchapter K of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986, as amended (the \"Code\"), rather than as ordinary income, either as disguised payments for services under Section 707(a)(2)(A) of the Code or as guaranteed payments under Section 707(c) of the Code.

Second, whether the Fee Waiver Program arrangement satisfies the economic substance doctrine as codified under Section 7701(o) of the Code.

This opinion is rendered at the **\"more likely than not\"** confidence level, meaning that we believe there is a **greater than 50% likelihood** that the federal income tax treatment described herein would be sustained on its merits if challenged by the Internal Revenue Service (\"IRS\") and litigated before a court of competent jurisdiction. This confidence level is consistent with the standard recognized for purposes of establishing reasonable cause and good faith reliance on a tax advisor\'s opinion under Section 6664(c) of the Code.

This opinion is being rendered in connection with the anticipated implementation of fee waiver elections beginning with the fiscal year commencing January 1, 2018, and is applicable to **Hargrove Capital Fund III, LP**, a Delaware limited partnership formed on June 1, 2015, with approximately \$820 million in committed capital, and **Hargrove Capital Fund IV, LP**, a Delaware limited partnership formed on September 15, 2017, with approximately \$1.35 billion in committed capital (each a \"Fund\" and collectively the \"Funds\"). We understand that HCP may in the future extend the Fee Waiver Program to additional investment funds within the Hargrove Capital family. This opinion would apply to any substantially similar fee waiver structures implemented for such future funds, provided the material terms and conditions are consistent in all respects with those described herein and the underlying facts and circumstances remain materially unchanged.

This opinion is based on the provisions of the Code, the Treasury Regulations promulgated thereunder, applicable Revenue Rulings, Revenue Procedures, and other administrative pronouncements, and relevant judicial decisions, each as in effect as of the date hereof, all of which are subject to change, possibly with retroactive effect. No assurance can be given that future legislative, regulatory, judicial, or administrative developments will not adversely affect the conclusions expressed in this opinion.

**[II. Statement of Facts]{.underline}**

In rendering this opinion, we have relied upon the following facts as represented to us by HCP and its counsel. Ridgeline has not independently verified these factual representations and has assumed their accuracy and completeness for purposes of this opinion.

**A. HCP Background**

HCP is a Delaware limited liability company formed on March 12, 2014, with its principal office located at 600 Lexington Avenue, 31st Floor, New York, NY 10022. HCP is classified as a partnership for federal income tax purposes and files an annual U.S. Return of Partnership Income on Form 1065. HCP serves as the management company for the Hargrove Capital Fund family of private equity investment funds and provides investment advisory, portfolio management, and related services to the Funds.

**B. Managing Partners and Ownership**

HCP\'s co-founders and managing partners are Elliot R. Hargrove, who holds a 42% profits interest in HCP, and Diane K. Sato, who holds a 38% profits interest in HCP. The remaining 20% profits interest is held collectively by other partners of HCP who participate in the firm\'s investment advisory and management activities. Mr. Hargrove and Ms. Sato exercise day-to-day management authority over HCP and make all material decisions regarding the operation of HCP and the Funds.

**C. The Funds**

Hargrove Capital Fund III, LP (\"Fund III\") is a Delaware limited partnership formed on June 1, 2015, with approximately \$820 million in committed capital from institutional and other qualified investors. The general partner of Fund III is Hargrove GP III LLC, an entity affiliated with HCP.

Hargrove Capital Fund IV, LP (\"Fund IV\") is a Delaware limited partnership formed on September 15, 2017, with approximately \$1.35 billion in committed capital. The general partner of Fund IV is Hargrove GP IV LLC, an entity affiliated with HCP. Fund IV is currently in its fundraising and initial investment period.

Both Funds pursue a mid-market private equity investment strategy, acquiring control or significant minority positions in privately held operating companies with enterprise values generally between \$100 million and \$750 million.

**D. Existing Management Fee Arrangements**

Under the existing limited partnership agreements governing each Fund, each Fund pays HCP an annual management fee calculated as a percentage of committed capital (during the investment period) or invested capital (after the investment period), as applicable. These management fees constitute ordinary income to HCP and, in turn, to its partners when allocated through HCP pursuant to HCP\'s operating agreement.

**E. Proposed Fee Waiver Structure**

HCP proposes to implement the Fee Waiver Program under which HCP\'s managing partners may elect, **prior to the start of each fiscal year**, to waive a portion of the management fees otherwise payable to HCP by the applicable Fund. In exchange for each dollar of waived management fees, HCP would receive a **priority profit allocation** from the relevant Fund equal in amount to the waived fee amount. The priority profit allocation would be payable **only from realized long-term capital gains** of the Fund. This feature is set forth in the proposed amendments to each Fund\'s limited partnership agreement and allocation waterfall provisions.

**F. Carry-Forward Provision**

If the relevant Fund does not generate sufficient realized long-term capital gains in a given fiscal year to satisfy the priority profit allocation attributable to that year\'s fee waiver, the unfulfilled amount will carry forward and be satisfied from realized long-term capital gains in subsequent fiscal years, until fully allocated or until the Fund\'s winding up and dissolution, whichever occurs first. There is no provision requiring acceleration, cash settlement, or payment of the unfulfilled allocation from any source other than realized long-term capital gains.

**G. Timing of Elections**

Waiver elections must be executed and delivered by HCP\'s managing partners **before the commencement of the fiscal year** to which the waiver relates. This prospective election requirement ensures that the waiver decision is made before the relevant partnership income has been earned or can reasonably be identified, and that the election is not retroactive in nature. We understand that the initial waiver elections for the fiscal year commencing January 1, 2018, are expected to be executed in December 2017.

**H. Absence of Deficit Restoration Obligation or Guarantee**

The priority profit allocation is **not** backed by any deficit restoration obligation on the part of any limited partner or the Fund itself, nor by any guarantee, indemnity, side letter, or other contractual mechanism that would assure payment of the priority allocation regardless of Fund performance. The limited partnership agreements do not require the Fund or any partner to make additional capital contributions for the purpose of funding priority allocations.

**I. Economic Risk**

The priority allocations bear genuine entrepreneurial risk because: (i) they depend entirely on the Fund\'s ability to generate realized long-term capital gains from its portfolio investments; (ii) Fund performance is uncertain and subject to market conditions, macroeconomic factors, deal execution risk, and the timing and terms of portfolio company exits; and (iii) there is no make-whole, clawback, or backstop mechanism running from the Fund, its limited partners, or any other person to HCP that would guarantee the eventual payment of the priority allocation in any amount.

**J. Anticipated Waiver Amounts**

HCP anticipates that the managing partners will waive management fees in material amounts beginning with tax year 2018. Specific dollar amounts have not been finalized as of the date of this opinion, but HCP has represented that the waived amounts could range from approximately \$5 million to \$20 million per year across the applicable Funds, depending on fund size, vintage year, and individual partner elections.

**K. Reliance on Representations**

The factual representations set forth in this Section II have been provided to Ridgeline by HCP and its counsel, Thornfield & Locke LLP. Ridgeline has relied upon these representations without independent verification. If any material fact differs from what has been represented to us, the conclusions expressed in this opinion may be affected.

**[III. Legal Analysis]{.underline}**

**[A. IRC § 707(a)(2)(A) --- Disguised Payments for Services]{.underline}**

**1. Statutory Framework**

Section 707(a)(2)(A) of the Code provides that if (i) a partner performs services for a partnership, (ii) there is a related direct or indirect allocation and distribution to such partner, and (iii) the performance of such services and the allocation and distribution, when viewed together, are properly characterized as a transaction occurring between the partnership and a partner acting other than in his capacity as a member of the partnership, then such transaction shall be treated as one between the partnership and a person who is not a partner. The practical effect of recharacterization under § 707(a)(2)(A) is that the allocation is treated as a payment of ordinary income for services rather than as a distributive share of partnership income. This provision was enacted as part of the Tax Reform Act of 1984, Pub. L. No. 98-369, and was intended to address abusive arrangements in which service partners disguise compensation as partnership allocations to convert ordinary income into capital gains or to obtain other tax benefits.

**2. Regulatory Framework --- The Six-Factor Test**

Treasury Regulations § 1.707-2(c) sets forth six factors to be considered in determining whether an allocation and distribution to a service-providing partner constitute a disguised payment for services. No single factor is determinative; rather, the factors are to be weighed in the aggregate based on all facts and circumstances. We analyze each factor below as applied to the Fee Waiver Program.

**Factor (1): Whether the allocation and distribution are subject to an appreciable risk that they will not be paid --- the entrepreneurial risk factor.**

This factor examines whether the partner\'s right to receive the allocation is contingent upon the partnership\'s overall economic performance, as opposed to being a relatively certain payment irrespective of partnership results. The greater the risk that the allocation will not be paid, the more the arrangement resembles a true partnership allocation rather than a payment for services.

Under the Fee Waiver Program, the priority profit allocations are payable **only** from realized long-term capital gains generated by the applicable Fund. If a Fund does not produce realized long-term capital gains --- whether due to adverse market conditions, unsuccessful portfolio investments, or delays in exit timing --- the priority allocation will not be satisfied. There is no alternative source of funding for the allocation, no deficit restoration obligation, and no guarantee or backstop of any kind. HCP is exposed to the same fundamental entrepreneurial risks that affect all partners whose returns depend upon the Fund\'s ability to generate investment gains. Fund III and Fund IV invest primarily in mid-market private equity transactions, a sector characterized by inherent performance variability and meaningful downside risk. Historical data for mid-market buyout funds demonstrates material dispersion of returns across vintage years, with some funds significantly underperforming their return targets.

This factor **strongly favors** treatment of the priority allocations as bona fide partnership allocations.

**Factor (2): Whether the partner, in its capacity as a partner, has a transactional relationship with the partnership that is the functional equivalent of a payment for services.**

This factor considers whether the economic arrangement between the partner and the partnership resembles a third-party service-provider relationship rather than a return on the partner\'s partnership interest. An arrangement that functions as a fee-for-service contract weighs toward disguised payment treatment, while an arrangement integrated into the partnership\'s allocation waterfall weighs toward partnership allocation treatment.

HCP is and remains a partner in the Funds through its affiliated general partner entities, Hargrove GP III LLC and Hargrove GP IV LLC. The fee waiver does not create a new or separate service relationship between HCP and the Funds. Rather, it modifies the form in which HCP receives a portion of its economic return as a participant in the Funds\' investment activities. The priority profit allocation is incorporated directly into the partnership\'s allocation waterfall provisions under the applicable limited partnership agreement, alongside the standard allocation provisions governing all partners\' shares of income, gain, loss, and deduction. The allocation is not structured as a separate fee-for-service arrangement, is not invoiced, and does not create an accounts receivable obligation on the Fund\'s balance sheet.

This factor **favors** treatment as a bona fide partnership allocation.

**Factor (3): Whether the allocation and distribution are subject to clawback or adjustment if the services are not performed as agreed.**

This factor evaluates whether the partner\'s entitlement to the allocation is conditioned on the partner\'s continued performance of services. If the allocation would be reduced or eliminated upon cessation of services, the arrangement more closely resembles a compensatory payment.

Under the Fee Waiver Program, once a waiver election has been executed and delivered for a given fiscal year, HCP\'s right to the corresponding priority profit allocation vests and is not contingent upon HCP\'s continued provision of management services to the Fund for any minimum duration. The priority allocation right survives any change in the management services arrangement, and there is no clawback or reduction mechanism tied to service levels. However, we acknowledge that this factor has somewhat limited analytical weight in the context of this particular arrangement because the fee waiver is structured as an allocation modification rather than as a freestanding service contract. The absence of a service-contingent clawback is consistent with the character of a partnership allocation.

This factor is **neutral to modestly favorable** for partnership allocation treatment.

**Factor (4): Whether the recipient\'s right to the allocation is subject to appreciable risk --- specifically, whether the allocation is \"reasonably certain\" to be fulfilled.**

This factor, which is closely related to but conceptually distinct from Factor (1), asks whether the priority allocation is effectively assured of being paid, such that the \"risk\" associated with the allocation is nominal or illusory rather than genuine. An allocation that is reasonably certain to be fulfilled --- for example, because the partnership has a reliable income stream or because the allocation is backstopped by a guarantee --- is more likely to be treated as a disguised payment. Conversely, an allocation that is genuinely uncertain and contingent on investment outcomes is more likely to be treated as a partnership allocation.

The priority allocations under the Fee Waiver Program are **not** reasonably certain to be fulfilled. They depend entirely on the realization of long-term capital gains from portfolio investments, which is inherently uncertain. There is no deficit restoration obligation, no guarantee by the Fund or any of its limited partners, and no side letter, credit facility, or other arrangement that would backstop the allocation or assure its eventual satisfaction. Private equity fund returns are variable and subject to meaningful downside risk. It is not uncommon for mid-market private equity funds to underperform expectations or to fail to generate sufficient realized gains to fully satisfy all priority allocations within the anticipated time horizon. Market dislocations, credit contractions, unfavorable regulatory developments, and portfolio-specific execution risks can all result in realized gains that fall materially short of projections.

**This is the most significant factor in the analysis, and it weighs heavily in HCP\'s favor.** The genuine uncertainty surrounding the priority allocations is the defining characteristic that distinguishes the Fee Waiver Program from arrangements properly treated as disguised payments for services.

**Factor (5): Whether the allocation is fixed in amount or is subject to adjustment based on the income of the partnership.**

This factor examines whether the partner\'s economic return from the arrangement is a predetermined, fixed sum --- characteristic of a fee --- or whether it varies with the partnership\'s financial performance --- characteristic of a partnership return.

The priority profit allocation is not fixed in amount. Although the nominal target of the allocation is set by reference to the dollar amount of waived fees, the actual amount allocated to HCP in any given year is limited to the Fund\'s realized long-term capital gains. If the Fund generates no realized long-term capital gains, the allocation is zero. If the Fund generates gains that are less than the waived fee amount, the allocation is limited to the available gains. The allocation thus varies directly with the income of the partnership, which is the hallmark of a partnership allocation. This characteristic also distinguishes the priority allocation from a guaranteed payment under § 707(c), which by definition is determined without regard to partnership income.

This factor **favors** treatment as a bona fide partnership allocation.

**Factor (6): The partner\'s interest in general and continuing partnership profits and losses.**

This factor considers whether the service partner has a meaningful, ongoing economic stake in the partnership\'s overall fortunes, beyond the specific allocation at issue. A partner with a substantial pre-existing and continuing interest in partnership profits and losses is more likely to receive allocations in its capacity as a partner rather than as a disguised service provider.

HCP, through its affiliated general partner entities Hargrove GP III LLC and Hargrove GP IV LLC, retains its general partner interest in each Fund, including its carried interest allocation (typically 20% of net profits above a preferred return hurdle) and its proportionate share of all other partnership profits and losses. The priority profit allocation does not displace, substitute for, or reduce HCP\'s broader partnership interest; it supplements it. HCP\'s overall economic relationship with the Funds extends far beyond the priority allocation and encompasses the full range of risks and rewards associated with general partner status. This deep and continuing partnership interest is inconsistent with a characterization of the priority allocation as a disguised payment for services.

This factor **favors** treatment as a bona fide partnership allocation.

**3. Overall § 707(a)(2)(A) Conclusion**

When the six regulatory factors are considered in the aggregate and in light of all facts and circumstances, the priority profit allocations under the Fee Waiver Program are **not** properly characterized as disguised payments for services under § 707(a)(2)(A). The allocations bear genuine entrepreneurial risk, are not reasonably certain to be fulfilled, are not fixed in amount but rather vary with partnership income, and are received by HCP in its capacity as a partner through its affiliated general partner entities. HCP maintains a substantial, continuing interest in the Funds\' overall profits and losses, and the allocation structure is integrated into the partnership\'s allocation waterfall rather than being structured as a separate fee arrangement.

It is our opinion that the priority profit allocations under the Fee Waiver Program **more likely than not** constitute bona fide allocations of partnership income and are **not** disguised payments for services under IRC § 707(a)(2)(A).

**4. Distinction from § 704(b) Analysis**

We note that the analysis under § 707(a)(2)(A) and Treasury Regulations § 1.707-2(c) is **distinct from** the \"substantial economic effect\" analysis under § 704(b) of the Code and Treasury Regulations § 1.704-1(b)(2). The concept of \"transitory allocations\" under the § 704(b) regulatory framework addresses a different question --- namely, whether partnership allocations have substantial economic effect and should be respected for tax purposes. The § 704(b) regulations and the § 707(a)(2)(A) regulations serve different statutory purposes and employ different analytical frameworks. The legislative history of the Tax Reform Act of 1984 confirms that Congress intended these provisions to operate independently, and that the § 707 disguised payment rules should not be conflated with the § 704(b) allocation rules. disguised payment rules should not be conflated with the § 704(b) allocation rules. This distinction is relevant in assessing the proper analytical framework for evaluating the Fee Waiver Program and should be kept in mind when considering any arguments regarding the allocations\' validity.

**[B. IRC § 707(c) --- Guaranteed Payments]{.underline}**

**1. Statutory Standard**

Section 707(c) of the Code defines guaranteed payments as payments to a partner for services or the use of capital, to the extent that such payments are **\"determined without regard to the income of the partnership.\"** Guaranteed payments are treated as ordinary income to the recipient partner and are deductible by the partnership (subject to applicable limitations) in the same manner as payments to a non-partner.

The critical statutory inquiry is whether the payment to the partner is fixed or determinable independently of the partnership\'s income. If the payment is contingent upon and determined by reference to partnership income, it is not a guaranteed payment under § 707(c).

**2. Analysis.** The priority profit allocations under the Fee Waiver Program are **not** guaranteed payments because they are, by definition, determined **with regard to** the income of the partnership. The allocations are payable only from realized long-term capital gains generated by the applicable Fund. If the Fund generates no such gains in a given fiscal year, the priority allocation for that year is zero. The entire amount, timing, and ultimate satisfaction of the allocation depend upon the Fund\'s investment performance, which is the quintessential example of a payment determined with regard to partnership income.

The allocation cannot be satisfied from management fees, interest income, short-term gains, or any other source of partnership income. It is exclusively tied to realized long-term capital gains. This structure is fundamentally inconsistent with the definition of a guaranteed payment under § 707(c), which contemplates a payment that the partner is entitled to receive regardless of whether the partnership generates income.

**3. The Carry-Forward Feature**

We anticipate that the government might argue that the carry-forward provision --- under which unfulfilled priority allocations carry forward to subsequent years and are satisfied from future realized long-term capital gains --- effectively guarantees eventual payment and therefore brings the arrangement within the scope of § 707(c). We do not find this argument persuasive.

The carry-forward provision merely extends the time period during which the Fund\'s realized long-term capital gains may be allocated to satisfy the priority allocation. It does not guarantee that sufficient gains will ever materialize. If the Fund winds down and liquidates without having generated sufficient realized long-term capital gains to satisfy all outstanding priority allocations, the unfulfilled amounts expire unsatisfied. The carry-forward is a timing mechanism, not a credit support mechanism. It does not convert a contingent, performance-dependent allocation into a guaranteed payment. To hold otherwise would effectively treat any multi-year allocation provision as a guaranteed payment, a result that finds no support in the statute, regulations, or case law.

**4. Conclusion.** It is our opinion that the priority profit allocations under the Fee Waiver Program **more likely than not** do not constitute guaranteed payments under IRC § 707(c). The allocations are determined with regard to the income of the partnership and are not assured of payment regardless of Fund performance.

**[C. Economic Substance Doctrine]{.underline}**

**1. Legal Framework**

The economic substance doctrine, as codified at IRC § 7701(o) (effective for transactions entered into after March 30, 2010), provides that a transaction shall be treated as having economic substance only if: (1) the transaction changes in a meaningful way (apart from Federal income tax effects) the taxpayer\'s economic position (the **\"objective prong\"**); and (2) the taxpayer has a substantial purpose (apart from Federal income tax effects) for entering into such transaction (the **\"subjective prong\"**). Section 7701(o) applies a **conjunctive test** --- both prongs must be satisfied. This codification was enacted as part of the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010, Pub. L. No. 111-152, § 1409, and clarified that the doctrine applies as a two-part conjunctive test, resolving a prior circuit split on whether the test was conjunctive or disjunctive.

**2. Objective Prong Analysis**

The Fee Waiver Program meaningfully changes HCP\'s economic position apart from Federal income tax effects in the following respects:

First, HCP exchanges a **certain** right --- the contractual entitlement to receive management fees, which are owed by the Fund regardless of investment performance --- for an **uncertain** right --- a priority profit allocation that is payable only from realized long-term capital gains, the existence and magnitude of which are contingent upon future investment outcomes. This exchange creates genuine and material downside risk for HCP. If the Fund underperforms its return targets or fails to generate realized long-term capital gains in sufficient amounts, HCP will receive less economic value from the priority allocation than it would have received had it simply collected the management fees.

Second, the economic position change is not de minimis. Given the anticipated waiver amounts of \$5 million to \$20 million per year, the difference in economic outcomes between collecting guaranteed management fees and receiving contingent priority allocations is substantial. HCP is foregoing a reliable revenue stream --- management fees that would be payable under the existing fund agreements regardless of Fund performance --- in exchange for revenue that is entirely dependent upon future investment results. This is a meaningful economic trade-off that exists independent of any tax consequences.

Third, Fund performance is not within HCP\'s unilateral control. The realization of long-term capital gains depends on macroeconomic conditions, industry dynamics, credit market availability, the performance of individual portfolio companies, and the timing and terms of exit transactions. These factors introduce genuine uncertainty into the economic outcome of the fee waiver arrangement.

We therefore conclude that the objective prong of the economic substance test is satisfied.

**3. Subjective Prong Analysis**

HCP has substantial non-tax business purposes for entering into the Fee Waiver Program:

**Alignment of Interests.** The Fee Waiver Program better aligns the economic interests of HCP\'s managing partners with those of the Funds\' limited partners by tying a meaningful portion of HCP\'s compensation to realized investment returns rather than to committed capital or invested capital. This alignment is a core principle of private equity fund governance and is viewed favorably by sophisticated institutional investors, including pension funds, endowments, sovereign wealth funds, and fund-of-funds managers.

**Limited Partner Relations and Fundraising.** Management fee waiver programs are widely used in the private equity industry as a mechanism to demonstrate general partner commitment to performance and to signal confidence in the investment program. The adoption of the Fee Waiver Program enhances HCP\'s competitive positioning in fundraising for future funds and strengthens HCP\'s relationships with existing limited partners who value evidence of GP alignment.

**Capital Efficiency.** By waiving management fees and accepting priority profit allocations, HCP effectively reinvests a portion of its management company economics into the Fund\'s investment pool. This reinvestment increases the capital available for deployment in portfolio investments and can enhance aggregate returns for all partners, including both general and limited partners.

These non-tax business purposes are genuine, substantial, and commercially rational, and they would motivate a reasonable business person to enter into the Fee Waiver Program apart from any tax benefits.

**4. Conclusion.** It is our opinion that the Fee Waiver Program **more likely than not** satisfies both prongs of the economic substance doctrine under IRC § 7701(o). The arrangement changes HCP\'s economic position in a meaningful way apart from tax effects and is supported by substantial non-tax business purposes.

**[D. Rev. Proc. 93-27 and Profits Interests]{.underline}**

**1. Background.** Revenue Procedure 93-27, 1993-2 C.B. 343, provides a safe harbor under which the IRS will not treat the receipt of a partnership profits interest in exchange for the provision of services to or for the benefit of the partnership as a taxable event at the time of grant, provided that: (i) the profits interest does not relate to a substantially certain and predictable stream of income from partnership assets, such as income from high-quality debt securities or a high-quality net lease; (ii) the partner does not dispose of the profits interest within two years of receipt; and (iii) the profits interest is not a limited partnership interest in a publicly traded partnership within the meaning of § 7704 of the Code.

This safe harbor reflects the IRS\'s administrative position that a profits interest --- i.e., a right to share in future partnership profits and gains but not in existing partnership assets --- is sufficiently speculative at the time of grant that it should not be treated as current compensation.

**2. Application to the Fee Waiver Program**

Although the Fee Waiver Program does not involve the grant of a new profits interest per se, the priority profit allocation is functionally analogous to a profits interest in that it represents a right to share in future partnership gains rather than a right to a current, fixed payment. The priority allocation has value only if and to the extent the Fund generates realized long-term capital gains --- precisely the type of contingent, profit-dependent economic interest that Rev. Proc. 93-27 treats as non-compensatory at the time of grant.

The priority allocations here clearly do **not** constitute a \"substantially certain and predictable stream of income\" because they depend entirely on uncertain future realized long-term capital gains from mid-market private equity investments. The inherent uncertainty of such gains is well established in the investment management industry and is supported by empirical data regarding the dispersion of private equity fund returns.

**3. Conclusion.** While Rev. Proc. 93-27 does not directly govern the Fee Waiver Program, it provides meaningful additional support, by analogy, for the proposition that profit-contingent allocations to service-providing partners are not inherently taxable as ordinary income. The underlying principle of Rev. Proc. 93-27 --- that contingent rights to future partnership profits should not be equated with current compensation --- reinforces the analysis set forth in Sections III.A and III.B above.

**[E. Character of Priority Allocations Under IRC § 702(b)]{.underline}**

**1. Statutory Rule**

Section 702(b) of the Code provides that the character of any item of income, gain, loss, deduction, or credit included in a partner\'s distributive share shall be determined as if such item were realized directly from the source from which realized by the partnership, or incurred in the same manner as incurred by the partnership. This rule ensures that the character of partnership items is preserved and flows through to the partners.

**2. Application.** To the extent the priority profit allocations under the Fee Waiver Program are funded from the applicable Fund\'s realized long-term capital gains --- i.e., gains from the sale or disposition of capital assets held for more than one year --- the allocations retain their character as long-term capital gains when allocated to HCP. Because HCP is itself classified as a partnership for federal income tax purposes, these long-term capital gains in turn flow through to HCP\'s individual partners and retain their character as long-term capital gains on the partners\' individual federal income tax returns.

**3. Conclusion.** Assuming, as we have concluded in Sections III.A and III.B above, that the priority profit allocations constitute bona fide allocations of partnership income and are not recharacterized as disguised payments for services or guaranteed payments, the allocations will be properly characterized as long-term capital gains to HCP and its partners under IRC § 702(b).

**[IV. Assumptions and Limitations]{.underline}**

This opinion is subject to the following assumptions and limitations, which should be carefully considered by HCP and its partners in evaluating the scope and applicability of our conclusions.

**Factual Assumptions.** This opinion is based entirely on the facts and representations described in Section II above. We have assumed that all such facts and representations are true, complete, and accurate in all material respects. If any material fact is different from what has been represented to us, or if the Fee Waiver Program is implemented in a manner that deviates in any material respect from the description set forth herein, our conclusions may be affected and this opinion should not be relied upon without consultation with Ridgeline.

**Prospective Election Timing.** This opinion assumes that all waiver elections will be duly executed and delivered by the electing managing partner(s) **prior to the start of the fiscal year** to which the waiver relates. The prospective nature of the election is a material element of the legal analysis set forth in this opinion, particularly with respect to the § 707(a)(2)(A) disguised payment analysis and the economic substance doctrine. If a waiver election is executed during or after the commencement of the applicable fiscal year, additional and potentially adverse issues may arise regarding the validity of the waiver, the character of the resulting allocation, and the applicability of the constructive receipt doctrine. **This opinion should not be relied upon for any waiver election that is not timely executed and delivered before the start of the relevant fiscal year.**

**No Deficit Restoration Obligation.** This opinion assumes that the Fee Waiver Program will not include any deficit restoration obligation, guarantee, indemnity, side letter, or other credit support mechanism --- whether formal or informal, written or oral --- that would assure payment of the priority profit allocation regardless of Fund performance. The absence of such features is a critical element of our analysis under the § 707(a)(2)(A) entrepreneurial risk factors and the economic substance doctrine. If any such feature is incorporated into the arrangement, our analysis may change materially, and this opinion should not be relied upon without further consultation.

**Applicable Law.** This opinion is based on the Internal Revenue Code, Treasury Regulations, Revenue Procedures, Revenue Rulings, judicial decisions, and other administrative guidance in effect as of November 1, 2017. Subsequent changes in law, regulation, or judicial or administrative interpretation --- whether prospective or retroactive --- could affect or modify our conclusions. We undertake no obligation to update this opinion in light of subsequent developments.

**\"More Likely Than Not\" Standard.** Our opinion is rendered at the \"more likely than not\" level of confidence, meaning we believe there is a greater than 50% likelihood that the federal income tax treatment described herein would be sustained on its merits if challenged by the IRS and litigated before a court of competent jurisdiction. This confidence level does not represent a guarantee of the outcome of any IRS examination, administrative proceeding, or litigation. There can be no assurance that the IRS will not take a contrary position or that a court would agree with our analysis in all respects.

**No Opinion on State, Local, or Foreign Taxes.** This opinion addresses only the federal income tax consequences of the Fee Waiver Program. We express no opinion on the state, local, or foreign tax implications of the arrangement, including but not limited to the applicability of any state or local income, franchise, or unincorporated business tax.

**Penalty Protection.** While this opinion may serve as a basis for establishing reasonable cause and good faith under IRC § 6664(c)(1) in the event that the IRS challenges the tax treatment described herein and asserts accuracy-related penalties under IRC § 6662, we express no separate opinion on whether the penalties described in § 6662 would be asserted or upheld, or whether a reasonable cause and good faith defense under § 6664(c) would ultimately be successful in any particular case. We note, however, that reliance on a reasoned, written opinion from a qualified tax advisor is a recognized and well-established basis for demonstrating reasonable cause and good faith under applicable case law and administrative guidance, including *United States v. Boyle*, 469 U.S. 241 (1985), and the regulations under § 1.6664-4.

**[V. Opinion and Conclusion]{.underline}**

Based on the facts and representations set forth in Section II, and subject to the assumptions and limitations described in Section IV, it is the opinion of Ridgeline Advisors LLP that:

1\. The management fee waiver priority profit allocations received by HCP under the Fee Waiver Program **more likely than not** constitute bona fide allocations of partnership income under Subchapter K of the Internal Revenue Code and are **not** disguised payments for services under IRC § 707(a)(2)(A). The six-factor analysis under Treasury Regulations § 1.707-2(c), considered in the aggregate, supports the conclusion that the priority allocations represent genuine partnership allocations bearing meaningful entrepreneurial risk, and not compensation for services rendered in a non-partner capacity.

2\. The management fee waiver priority profit allocations **more likely than not** are **not** guaranteed payments under IRC § 707(c). The allocations are determined with regard to the income of the partnership --- specifically, they are payable only from realized long-term capital gains --- and therefore do not fall within the statutory definition of guaranteed payments.

3\. The Fee Waiver Program **more likely than not** satisfies the economic substance doctrine as codified under IRC § 7701(o). The arrangement meaningfully changes HCP\'s economic position apart from Federal income tax effects (objective prong) and is supported by substantial non-tax business purposes, including alignment of interests with limited partners, enhanced fundraising positioning, and capital efficiency (subjective prong).

4\. To the extent the priority profit allocations are funded from the Funds\' realized long-term capital gains, the allocations **more likely than not** will be properly characterized as long-term capital gains to HCP and to HCP\'s individual partners under IRC § 702(b), preserving the character of the underlying gain as it flows through to the partners.

**Reliance.** HCP and its partners may rely on this opinion in reporting the management fee waiver priority profit allocations as long-term capital gains on HCP\'s Forms 1065 (U.S. Return of Partnership Income) and on the partners\' individual returns (Forms 1040 and Schedules K-1) for the applicable tax years, commencing with tax year 2018 and continuing for each subsequent tax year in which the Fee Waiver Program is in effect and the material terms are consistent with those described herein.

**Reliance for Penalty Protection.** This opinion is intended to, and may, serve as a basis for establishing reasonable cause and good faith under IRC § 6664(c)(1) in the event the IRS challenges the federal income tax treatment described herein and asserts accuracy-related penalties under IRC § 6662. We note that the \"more likely than not\" confidence level at which this opinion is rendered exceeds the threshold generally recognized as sufficient for reasonable cause reliance on a tax advisor\'s opinion under applicable Treasury Regulations and judicial authority. HCP and its partners should retain this opinion letter in their records as evidence of their reliance on professional tax advice in connection with the Fee Waiver Program.

from docx import Document
from docx.shared import Pt, Inches, RGBColor
from docx.enum.text import WD_ALIGN_PARAGRAPH
from docx.enum.table import WD_TABLE_ALIGNMENT
from docx.oxml.ns import qn
from docx.oxml import OxmlElement

doc = Document()
sec = doc.sections[0]
sec.left_margin = sec.right_margin = Inches(1)
sec.top_margin = sec.bottom_margin = Inches(1)

st = doc.styles['Normal']
st.font.name = 'Times New Roman'
st.font.size = Pt(11.5)
st.element.rPr.rFonts.set(qn('w:eastAsia'), 'Times New Roman')
for name, size in [('Heading 1', 14), ('Heading 2', 12.5), ('Heading 3', 11.5)]:
    h = doc.styles[name]
    h.font.name = 'Times New Roman'

    h.font.bold = True
    h.font.color.rgb = RGBColor(0, 0, 0)
    rpr = h.element.get_or_add_rPr()
    rf = rpr.find(qn('w:rFonts'))
    if rf is None:
        rf = OxmlElement('w:rFonts'); rpr.append(rf)
    for a in ('w:ascii', 'w:hAnsi', 'w:eastAsia', 'w:cs'):
        rf.set(qn(a), 'Times New Roman')

def shade(cell, color):
    tcPr = cell._tc.get_or_add_tcPr()
    shd = OxmlElement('w:shd')
    shd.set(qn('w:val'), 'clear'); shd.set(qn('w:color'), 'auto'); shd.set(qn('w:fill'), color)
    tcPr.append(shd)

def P(text='', bold=False, italic=False, align=None, size=None, space_after=6, indent=None):
    p = doc.add_paragraph()
    add_runs(p, text, bold, italic, size)
    p.paragraph_format.space_after = Pt(space_after)
    if align == 'center':
        p.alignment = WD_ALIGN_PARAGRAPH.CENTER
    if indent:
        p.paragraph_format.left_indent = Inches(indent)
    return p

def add_runs(p, text, bold=False, italic=False, size=None):
    # simple markup: **bold** and *italic*
    import re
    parts = re.split(r'(\*\*[^*]+\*\*|\*[^*]+\*)', text)
    for part in parts:
        if not part:
            continue
        if part.startswith('**') and part.endswith('**'):
            r = p.add_run(part[2:-2]); r.bold = True; r.italic = italic
        elif part.startswith('*') and part.endswith('*') and len(part) > 2:
            r = p.add_run(part[1:-1]); r.italic = True; r.bold = bold
        else:
            r = p.add_run(part); r.bold = bold; r.italic = italic
        if size:
            r.font.size = Pt(size)

def B(text, level=0):
    p = doc.add_paragraph(style='List Bullet' if level == 0 else 'List Bullet 2')
    add_runs(p, text)
    p.paragraph_format.space_after = Pt(3)
    return p

def N(text):
    p = doc.add_paragraph(style='List Number')
    add_runs(p, text)
    p.paragraph_format.space_after = Pt(3)
    return p

def H(text, level=1):
    return doc.add_heading(text, level=level)

def table(headers, rows, widths=None, header_fill='D9D9D9', size=9.5):
    t = doc.add_table(rows=1, cols=len(headers))
    t.style = 'Table Grid'
    t.alignment = WD_TABLE_ALIGNMENT.CENTER
    for i, h in enumerate(headers):
        c = t.rows[0].cells[i]
        c.text = ''
        add_runs(c.paragraphs[0], h, bold=True, size=size)
        shade(c, header_fill)
    for row in rows:
        cells = t.add_row().cells

issue('A-1', 'The Brief Misdates the Fund IV TY 2020 Election and Conflates It with the Fund V Election',
 ['SUMF ¶ 17: “Both the Fund IV and Fund V waiver elections for Tax Year 2020 were executed after the start of the fiscal year. . . . [T]he Fund IV election was likewise executed after the commencement of the 2020 fiscal year.”',
  'Arg. IV.C.2 (“Second”): “The TY 2020 elections for both Fund IV and Fund V were executed after the commencement of the fiscal year, demonstrating that the waivers were retroactive adjustments rather than genuine prospective business decisions.” See also n.13.'],
 ['The Fund IV TY 2020 election (Form HCP-2020-IV-005) was executed on **December 10, 2019**, three weeks before the fiscal year began. The government\'s own exhibit list says so: Quillen Decl. ¶ 89, Ex. 5-E (“Date: December 10, 2019. Countersigned by Hargrove GP IV LLC”). HCP\'s compiled summary marks it “Executed Prior to Fiscal Year Start: Yes.”',
  'Quillen herself never claims the Fund IV election was late. Her ¶ 32 omits the date, and ¶ 34 contrasts *only* the Fund V election with “the TY 2018 and TY 2019 elections.” The January 15, 2020 Greystone borrowing base certificate already referenced the TY 2020 election (Quillen Decl. ¶ 79), which is independent third-party corroboration that the Fund IV election existed at the start of the year.',
  'The Brief notably gives a specific date for Fund V but none for Fund IV (“likewise executed after”), which suggests counsel inferred rather than checked.'],
 'Critical',
 'The “retroactive election” theme is a pillar of the economic substance argument (Arg. IV.C.2) and the timing argument under the Treas. Reg. § 1.707-2 framework (n.13). Correcting the record confines any timing argument to a single election worth $6,000,000 (12.6% of the adjustment) and leaves $41,612,000 (87.4%) indisputably prospective. It is also a clean, document-based credibility hit that the Court can verify in seconds.',
 ['Lead the Counterstatement of Facts with an election-by-election table (Part III.A above) citing Exs. 5-A through 5-F and the Election Forms. Characterize the error precisely and without hyperbole: the government “conflated” two elections with different execution dates.',
  'In the argument, use the corrected facts to show that the government\'s own legal standard (n.13: a genuine waiver “must be made before the period to which it relates”) is satisfied for every election except Fund V, which is addressed separately (Issue A-2).',
  'Obtain a short declaration from HCP\'s CFO or the GP IV signatory authenticating the December 10, 2019 execution and delivery to the GP.']
)

issue('A-2', 'The Brief\'s Characterization of the Fund V Election as “Retroactive” Ignores That Fund V Did Not Exist Until February 1, 2020',
 ['SUMF ¶ 17: the Fund V election “was signed on January 28, 2020, twenty-eight days into the fiscal year.” Arg. IV.C.2: “This retroactive timing is inconsistent with a genuine pre-commitment to accept investment risk and is instead consistent with a post hoc adjustment.”'],
 ['The government\'s own SUMF ¶ 5 and Quillen Decl. ¶ 15 state that Fund V was formed on **February 1, 2020**. The Election Form itself recites that Fund V was “formed on February 1, 2020” and that its LPA was “to be dated on or about February 1, 2020.” The election therefore preceded the Fund\'s legal existence, its LPA, any capital call, any investment, and any accrual of management fees. A partnership cannot have a taxable year that begins before it exists [cite-check: Treas. Reg. § 1.708-1 / § 1.6031(a)-1 regarding commencement of partnership taxable year].',
  'The “hindsight” rationale (Quillen Decl. ¶ 36: retroactive election “may suggest that the election was made with the benefit of hindsight regarding the fund\'s anticipated investment activity”) is impossible on these facts: on January 28, 2020, Fund V had no portfolio, no investments, and no track record. Indeed, the outcome proves the point — Fund V realized nothing in 2020 (Issue A-3).',
  'Caution: HCP\'s own compiled summary marks this election “No” and describes it as “twenty-eight days after the commencement of the fiscal year beginning January 1, 2020,” and the Form recites a fiscal year “commencing January 1, 2020” and a representation (§ 5(a)) that the election was made “prior to the commencement of the fiscal year.” We cannot dispute the date, and the form\'s internal recitals are imperfect.'],
 'Significant',
 'This is the only election with any timing issue. Properly framed, it is a drafting artifact rather than evidence of hindsight. Improperly framed (e.g., denying it was late), it would cost credibility, because our own documents concede the date.',
 ['Concede the execution date; reframe its significance. Argue that the relevant period for prospectivity is the period during which services were rendered and fees accrued, which could not begin before Fund V\'s formation on February 1, 2020.',
  'Confirm with HCP: Fund V\'s first closing date, LPA execution date, management fee commencement date, first capital call, and first investment date. If no fees accrued before February 1, 2020, obtain a declaration to that effect.',
  'Coordinate with the penalty analysis: the Ridgeline Opinion expressly says it “should not be relied upon for any waiver election that is not timely executed” (see Issue D-10).']
)

issue('A-3', 'The Brief Asserts That Fund V Had “Substantial Capital Gains Activity” in 2020; the Government\'s Own Exhibit 4 Shows Zero Realized Gains',
 ['SUMF ¶ 25: Fund V “had substantial capital gains activity during Tax Year 2020, providing the basis for the $6,000,000 priority allocation to HCP.”',
  'Arg. IV.C.2 (“Fourth”): “[A]ll three Funds generated substantial capital gains during the relevant tax years . . . . HCP\'s decision to participate in the waiver program only when the Funds had sufficient realized gains . . . further evidences the tax-driven nature of the arrangement.”'],
 ['Quillen Decl. ¶ 40 and Ex. 4: Fund V realized **$0** in gains (short- or long-term) and $0 in losses in TY 2020; its portfolio was entirely unrealized; the ~$41 million of unrealized appreciation was “subsequently written down in Q2 2021.” ¶ 41: the $6,000,000 allocation “could not have been satisfied from realized gains” and was carried forward. ¶ 44: the Fund V allocation “remained unsatisfied.” Ashford Decl. ¶¶ 22–23, 47 agree.',
  'The Brief\'s own carried-interest section contradicts SUMF ¶ 25, describing Fund V as having no “realized investment returns” and a “nonexistent” track record (Arg. IV.B).',
  'Substantively, Fund V is the only fund-year in which the contingency was tested, and HCP lost: it gave up $6,000,000 of fee income that would have been payable regardless of performance and received nothing in 2020, with the unrealized gains that might have funded a future allocation written down months later.'],
 'Critical',
 'This misstatement goes to the heart of the entrepreneurial-risk inquiry (the primary factor under Prop. Treas. Reg. § 1.707-2(c)) and to the objective prong of § 7701(o)(1)(A). The government\'s own declarant establishes, at a minimum, a genuine dispute about whether HCP bore meaningful risk.',
 ['Make Fund V the centerpiece of the risk argument: “The one time the contingency was tested, HCP lost.” Quote Quillen ¶¶ 40–41 and Ex. 4 verbatim.',
  'Use the point to rebut the “calibration” theory (Issue C-5) and Professor Ashford\'s claim that the carry-forward converted risk into “timing” (Issue D-4).',
  'Before relying on it, resolve the TY 2020 reporting problem discussed at Issue D-8; we must be able to explain why HCP reported the $6,000,000 as long-term capital gain.']
)

issue('A-4', 'The Brief Invents a “Compounding Return Equal to the Applicable Federal Rate” and Misstates the Carry-Forward as Having “No Expiration”',
 ['SUMF ¶ 11: “There was no expiration date on the carry-forward, and the unfulfilled amount accumulated with a compounding return equal to the applicable federal rate.”',
  'Repeated in Factor (1) (“with no expiration date and with a compounding return at the applicable federal rate”), Factor (2) (“the Carry-Forward Provision with its compounding return at the applicable federal rate further underscored the preferential nature”; HCP “occupied a creditor-like position”), Factor (6) (“Unfulfilled allocations were carried forward indefinitely and accrued a compounding return”), and Arg. IV.B (“carried forward indefinitely with a compounding return”).'],
 ['Section 4 of every Election Form provides only that an unfulfilled amount carries forward and is satisfied from future net long-term capital gains “until fully allocated,” and that the carry-forward “shall remain an obligation of the Fund until the Priority Allocation has been satisfied in its entirety **or until the dissolution and final liquidation of the Fund, whichever occurs first**.” There is no interest, no AFR accrual, and no compounding.',
  'The Ridgeline Opinion (§ II.F; § III.B.3) confirms: no acceleration, no cash settlement, no payment from any source other than realized long-term capital gains; unfulfilled amounts “expire unsatisfied” on liquidation.',
  'Neither of the government\'s declarants supports the AFR term. Quillen Decl. ¶ 23 and Ashford Decl. ¶¶ 16, 40 describe the carry-forward without any return. (Their statement that it had “no stated expiration” is itself inaccurate in light of the liquidation cut-off.)'],
 'Critical',
 'The AFR “return” is the sole factual basis for the Brief\'s “preferred return” and “creditor-like” characterizations (Factor 2) and a principal support for the “no ceiling” argument (Factor 6). Without it, the carry-forward is an unsecured, non-interest-bearing, subordinated-to-realization, expiring contingent right — which is the antithesis of a debt claim. This misstatement also damages the government\'s credibility because the operative documents are short and unambiguous.',
 ['Quote § 4 of an Election Form in full in the Counterstatement and the argument. Point out that no declarant supports the AFR assertion.',
  'Emphasize the liquidation cut-off: a fund that winds up without sufficient net long-term capital gains extinguishes the claim. Ask Dr. Chu to model the time value cost of an interest-free deferral (even a fully satisfied carry-forward is economically worth less than the waived fee).',
  'Confirm with HCP and Ridgeline that the LPA amendments (Ex. 6) contain no different or additional carry-forward terms (e.g., an interest accrual) that the government may have drawn on.']
)

issue('A-5', 'The Brief Wrongly Asserts That Only a “Total and Permanent Loss” of Fund Capital Could Defeat the Priority Allocation',
 ['SUMF ¶ 12: “barring a total and permanent loss of a Fund\'s invested capital, HCP would eventually receive the full dollar amount.” Factor (1): “The only circumstance under which HCP would fail to receive the full priority allocation was if a Fund suffered a total and permanent loss of all invested capital.”'],
 ['The allocation is payable only from “net long-term capital gains (as defined under Section 1222)” (Election Forms § 3). A fund can lose money, merely return its capital, realize only short-term gains or ordinary income, or have net capital losses in its remaining years — any of which defeats the allocation without a “total loss.” Because the claim expires at liquidation, a fund with a 0.9x or 1.0x outcome would never satisfy it.',
  'The Brief\'s own description of Fund III as a “below-median” “difficult” vintage (SUMF ¶ 25; Quillen Decl. ¶ 13) and the Fund V write-down (Ex. 4) show that sub-par outcomes are realistic, not “catastrophic.”'],
 'Significant',
 'This overstatement is the predicate for the conclusion that risk was “negligible” (Factor 1). Correcting it reframes the risk question as an ordinary investment-performance question, which is quintessentially factual.',
 ['Have Dr. Chu quantify, at each election date, the probability that each Fund would fail to generate sufficient net long-term capital gains over its remaining life, using vintage-year dispersion data (the government\'s own Preqin/McKinsey sources can be used for this purpose).',
  'Cite the Election Forms\' § 5(b) representation that HCP “assumes the entrepreneurial risk that the Priority Allocation may never be satisfied in whole or in part.”']
)
