 ['SUMF ¶ 25: Fund III\'s $298 million of realized net gains “represented a net multiple on invested capital of approximately 0.36x on total committed capital, a below-median performance” “as of the end of Tax Year 2020.” Arg. IV.B: “a net multiple of approximately 0.36x.” Ashford Decl. ¶ 21: Fund IV “net multiple of approximately 0.55x.”'],
 ['0.36 is simply $298M ÷ $820M — a ratio of realized *gains* to *committed* capital. A multiple on invested capital (MOIC) measures total value returned (including return of capital) against capital invested; a fund with $298 million of net gains on fully invested capital would have a MOIC of roughly 1.36x, not 0.36x. The phrase “net multiple on invested capital . . . on total committed capital” is internally incoherent. The same error infects Ashford\'s 0.55x for Fund IV ($742M ÷ $1.35B).',
  'The measurement date is inconsistent: “as of the end of Tax Year 2020” (Brief), “as of the close of its investment period on June 1, 2019” (Ashford Decl. ¶ 20), and “[b]y the close of the examination period” (Quillen Decl. ¶ 13). The Brief also cites Ex. 10 (internal emails) for these figures.'],
 'Minor',
 'The mislabeling does not change the outcome of any legal issue, but it suggests the government does not understand the performance data on which its “below-median” narrative depends, and a sub-1.0x multiple implies a loss that did not occur.',
 ['Correct the metric in the Counterstatement; have Dr. Chu state Fund III\'s actual MOIC, TVPI, and DPI. Avoid overplaying — a short footnote suffices.',
  'Do not contest the judicial notice request for the Preqin/McKinsey data (Part VIII); contest only the inference.']
)

issue('A-8', 'The Brief Attributes Fund IV\'s Subscription Credit Facility to Fund V',
 ['SUMF ¶ 25 & n.7: “Fund V utilized a subscription credit facility provided by Greystone National Bank . . . . Quillen Decl. ¶ 33; Ex. 13.”'],
 ['Quillen Decl. ¶¶ 78–80 and Ex. 13: the Greystone facility is between **Fund IV**, as borrower, and Greystone, entered December 1, 2017 and amended June 15, 2019 and January 10, 2020. There is no Fund V facility in the record.'],
 'Minor',
 'Low substantive impact, but it is another verifiable inaccuracy and it bears on the government\'s apparent intent to argue that the facility “integrated” the waiver into fund finance (Quillen Decl. ¶ 79).',
 ['Note in the Counterstatement. Separately review Ex. 13 in full (see Issue D-11) before the government reframes the borrowing base disclosure as credit support.']
)

issue('A-9', 'The Brief Misidentifies HCP\'s Partnership Representative and Uses Repealed TEFRA Terminology',
 ['Prelim. Stmt.: “Notice of the FPAA was served on Diane K. Sato, Tax Matters Partner of HCP.” SUMF ¶ 7: “Diane K. Sato served as HCP\'s Tax Matters Partner during the tax years at issue.” Quillen Decl. ¶¶ 11, 59.'],
 ['All three years are governed by the BBA centralized partnership audit regime (tax years beginning after December 31, 2017). The “tax matters partner” role was repealed for those years; the BBA requires a **partnership representative** (§ 6223). Exhibit 7 (TY 2018 Form 1065, p. 5) designates “Partnership Representative: **Elliot R. Hargrove**.” Quillen herself acknowledges the PR designation (¶¶ 12, 47) while simultaneously asserting that Sato was TMP “since the entity\'s formation in 2014” (¶ 11) and that all notices “including the [FPAA] were served upon Ms. Sato in her capacity as Tax Matters Partner” (¶ 59).'],
 'Significant',
 'Standing alone this is a terminology error, but it signals that the IRS may have run this examination under TEFRA procedures and supports the procedural and limitations arguments at Issue B-14. Its ultimate weight depends on facts we must confirm (to whom the FPA was actually mailed; PR designations for TY 2019 and TY 2020).',
 ['Raise it as part of the procedural-validity argument (Issue B-14), not as a stand-alone point.',
  'Pull the TY 2019 and TY 2020 Forms 1065 to confirm the PR designation for each year and confirm whether any designation was revoked or changed.']
)

issue('A-10', 'The Brief Misstates Who Owns the Funds\' General Partners',
 ['SUMF ¶¶ 3–4: Hargrove GP III LLC and Hargrove GP IV LLC are “wholly owned and controlled by Hargrove and Sato.” Ashford Decl. ¶ 12 (GPs “controlled by Messrs. Hargrove and Sato”).'],
 ['Quillen Decl. ¶¶ 13–15: each GP (III, IV and V) is “a Delaware limited liability company **wholly owned by HCP**.” The Ridgeline Opinion (§ III.A.2, Factors 2 and 6) likewise treats HCP as a partner in the Funds “through its affiliated general partner entities.”'],
 'Significant',
 'HCP\'s status as a partner of each Fund is a predicate of the government\'s own theories (§ 707(a)(2)(A) applies only where “a partner performs services”; § 707(c) applies only to payments “to a partner”), and of HCP\'s position that the priority allocations are distributive shares under § 702(b). The government\'s version (GPs owned by the individuals) would undermine both sides\' frameworks and is contradicted by its declarant.',
 ['Correct the record using Ex. 3 (organizational chart) and the GP LLC agreements, and establish that each GP is a single-member LLC owned by HCP and disregarded for tax purposes (confirm no Form 8832 election). Frame this affirmatively (HCP is a partner with a continuing interest in Fund profits and losses, including its carried interest) rather than as a “gotcha.”',
  'Confirm whether the priority allocations were made to HCP directly or to the GP as HCP\'s designee (Election Forms § 3 permits either), and conform our characterization.']
)

issue('A-11', 'The Brief Refers to “Waiver Side Letters” That Do Not Exist',
 ['SUMF ¶ 10: the program terms are “set forth in the side letters executed between HCP and each Fund (collectively, the ‘Waiver Side Letters’).” SUMF ¶ 11 (“The Waiver Side Letters contained a ‘carry-forward’ or ‘make-whole’ provision”).'],
 ['The operative instruments are the Election Forms (executed under § 8.4(b) of each Fund\'s LPA) and the LPA amendments (Quillen Decl. ¶ 24; Ex. 6). The Ridgeline Opinion\'s analysis expressly assumes there is no “guarantee, indemnity, side letter, or other contractual mechanism” supporting the allocation (§ II.H; § IV). The government\'s declarant never uses the term “side letter.”'],
 'Significant',
 'The label is not harmless: in private fund practice “side letters” connote bespoke, off-LPA arrangements, and the Ridgeline Opinion and *Pinnacle* both treat side arrangements and credit support as decisive. An uncorrected reference could become a “fact” in the Court\'s opinion.',
 ['Respond to SUMF ¶¶ 10–11 as “Disputed” and identify the actual instruments. Confirm with HCP that no side letters relating to the waiver program exist with any LP (if any LP side letters mention the program, we need to know now).']
)

issue('A-12', 'The Brief Dates the Program to 2016, Contradicting the Government\'s Declarant and the Ridgeline Opinion',
 ['SUMF ¶ 9: “Beginning in 2016, HCP implemented a management fee waiver program.” Ashford Decl. ¶ 14 (same) and ¶ 74 (“HCP elected to waive fees in every year from 2016 through the tax years at issue”).'],
 ['Quillen Decl. ¶ 65: the Ridgeline Opinion “was obtained by HCP prior to the execution of any management fee waiver elections,” and “the earliest waiver elections (for TY 2018) were executed on December 15, 2017.” The Ridgeline Opinion (November 1, 2017) describes a “proposed” program with initial elections “expected to be executed in December 2017.” Fund IV did not exist until September 2017. Quillen ¶ 21 refers to “late 2016,” an internal inconsistency within the government\'s own record.'],
 'Minor',
 'The point matters chiefly because Professor Ashford\'s “routine and repeated annually” theory (¶ 74) depends on a multi-year history the record does not support.',
 ['Confirm with HCP that no waivers were made before TY 2018 (if any 2016 or 2017 waivers exist, we need the documents immediately). If confirmed, use the point to impeach Ashford ¶ 74 as lacking foundation.']
)

issue('A-13', 'The Brief Overstates the Absence of Limited Partner Involvement',
 ['SUMF ¶ 21: “No limited partners of the Funds participated in the waiver decisions. . . . The limited partnership agreements of each Fund authorized the general partner . . . to approve such arrangements without limited partner consent.” (citing Quillen Decl. ¶ 27).'],
 ['Each Election Form § 5(c) provides that an election is irrevocable and “may not be modified, amended, or rescinded without the prior written consent of the General Partner **and the Advisory Committee of the Fund**.” The priority allocation mechanism was “authorized by amendments to the LPAs” (Quillen Decl. ¶¶ 21, 24; Ex. 6); an amendment giving the manager a first-dollar priority over LP capital gains ordinarily requires LP consent. The program was disclosed to Fund IV\'s lender (Quillen Decl. ¶ 79). Quillen ¶ 27 (cited) says nothing about LP involvement.'],
 'Significant',
 'LP and Advisory Committee involvement is evidence of arm\'s-length dealing, of genuine economic effect on the LPs (Issue C-6), and of a non-tax business purpose (LP alignment). It also undercuts the “paper exercise” theme.',
 ['Obtain the LPA amendment consent records, any LPAC minutes or consents, and LP communications describing the program (annual meeting materials, quarterly letters, fundraising materials for Fund V). Use them in the Counterstatement; dispute SUMF ¶ 21.']
)

issue('A-14', 'The Brief Misstates the Business Purposes HCP Identified',
 ['Arg. IV.C.2 (“First”): “HCP has never articulated any business justification . . . other than tax savings. . . . HCP\'s responses . . . cited only ‘alignment of interests’ . . . . Quillen Decl. ¶ 44.”'],
 ['Quillen Decl. ¶ 44 says nothing about HCP\'s stated business purposes. The Ridgeline Opinion, which HCP produced and cited in its protest (Quillen Decl. ¶¶ 60, 70), identifies three non-tax purposes: alignment of interests, LP relations and fundraising, and capital efficiency (§ III.C.3). HCP\'s protest argued that the allocations were “subject to entrepreneurial risk” (Quillen Decl. ¶ 60). The government\'s own footnote 8 concedes that fee waivers are “increasingly common” among “a significant number of mid-market and large-cap fund managers.”'],
 'Significant',
 'Business purpose is a fact issue on which the government bears the summary-judgment burden of showing no genuine dispute. Mischaracterizing HCP\'s stated purposes, with a citation that does not support the point, invites the Court to find a dispute.',
 ['Submit declarations from Hargrove and Sato (and ideally an LP or placement agent) describing the non-tax reasons for the program, contemporaneous LP communications, and Fund V fundraising materials. Use footnote 8\'s industry-practice concession affirmatively.']
)

issue('A-15', 'Mr. Hargrove\'s Professional Background Is Asserted Without Record Support',
 ['SUMF ¶ 6; Arg. IV.C.2 (“Third”) & n.14; Part V.B.4: Hargrove “practiced as a tax attorney at Thornfield & Locke LLP . . . for approximately eight years.”'],
 ['The only citations (Quillen Decl. ¶ 9; Ex. 5) concern HCP\'s formation and the Election Forms. Nothing in the Quillen or Ashford Declarations addresses Mr. Hargrove\'s background.'],
 'Minor',
 'As a matter of evidence, the assertion is unsupported and may be disregarded on summary judgment. But the underlying fact (if accurate) is legitimately relevant to the penalty inquiry and has serious internal implications for this firm (Issue D-12).',
 ['In the Counterstatement, respond “Disputed — no record support,” without denying the fact if it is true. Do **not** argue that a taxpayer\'s expertise is irrelevant to reasonable cause; it is a standard factor (Part VIII).']
)

issue('A-16', 'The Brief Overstates the Scope of the “Conversion”: HCP Waived Only Part of Its Fees and Reported the Rest as Ordinary Income',
 ['Prelim. Stmt.; SUMF ¶ 18: waived amounts “tracked the growth in management fees payable to HCP as the Funds increased in size.” Arg. IV.C.3: the arrangement “did not change the amount of compensation HCP received.”'],
 ['Quillen Decl. ¶ 46: the TY 2018 return reported ordinary management fee income for “fees that were not subject to waiver elections.” Using the government\'s 2.0% investment-period rate (Quillen Decl. ¶ 18), Fund IV\'s annual fee alone was roughly $27 million, of which $5.2 million was waived for 2018. Waived amounts also *fell* in 2020 ($16.362M) from 2019 ($18.85M) even though Fund V ($1.75B) was added — the opposite of “tracking growth.” And for Fund V in 2020, HCP\'s compensation demonstrably *did* change: it received nothing in place of $6 million of fees.'],
 'Minor',
 'Useful color showing that the program was a calibrated, partial at-risk commitment rather than wholesale relabeling of fee income.',
 ['Have HCP\'s CFO prepare a schedule of fees earned, waived, and collected by Fund and year (confirm fee base and rates). Use sparingly in the business purpose discussion.']
)
PYEOF
echo ok
OUTER
)"
input.description: Write Category A factual errors script

toolu_01R6Ctb1Jt3dzfxVZo539Qsk.command:
S=/home/user/Lawless_Research_Lab/harvey_lab/sbx.sh; R=/home/user/Lawless_Research_Lab/harvey_lab/vendor/harvey-labs/results/tax/identify-tax-issues-in-counterpartys-summary-judgment-brief/claude-code-session/20261016-025653; $S $R "$(cat <<'OUTER'
cat > /workspace/build/part3.py <<'PYEOF'
H('IV. Category (A): Factual Errors', 1)

issue('A-1', 'The Brief Misdates the Fund IV TY 2020 Election and Conflates It with the Fund V Election',
 ['SUMF \u00b6 17: \u201cBoth the Fund IV and Fund V waiver elections for Tax Year 2020 were executed after the start of the fiscal year. . . . [T]he Fund IV election was likewise executed after the commencement of the 2020 fiscal year.\u201d',
  'Arg. IV.C.2 (\u201cSecond\u201d): \u201cThe TY 2020 elections for both Fund IV and Fund V were executed after the commencement of the fiscal year, demonstrating that the waivers were retroactive adjustments rather than genuine prospective business decisions.\u201d See also n.13.'],
 ['The Fund IV TY 2020 election (Form HCP-2020-IV-005) was executed on **December 10, 2019**, three weeks before the fiscal year began. The government\'s own exhibit list says so: Quillen Decl. \u00b6 89, Ex. 5-E (\u201cDate: December 10, 2019. Countersigned by Hargrove GP IV LLC\u201d). HCP\'s compiled summary marks it \u201cExecuted Prior to Fiscal Year Start: Yes.\u201d',
  'Quillen herself never claims the Fund IV election was late. Her \u00b6 32 omits the date, and \u00b6 34 contrasts *only* the Fund V election with \u201cthe TY 2018 and TY 2019 elections.\u201d The January 15, 2020 Greystone borrowing base certificate already referenced the TY 2020 election (Quillen Decl. \u00b6 79), which is independent third-party corroboration that the Fund IV election existed at the start of the year.',
  'The Brief notably gives a specific date for Fund V but none for Fund IV (\u201clikewise executed after\u201d), which suggests counsel inferred rather than checked.'],
 'Critical',
 'The \u201cretroactive election\u201d theme is a pillar of the economic substance argument (Arg. IV.C.2) and the timing argument under the Treas. Reg. \u00a7 1.707-2 framework (n.13). Correcting the record confines any timing argument to a single election worth $6,000,000 (12.6% of the adjustment) and leaves $41,612,000 (87.4%) indisputably prospective. It is also a clean, document-based credibility hit that the Court can verify in seconds.',
 ['Lead the Counterstatement of Facts with an election-by-election table (Part III.A above) citing Exs. 5-A through 5-F and the Election Forms. Characterize the error precisely and without hyperbole: the government \u201cconflated\u201d two elections with different execution dates.',
  'In the argument, use the corrected facts to show that the government\'s own legal standard (n.13: a genuine waiver \u201cmust be made before the period to which it relates\u201d) is satisfied for every election except Fund V, which is addressed separately (Issue A-2).',
  'Obtain a short declaration from HCP\'s CFO or the GP IV signatory authenticating the December 10, 2019 execution and delivery to the GP.']
)

issue('A-2', 'The Brief\'s Characterization of the Fund V Election as \u201cRetroactive\u201d Ignores That Fund V Did Not Exist Until February 1, 2020',
 ['SUMF \u00b6 17: the Fund V election \u201cwas signed on January 28, 2020, twenty-eight days into the fiscal year.\u201d Arg. IV.C.2: \u201cThis retroactive timing is inconsistent with a genuine pre-commitment to accept investment risk and is instead consistent with a post hoc adjustment.\u201d'],
 ['The government\'s own SUMF \u00b6 5 and Quillen Decl. \u00b6 15 state that Fund V was formed on **February 1, 2020**. The Election Form itself recites that Fund V was \u201cformed on February 1, 2020\u201d and that its LPA was \u201cto be dated on or about February 1, 2020.\u201d The election therefore preceded the Fund\'s legal existence, its LPA, any capital call, any investment, and any accrual of management fees. A partnership cannot have a taxable year that begins before it exists [cite-check: Treas. Reg. \u00a7 1.708-1 / \u00a7 1.6031(a)-1 regarding commencement of partnership taxable year].',
  'The \u201chindsight\u201d rationale (Quillen Decl. \u00b6 36: retroactive election \u201cmay suggest that the election was made with the benefit of hindsight regarding the fund\'s anticipated investment activity\u201d) is impossible on these facts: on January 28, 2020, Fund V had no portfolio, no investments, and no track record. Indeed, the outcome proves the point \u2014 Fund V realized nothing in 2020 (Issue A-3).',
  'Caution: HCP\'s own compiled summary marks this election \u201cNo\u201d and describes it as \u201ctwenty-eight days after the commencement of the fiscal year beginning January 1, 2020,\u201d and the Form recites a fiscal year \u201ccommencing January 1, 2020\u201d and a representation (\u00a7 5(a)) that the election was made \u201cprior to the commencement of the fiscal year.\u201d We cannot dispute the date, and the form\'s internal recitals are imperfect.'],
 'Significant',
 'This is the only election with any timing issue. Properly framed, it is a drafting artifact rather than evidence of hindsight. Improperly framed (e.g., denying it was late), it would cost credibility, because our own documents concede the date.',
 ['Concede the execution date; reframe its significance. Argue that the relevant period for prospectivity is the period during which services were rendered and fees accrued, which could not begin before Fund V\'s formation on February 1, 2020.',
  'Confirm with HCP: Fund V\'s first closing date, LPA execution date, management fee commencement date, first capital call, and first investment date. If no fees accrued before February 1, 2020, obtain a declaration to that effect.',
  'Coordinate with the penalty analysis: the Ridgeline Opinion expressly says it \u201cshould not be relied upon for any waiver election that is not timely executed\u201d (see Issue D-10).']
)

issue('A-3', 'The Brief Asserts That Fund V Had \u201cSubstantial Capital Gains Activity\u201d in 2020; the Government\'s Own Exhibit 4 Shows Zero Realized Gains',
 ['SUMF \u00b6 25: Fund V \u201chad substantial capital gains activity during Tax Year 2020, providing the basis for the $6,000,000 priority allocation to HCP.\u201d',
  'Arg. IV.C.2 (\u201cFourth\u201d): \u201c[A]ll three Funds generated substantial capital gains during the relevant tax years . . . . HCP\'s decision to participate in the waiver program only when the Funds had sufficient realized gains . . . further evidences the tax-driven nature of the arrangement.\u201d'],
 ['Quillen Decl. \u00b6 40 and Ex. 4: Fund V realized **$0** in gains (short- or long-term) and $0 in losses in TY 2020; its portfolio was entirely unrealized; the ~$41 million of unrealized appreciation was \u201csubsequently written down in Q2 2021.\u201d \u00b6 41: the $6,000,000 allocation \u201ccould not have been satisfied from realized gains\u201d and was carried forward. \u00b6 44: the Fund V allocation \u201cremained unsatisfied.\u201d Ashford Decl. \u00b6\u00b6 22\u201323, 47 agree.',
  'The Brief\'s own carried-interest section contradicts SUMF \u00b6 25, describing Fund V as having no \u201crealized investment returns\u201d and a \u201cnonexistent\u201d track record (Arg. IV.B).',
  'Substantively, Fund V is the only fund-year in which the contingency was tested, and HCP lost: it gave up $6,000,000 of fee income that would have been payable regardless of performance and received nothing in 2020, with the unrealized gains that might have funded a future allocation written down months later.'],
 'Critical',
 'This misstatement goes to the heart of the entrepreneurial-risk inquiry (the primary factor under Prop. Treas. Reg. \u00a7 1.707-2(c)) and to the objective prong of \u00a7 7701(o)(1)(A). The government\'s own declarant establishes, at a minimum, a genuine dispute about whether HCP bore meaningful risk.',
 ['Make Fund V the centerpiece of the risk argument: \u201cThe one time the contingency was tested, HCP lost.\u201d Quote Quillen \u00b6\u00b6 40\u201341 and Ex. 4 verbatim.',
  'Use the point to rebut the \u201ccalibration\u201d theory (Issue C-5) and Professor Ashford\'s claim that the carry-forward converted risk into \u201ctiming\u201d (Issue D-4).',
  'Before relying on it, resolve the TY 2020 reporting problem discussed at Issue D-8; we must be able to explain why HCP reported the $6,000,000 as long-term capital gain.']
)

issue('A-4', 'The Brief Invents a \u201cCompounding Return Equal to the Applicable Federal Rate\u201d and Misstates the Carry-Forward as Having \u201cNo Expiration\u201d',
 ['SUMF \u00b6 11: \u201cThere was no expiration date on the carry-forward, and the unfulfilled amount accumulated with a compounding return equal to the applicable federal rate.\u201d',
  'Repeated in Factor (1) (\u201cwith no expiration date and with a compounding return at the applicable federal rate\u201d), Factor (2) (\u201cthe Carry-Forward Provision with its compounding return at the applicable federal rate further underscored the preferential nature\u201d; HCP \u201coccupied a creditor-like position\u201d), Factor (6) (\u201cUnfulfilled allocations were carried forward indefinitely and accrued a compounding return\u201d), and Arg. IV.B (\u201ccarried forward indefinitely with a compounding return\u201d).'],
 ['Section 4 of every Election Form provides only that an unfulfilled amount carries forward and is satisfied from future net long-term capital gains \u201cuntil fully allocated,\u201d and that the carry-forward \u201cshall remain an obligation of the Fund until the Priority Allocation has been satisfied in its entirety **or until the dissolution and final liquidation of the Fund, whichever occurs first**.\u201d There is no interest, no AFR accrual, and no compounding.',
  'The Ridgeline Opinion (\u00a7 II.F; \u00a7 III.B.3) confirms: no acceleration, no cash settlement, no payment from any source other than realized long-term capital gains; unfulfilled amounts \u201cexpire unsatisfied\u201d on liquidation.',
  'Neither of the government\'s declarants supports the AFR term. Quillen Decl. \u00b6 23 and Ashford Decl. \u00b6\u00b6 16, 40 describe the carry-forward without any return. (Their statement that it had \u201cno stated expiration\u201d is itself inaccurate in light of the liquidation cut-off.)'],
 'Critical',
 'The AFR \u201creturn\u201d is the sole factual basis for the Brief\'s \u201cpreferred return\u201d and \u201ccreditor-like\u201d characterizations (Factor 2) and a principal support for the \u201cno ceiling\u201d argument (Factor 6). Without it, the carry-forward is an unsecured, non-interest-bearing, subordinated-to-realization, expiring contingent right \u2014 which is the antithesis of a debt claim. This misstatement also damages the government\'s credibility because the operative documents are short and unambiguous.',
 ['Quote \u00a7 4 of an Election Form in full in the Counterstatement and the argument. Point out that no declarant supports the AFR assertion.',
  'Emphasize the liquidation cut-off: a fund that winds up without sufficient net long-term capital gains extinguishes the claim. Ask Dr. Chu to model the time value cost of an interest-free deferral (even a fully satisfied carry-forward is economically worth less than the waived fee).',
  'Confirm with HCP and Ridgeline that the LPA amendments (Ex. 6) contain no different or additional carry-forward terms (e.g., an interest accrual) that the government may have drawn on.']
)

issue('A-5', 'The Brief Wrongly Asserts That Only a \u201cTotal and Permanent Loss\u201d of Fund Capital Could Defeat the Priority Allocation',
 ['SUMF \u00b6 12: \u201cbarring a total and permanent loss of a Fund\'s invested capital, HCP would eventually receive the full dollar amount.\u201d Factor (1): \u201cThe only circumstance under which HCP would fail to receive the full priority allocation was if a Fund suffered a total and permanent loss of all invested capital.\u201d'],
 ['The allocation is payable only from \u201cnet long-term capital gains (as defined under Section 1222)\u201d (Election Forms \u00a7 3). A fund can lose money, merely return its capital, realize only short-term gains or ordinary income, or have net capital losses in its remaining years \u2014 any of which defeats the allocation without a \u201ctotal loss.\u201d Because the claim expires at liquidation, a fund with a 0.9x or 1.0x outcome would never satisfy it.',
  'The Brief\'s own description of Fund III as a \u201cbelow-median\u201d \u201cdifficult\u201d vintage (SUMF \u00b6 25; Quillen Decl. \u00b6 13) and the Fund V write-down (Ex. 4) show that sub-par outcomes are realistic, not \u201ccatastrophic.\u201d'],
 'Significant',
 'This overstatement is the predicate for the conclusion that risk was \u201cnegligible\u201d (Factor 1). Correcting it reframes the risk question as an ordinary investment-performance question, which is quintessentially factual.',
 ['Have Dr. Chu quantify, at each election date, the probability that each Fund would fail to generate sufficient net long-term capital gains over its remaining life, using vintage-year dispersion data (the government\'s own Preqin/McKinsey sources can be used for this purpose).',
  'Cite the Election Forms\' \u00a7 5(b) representation that HCP \u201cassumes the entrepreneurial risk that the Priority Allocation may never be satisfied in whole or in part.\u201d']
)

issue('A-6', 'The Brief Says the Carry-Forward \u201cEnsured\u201d Fund III Shortfalls Were Satisfied; the Government\'s Declarant Says There Were No Fund III Shortfalls',
 ['SUMF \u00b6 26: \u201cNotwithstanding Fund III\'s relatively modest returns, HCP received the full amount of the priority profit allocations attributable to Fund III waiver elections. The Carry-Forward Provision ensured that any shortfall . . . was carried forward and eventually satisfied from subsequent gains.\u201d (citing Quillen Decl. \u00b6 34).'],
 ['Quillen Decl. \u00b6 42: Fund III\'s allocations \u201cwere funded from actual realized long-term capital gains of the fund\u201d in TY 2018 and TY 2019, and \u201cthe priority allocations in both years were allocated from realized long-term capital gains.\u201d \u00b6 43 says the same for Fund IV. The carry-forward was never triggered for Fund III or Fund IV. The only carry-forward in the record is Fund V\'s, which remains unsatisfied.',
  'The cited paragraph (\u00b6 34) concerns the Fund V election date.'],
 'Significant',
 'The government uses Fund III to argue that the carry-forward \u201cguaranteed\u201d payment even for a poor performer. The record shows no such thing; the carry-forward has never paid HCP a dollar.',
 ['Point out that the carry-forward\'s \u201cguarantee\u201d function is entirely hypothetical on this record, and that the one actual carry-forward (Fund V) remains unpaid.',
  'Pair with the ex ante/ex post methodological critique of Professor Ashford (Issue D-4).']
)

issue('A-7', 'Fund III and Fund IV Performance Metrics Are Mislabeled and Inconsistently Dated',
 ['SUMF \u00b6 25: Fund III\'s $298 million of realized net gains \u201crepresented a net multiple on invested capital of approximately 0.36x on total committed capital, a below-median performance\u201d \u201cas of the end of Tax Year 2020.\u201d Arg. IV.B: \u201ca net multiple of approximately 0.36x.\u201d Ashford Decl. \u00b6 21: Fund IV \u201cnet multiple of approximately 0.55x.\u201d'],
 ['0.36 is simply $298M \u00f7 $820M \u2014 a ratio of realized *gains* to *committed* capital. A multiple on invested capital (MOIC) measures total value returned (including return of capital) against capital invested; a fund with $298 million of net gains on fully invested capital would have a MOIC of roughly 1.36x, not 0.36x. The phrase \u201cnet multiple on invested capital . . . on total committed capital\u201d is internally incoherent. The same error infects Ashford\'s 0.55x for Fund IV ($742M \u00f7 $1.35B).',
  'The measurement date is inconsistent: \u201cas of the end of Tax Year 2020\u201d (Brief), \u201cas of the close of its investment period on June 1, 2019\u201d (Ashford Decl. \u00b6 20), and \u201c[b]y the close of the examination period\u201d (Quillen Decl. \u00b6 13). The Brief also cites Ex. 10 (internal emails) for these figures.'],
 'Minor',
 'The mislabeling does not change the outcome of any legal issue, but it suggests the government does not understand the performance data on which its \u201cbelow-median\u201d narrative depends, and a sub-1.0x multiple implies a loss that did not occur.',
 ['Correct the metric in the Counterstatement; have Dr. Chu state Fund III\'s actual MOIC, TVPI, and DPI. Avoid overplaying \u2014 a short footnote suffices.',
  'Do not contest the judicial notice request for the Preqin/McKinsey data (Part VIII); contest only the inference.']
)

issue('A-8', 'The Brief Attributes Fund IV\'s Subscription Credit Facility to Fund V',
 ['SUMF \u00b6 25 & n.7: \u201cFund V utilized a subscription credit facility provided by Greystone National Bank . . . . Quillen Decl. \u00b6 33; Ex. 13.\u201d'],
 ['Quillen Decl. \u00b6\u00b6 78\u201380 and Ex. 13: the Greystone facility is between **Fund IV**, as borrower, and Greystone, entered December 1, 2017 and amended June 15, 2019 and January 10, 2020. There is no Fund V facility in the record.'],
 'Minor',
 'Low substantive impact, but it is another verifiable inaccuracy and it bears on the government\'s apparent intent to argue that the facility \u201cintegrated\u201d the waiver into fund finance (Quillen Decl. \u00b6 79).',
 ['Note in the Counterstatement. Separately review Ex. 13 in full (see Issue D-11) before the government reframes the borrowing base disclosure as credit support.']
)

issue('A-9', 'The Brief Misidentifies HCP\'s Partnership Representative and Uses Repealed TEFRA Terminology',
 ['Prelim. Stmt.: \u201cNotice of the FPAA was served on Diane K. Sato, Tax Matters Partner of HCP.\u201d SUMF \u00b6 7: \u201cDiane K. Sato served as HCP\'s Tax Matters Partner during the tax years at issue.\u201d Quillen Decl. \u00b6\u00b6 11, 59.'],
 ['All three years are governed by the BBA centralized partnership audit regime (tax years beginning after December 31, 2017). The \u201ctax matters partner\u201d role was repealed for those years; the BBA requires a **partnership representative** (\u00a7 6223). Exhibit 7 (TY 2018 Form 1065, p. 5) designates \u201cPartnership Representative: **Elliot R. Hargrove**.\u201d Quillen herself acknowledges the PR designation (\u00b6\u00b6 12, 47) while simultaneously asserting that Sato was TMP \u201csince the entity\'s formation in 2014\u201d (\u00b6 11) and that all notices \u201cincluding the [FPAA] were served upon Ms. Sato in her capacity as Tax Matters Partner\u201d (\u00b6 59).'],
 'Significant',
 'Standing alone this is a terminology error, but it signals that the IRS may have run this examination under TEFRA procedures and supports the procedural and limitations arguments at Issue B-14. Its ultimate weight depends on facts we must confirm (to whom the FPA was actually mailed; PR designations for TY 2019 and TY 2020).',
 ['Raise it as part of the procedural-validity argument (Issue B-14), not as a stand-alone point.',
  'Pull the TY 2019 and TY 2020 Forms 1065 to confirm the PR designation for each year and confirm whether any designation was revoked or changed.']
)

issue('A-10', 'The Brief Misstates Who Owns the Funds\' General Partners',
 ['SUMF \u00b6\u00b6 3\u20134: Hargrove GP III LLC and Hargrove GP IV LLC are \u201cwholly owned and controlled by Hargrove and Sato.\u201d Ashford Decl. \u00b6 12 (GPs \u201ccontrolled by Messrs. Hargrove and Sato\u201d).'],
 ['Quillen Decl. \u00b6\u00b6 13\u201315: each GP (III, IV and V) is \u201ca Delaware limited liability company **wholly owned by HCP**.\u201d The Ridgeline Opinion (\u00a7 III.A.2, Factors 2 and 6) likewise treats HCP as a partner in the Funds \u201cthrough its affiliated general partner entities.\u201d'],
 'Significant',
 'HCP\'s status as a partner of each Fund is a predicate of the government\'s own theories (\u00a7 707(a)(2)(A) applies only where \u201ca partner performs services\u201d; \u00a7 707(c) applies only to payments \u201cto a partner\u201d), and of HCP\'s position that the priority allocations are distributive shares under \u00a7 702(b). The government\'s version (GPs owned by the individuals) would undermine both sides\' frameworks and is contradicted by its declarant.',
 ['Correct the record using Ex. 3 (organizational chart) and the GP LLC agreements, and establish that each GP is a single-member LLC owned by HCP and disregarded for tax purposes (confirm no Form 8832 election). Frame this affirmatively (HCP is a partner with a continuing interest in Fund profits and losses, including its carried interest) rather than as a \u201cgotcha.\u201d',
  'Confirm whether the priority allocations were made to HCP directly or to the GP as HCP\'s designee (Election Forms \u00a7 3 permits either), and conform our characterization.']
)

issue('A-11', 'The Brief Refers to \u201cWaiver Side Letters\u201d That Do Not Exist',
 ['SUMF \u00b6 10: the program terms are \u201cset forth in the side letters executed between HCP and each Fund (collectively, the \u2018Waiver Side Letters\u2019).\u201d SUMF \u00b6 11 (\u201cThe Waiver Side Letters contained a \u2018carry-forward\u2019 or \u2018make-whole\u2019 provision\u201d).'],
 ['The operative instruments are the Election Forms (executed under \u00a7 8.4(b) of each Fund\'s LPA) and the LPA amendments (Quillen Decl. \u00b6 24; Ex. 6). The Ridgeline Opinion\'s analysis expressly assumes there is no \u201cguarantee, indemnity, side letter, or other contractual mechanism\u201d supporting the allocation (\u00a7 II.H; \u00a7 IV). The government\'s declarant never uses the term \u201cside letter.\u201d'],
 'Significant',
 'The label is not harmless: in private fund practice \u201cside letters\u201d connote bespoke, off-LPA arrangements, and the Ridgeline Opinion and *Pinnacle* both treat side arrangements and credit support as decisive. An uncorrected reference could become a \u201cfact\u201d in the Court\'s opinion.',
 ['Respond to SUMF \u00b6\u00b6 10\u201311 as \u201cDisputed\u201d and identify the actual instruments. Confirm with HCP that no side letters relating to the waiver program exist with any LP (if any LP side letters mention the program, we need to know now).']
)

issue('A-12', 'The Brief Dates the Program to 2016, Contradicting the Government\'s Declarant and the Ridgeline Opinion',
 ['SUMF \u00b6 9: \u201cBeginning in 2016, HCP implemented a management fee waiver program.\u201d Ashford Decl. \u00b6 14 (same) and \u00b6 74 (\u201cHCP elected to waive fees in every year from 2016 through the tax years at issue\u201d).'],
 ['Quillen Decl. \u00b6 65: the Ridgeline Opinion \u201cwas obtained by HCP prior to the execution of any management fee waiver elections,\u201d and \u201cthe earliest waiver elections (for TY 2018) were executed on December 15, 2017.\u201d The Ridgeline Opinion (November 1, 2017) describes a \u201cproposed\u201d program with initial elections \u201cexpected to be executed in December 2017.\u201d Fund IV did not exist until September 2017. Quillen \u00b6 21 refers to \u201clate 2016,\u201d an internal inconsistency within the government\'s own record.'],
 'Minor',
 'The point matters chiefly because Professor Ashford\'s \u201croutine and repeated annually\u201d theory (\u00b6 74) depends on a multi-year history the record does not support.',
 ['Confirm with HCP that no waivers were made before TY 2018 (if any 2016 or 2017 waivers exist, we need the documents immediately). If confirmed, use the point to impeach Ashford \u00b6 74 as lacking foundation.']
)

issue('A-13', 'The Brief Overstates the Absence of Limited Partner Involvement',
 ['SUMF \u00b6 21: \u201cNo limited partners of the Funds participated in the waiver decisions. . . . The limited partnership agreements of each Fund authorized the general partner . . . to approve such arrangements without limited partner consent.\u201d (citing Quillen Decl. \u00b6 27).'],
 ['Each Election Form \u00a7 5(c) provides that an election is irrevocable and \u201cmay not be modified, amended, or rescinded without the prior written consent of the General Partner **and the Advisory Committee of the Fund**.\u201d The priority allocation mechanism was \u201cauthorized by amendments to the LPAs\u201d (Quillen Decl. \u00b6\u00b6 21, 24; Ex. 6); an amendment giving the manager a first-dollar priority over LP capital gains ordinarily requires LP consent. The program was disclosed to Fund IV\'s lender (Quillen Decl. \u00b6 79). Quillen \u00b6 27 (cited) says nothing about LP involvement.'],
 'Significant',
 'LP and Advisory Committee involvement is evidence of arm\'s-length dealing, of genuine economic effect on the LPs (Issue C-6), and of a non-tax business purpose (LP alignment). It also undercuts the \u201cpaper exercise\u201d theme.',
 ['Obtain the LPA amendment consent records, any LPAC minutes or consents, and LP communications describing the program (annual meeting materials, quarterly letters, fundraising materials for Fund V). Use them in the Counterstatement; dispute SUMF \u00b6 21.']
)

issue('A-14', 'The Brief Misstates the Business Purposes HCP Identified',
 ['Arg. IV.C.2 (\u201cFirst\u201d): \u201cHCP has never articulated any business justification . . . other than tax savings. . . . HCP\'s responses . . . cited only \u2018alignment of interests\u2019 . . . . Quillen Decl. \u00b6 44.\u201d'],
 ['Quillen Decl. \u00b6 44 says nothing about HCP\'s stated business purposes. The Ridgeline Opinion, which HCP produced and cited in its protest (Quillen Decl. \u00b6\u00b6 60, 70), identifies three non-tax purposes: alignment of interests, LP relations and fundraising, and capital efficiency (\u00a7 III.C.3). HCP\'s protest argued that the allocations were \u201csubject to entrepreneurial risk\u201d (Quillen Decl. \u00b6 60). The government\'s own footnote 8 concedes that fee waivers are \u201cincreasingly common\u201d among \u201ca significant number of mid-market and large-cap fund managers.\u201d'],
 'Significant',
 'Business purpose is a fact issue on which the government bears the summary-judgment burden of showing no genuine dispute. Mischaracterizing HCP\'s stated purposes, with a citation that does not support the point, invites the Court to find a dispute.',
 ['Submit declarations from Hargrove and Sato (and ideally an LP or placement agent) describing the non-tax reasons for the program, contemporaneous LP communications, and Fund V fundraising materials. Use footnote 8\'s industry-practice concession affirmatively.']
)

issue('A-15', 'Mr. Hargrove\'s Professional Background Is Asserted Without Record Support',
 ['SUMF \u00b6 6; Arg. IV.C.2 (\u201cThird\u201d) & n.14; Part V.B.4: Hargrove \u201cpracticed as a tax attorney at Thornfield & Locke LLP . . . for approximately eight years.\u201d'],
 ['The only citations (Quillen Decl. \u00b6 9; Ex. 5) concern HCP\'s formation and the Election Forms. Nothing in the Quillen or Ashford Declarations addresses Mr. Hargrove\'s background.'],

 'As a matter of evidence, the assertion is unsupported and may be disregarded on summary judgment. But the underlying fact (if accurate) is legitimately relevant to the penalty inquiry and has serious internal implications for this firm (Issue D-12).',
 ['In the Counterstatement, respond \u201cDisputed \u2014 no record support,\u201d without denying the fact if it is true. Do **not** argue that a taxpayer\'s expertise is irrelevant to reasonable cause; it is a standard factor (Part VIII).']
)

 ['Prelim. Stmt.; SUMF \u00b6 18: waived amounts \u201ctracked the growth in management fees payable to HCP as the Funds increased in size.\u201d Arg. IV.C.3: the arrangement \u201cdid not change the amount of compensation HCP received.\u201d'],
 ['Quillen Decl. \u00b6 46: the TY 2018 return reported ordinary management fee income for \u201cfees that were not subject to waiver elections.\u201d Using the government\'s 2.0% investment-period rate (Quillen Decl. \u00b6 18), Fund IV\'s annual fee alone was roughly $27 million, of which $5.2 million was waived for 2018. issue('B-1', 'The Brief Inverts Rev. Proc. 93-27, Which Provides That Receipt of a Profits Interest Is Generally *Not* a Taxable Event',
 ['Arg. IV.A.4: “[T]he IRS has long recognized that profits interests received in exchange for services are taxed at the time of receipt if they have a determinable value. See Rev. Proc. 93-27, 1993-2 C.B. 343.”',
  'Ashford Decl. ¶¶ 50–55 (Opinion 3): Rev. Proc. 93-27 “establishes that profits interests received in exchange for services are taxed at the time of receipt if they have a determinable value” and “supports the conclusion that the profits interests received in exchange for waived fees should be taxed upon receipt.”'],
 ['Rev. Proc. 93-27 § 4.01 provides that, if a person receives a profits interest for services to or for the benefit of a partnership in a partner capacity, the IRS **will not treat the receipt as a taxable event**. Section 4.02 lists three exceptions: (1) the profits interest relates to a substantially certain and predictable stream of income from partnership assets, *such as income from high-quality debt securities or a high-quality net lease*; (2) the partner disposes of the interest within two years; or (3) the interest is a limited partnership interest in a publicly traded partnership. Rev. Proc. 2001-43 supplements it. The “determinable value” language is not in the revenue procedure; it echoes the pre-1993 *Diamond*/*Campbell* case law that Rev. Proc. 93-27 was issued to address. The Ridgeline Opinion describes Rev. Proc. 93-27 correctly (§ III.D).',
  'Professor Ashford\'s reliance on the first exception is misplaced: it addresses income streams from *partnership assets* of the high-grade-debt/net-lease type, not contingent realized gains from a mid-market buyout portfolio — the paradigm of uncertain income.',
  'When Treasury proposed the § 707(a)(2)(A) regulations in 2015, the preamble announced that the IRS *intended* to issue a revenue procedure adding a new exception to Rev. Proc. 93-27 for profits interests issued in conjunction with a partner forgoing payment of a substantially fixed amount (i.e., fee waivers). 80 Fed. Reg. 43652 (July 23, 2015) [cite-check]. To my knowledge, no such revenue procedure has issued. The government\'s position therefore requires an exception the IRS itself acknowledged does not yet exist.',
  'Even on its own terms, a “taxed at receipt” theory would (i) tax HCP on the fair market value of the interest at grant, not on $47,612,000 of later allocations, and (ii) place the income in the year of grant — e.g., TY 2017 for the December 2017 elections (a year not in the FPAA and outside the BBA regime), TY 2018 for the November 2018 elections, and TY 2019 for the December 2019 Fund IV election. That is irreconcilable with the FPAA\'s adjustments.'],
 'Critical',
 'This is the clearest misstatement of law in the Brief. Exposing that the government and its expert have described an authority as standing for the opposite of what it says will color the Court\'s view of every other legal proposition in the motion, and it eliminates an entire theory (Ashford Opinion 3).',
 ['Quote §§ 4.01–4.02 of Rev. Proc. 93-27 verbatim and juxtapose them with the Brief\'s sentence. Note the 2015 preamble\'s announced (and unissued) fee-waiver exception.',
  'Point out the timing/valuation incoherence of a “taxed at receipt” theory and that it is not the basis of the FPAA (Quillen Decl. ¶ 61).',
  'Tone: measured. One clean paragraph is more effective than rhetoric.']
)

issue('B-2', 'The Brief Misstates the Treas. Reg. § 1.707-2(c) Factors, Omits Factor (4), Imports the § 704(b) “Transitory Allocation” Framework, and Ignores That the Regulation Is Only Proposed',
 ['Arg. IV.A.2: “The Treasury Regulations provide a six-factor test . . . . The government submits that each applicable factor weighs decisively in favor of recharacterization.” The Brief then labels Factors (1), (2), (3), (5) and (6) and, in place of Factor (4), inserts a heading “The Priority Allocations Constitute Transitory Allocations Lacking Substantial Economic Effect,” relying on Treas. Reg. § 1.704-1(b)(2)(iii). Arg. IV.A.5: “Every applicable factor . . . weighs in favor” — listing five.'],
 ['**Status.** Section 1.707-2 is a *proposed* regulation (REG-115452-14, 80 Fed. Reg. 43652 (July 23, 2015)) that has never been finalized. By its terms it would apply to arrangements entered into or modified after final regulations are published [cite-check proposed effective date provision]. Proposed regulations are not binding and receive no deference, although they may be considered for their persuasive value. The Brief repeatedly calls them “the Treasury Regulations” and “the implementing regulations.”',
  '**Content.** Prop. Treas. Reg. § 1.707-2(c) makes **significant entrepreneurial risk** the most important factor ((c)(1)) and then lists five secondary factors: whether the service provider (2) holds a transitory or short-duration interest; (3) receives allocations and distributions in a time frame comparable to a non-partner service provider; (4) became a partner primarily to obtain tax benefits not otherwise available; (5) has a continuing interest in general partnership profits that is small relative to the allocation; and (6) receives different allocations for different services with significantly different entrepreneurial risk [cite-check exact text]. The government\'s Factors (2) (“guaranteed payment or preferred return”), (3) (“converting ordinary income to capital gain”), (5) (“relatively fixed in relation to the services”), and (6) (“subject to a ceiling”) do not appear in the proposed regulation. Several are drawn loosely from the (c)(1) list of facts that create a presumption of insufficient risk, and one is inverted: under the proposed regulation it is a *cap* (“capped allocations . . . if the cap would reasonably be expected to apply in most years”) that signals insufficient risk, so the *absence* of a ceiling cannot support recharacterization.',
  '**Omitted factors favor HCP.** The factors the Brief skips are the ones HCP wins: HCP\'s interest in the Funds (through its wholly owned GPs) is long-term, not transitory; the GPs were partners with carried interests independent of the waiver, so HCP did not “become a partner” to obtain tax benefits; and the value of HCP\'s continuing interest in general Fund profits (including its 20% carry, Ridgeline § III.A.2 Factor 6) is not small relative to the priority allocations.',
  '**Imported framework.** The § 704(b) transitory-allocation rule (Treas. Reg. § 1.704-1(b)(2)(iii)(c)) asks whether an *allocation among partners* is likely to be offset by *subsequent allocations* so that capital accounts end where they would have been. A waived management fee is not a partnership allocation, so it cannot be an “offsetting allocation.” Moreover, the remedy for an allocation lacking substantial economic effect is reallocation in accordance with the partners\' interests in the partnership, not recharacterization of capital gain as ordinary income — and the FPAA made no § 704(b) adjustment (Quillen Decl. ¶ 61). The Ridgeline Opinion specifically warned that the two frameworks are “distinct” and “should not be conflated” (§ III.A.4).'],
 'Critical',
 'The § 707(a)(2)(A) argument is the government\'s lead theory. A Court that sees the government has mis-described the test it asks the Court to apply, omitted the factors that favor the taxpayer, and substituted an unrelated framework is unlikely to find the issue suitable for summary judgment.',
 ['Set out the proposed regulation\'s actual text in a table and walk through each factor, with record citations. Note the regulation\'s proposed status in one sentence, but argue primarily that HCP prevails even under the IRS\'s own proposed standard (see caution below).',
  '**Caution:** the Ridgeline Opinion also cites “Treasury Regulations § 1.707-2(c)” as if final and uses its own, non-textual factor labels (e.g., “clawback,” “reasonably certain”). The opposition should rely on the regulatory text, not on Ridgeline\'s labels, and should not overemphasize the “proposed” point in a way that suggests HCP\'s adviser misunderstood the law. The (c)(1) presumption list also contains facts the government may invoke in reply (see Issue D-3).']
)

issue('B-3', 'The Brief Treats Character Conversion as a “Dispositive” Factor, Which Would Make § 707(a)(2)(A) Swallow § 702(b)',
 ['Arg. IV.A.2, Factor (3): “This factor is dispositive in the present case.” Quoting *Pinnacle Partners* for the proposition that conversion “weighs heavily.”'],
 ['Every allocation of long-term capital gain to a service partner (including every carried interest) “converts” what could have been fee income into capital gain. Section 702(b) prescribes that result for distributive shares, and in § 1061 (2017) Congress addressed carried interest by lengthening the holding period, not by making the income ordinary. A test under which conversion is “dispositive” would recharacterize every carried interest. Character conversion is the *consequence* of respecting the allocation, not a factor in deciding whether to respect it. The quoted *Pinnacle* language does not appear in Exhibit 12.'],
 'Significant',
 'Undercuts the analytical core of the Brief\'s § 707(a)(2)(A) section and its § 702(b) section (Issue B-8).',
 ['Pair with the carried-interest contradiction (Issue C-2): the government concedes carried interest receives capital gain treatment, so conversion alone cannot be disqualifying.']
)

issue('B-4', 'The Brief Misrepresents *Pinnacle Partners*: The Holding Turned on a Deficit Restoration Obligation and Was Expressly Limited to Its Facts',
 ['Arg. IV.A.3: the *Pinnacle* arrangement was “substantially identical to HCP\'s Fee Waiver Program”; *Pinnacle* “categorically establishes that management fee waivers of this type fail to shift meaningful entrepreneurial risk.” Factor (1): *Pinnacle* found “a substantially identical carry-forward mechanism eliminated meaningful risk.” Part V.B.3–4 (penalty).'],
 ['The government\'s own Exhibit 12 (and Quillen Decl. ¶¶ 75–76) shows the decisive fact was a **deficit restoration obligation** that “effectively guaranteed that Pinnacle Partners would receive the full amount of the waived fees regardless of the fund\'s investment performance,” and that “[t]he court emphasizes that its holding is based on the specific facts before it, including the presence of the deficit restoration obligation.” The Brief never mentions the DRO.',
  'HCP\'s arrangement has no DRO, guarantee, indemnity, or credit support (Ridgeline Opinion §§ II.H, III.A.2; Election Forms §§ 3–4). Exhibit 12 does not mention any carry-forward provision at all, so the Brief\'s assertion that *Pinnacle* involved a “substantially identical carry-forward mechanism” is unsupported by the excerpts the government chose to file.',
  'The quotations the Brief attributes to *Pinnacle* (e.g., the carry-forward “ensured that the manager would ultimately receive the full amount”; “a re-labeling exercise designed to achieve a tax result”) do not appear in Exhibit 12. We need the full opinion to determine whether they exist.',
  '*Pinnacle* is a Tax Court memorandum opinion (not precedential even in the Tax Court, and not binding on this Court), and it was decided June 14, 2019 (Quillen Decl. ¶ 71) — after the Ridgeline Opinion and after the TY 2018 and TY 2019 elections were executed.'],
 'Critical',
 '*Pinnacle* is the only fee-waiver case the government cites and it anchors both the merits and the penalty arguments (“substantial authority,” negligence). Its own excerpt distinguishes it.',
 ['Quote the two Exhibit 12 passages in full. Argue that *Pinnacle* supports HCP: by limiting its holding to the DRO, the court implicitly recognized that a fee waiver without a backstop can bear real entrepreneurial risk.',
  'Obtain and read the complete *Pinnacle* opinion immediately to verify the government\'s quotations and pin cites, and to identify any additional distinguishing facts (election timing, binding nature, allocation source). If the quoted language does not exist, say so precisely.']
)

issue('B-5', 'The § 707(c) Guaranteed-Payment Remedy Is Legally Unavailable and Is Not the Basis of the FPAA',
 ['Part V.A: “The priority allocations are, in substance, guaranteed payments within the meaning of IRC § 707(c). They were determined without regard to the partnership\'s income . . . . Recharacterization of the priority allocations as guaranteed payments is therefore the appropriate remedy.” Ashford Decl. ¶¶ 37–48 (Opinion 2).'],
 ['Section 707(c) reaches only payments “determined without regard to the income of the partnership.” The priority allocation is payable “solely from the Fund\'s net long-term capital gains” (Election Forms § 3), and if there are none the allocation is zero for that year and may never be paid. The government concedes as much (SUMF ¶ 10: “payable solely from realized long-term capital gains”), and Professor Ashford acknowledges that the allocations “appear to be ‘determined with regard to the income of the partnership’” (¶ 42). An amount computed by reference to partnership income is a distributive share, not a guaranteed payment [cite-check: Treas. Reg. § 1.707-1(c); Rev. Rul. 69-180].',
  'Sections 707(a) and 707(c) are mutually exclusive: § 707(a)(2)(A) treats the recipient as a non-partner; § 707(c) treats the recipient as a partner receiving a fixed payment. The Brief asks for both.',
  'The FPAA rests on § 707(a)(2)(A) and economic substance (Quillen Decl. ¶ 61). A § 707(c) recharacterization is a new theory on which the government should bear the burden (Issue B-15).',
  'A guaranteed-payment remedy would carry correlative consequences the government ignores (a § 162 deduction or § 263 capitalization at the Fund level, which reduces the LPs\' gains). The government seeks only the one-sided adjustment to HCP.'],
 'Significant',
 'The remedy section is where the government tells the Court what judgment to enter. A remedy that is unavailable as a matter of statutory text, and inconsistent with the liability theory, is a strong reason to deny the motion as framed.',
 ['Argue that, because the government itself cannot identify which provision governs the recharacterization, it has not shown entitlement to judgment as a matter of law. Use the statutory text and Ashford ¶ 42\'s concession.']
)

issue('B-6', 'The Economic Substance Argument Does Not Satisfy § 7701(o) or Address Second Circuit Law',
 ['Arg. IV.C (relying on *Gregory*, *ASA Investerings* (D.C. Cir.), *Frank Lyon*; TOA also lists *Coltec* (Fed. Cir.) and *Klamath* (5th Cir.)). Ashford Decl. ¶ 27 (“I focus primarily on whether HCP had a substantial non-tax business purpose”).'],
 ['**No relevance analysis.** Section 7701(o)(5)(C) provides that whether the doctrine is “relevant” to a transaction is determined as if § 7701(o) had never been enacted. The Brief simply assumes relevance. The legislative history (Joint Committee on Taxation, JCX-18-10, at 152–53 (2010) [cite-check]) states that codification was not intended to disturb basic business choices respected under longstanding practice. The choice between taking compensation as a fee or as a profits-based partnership allocation is precisely such a choice; Congress has repeatedly legislated in this space (§§ 707(a)(2)(A), 1061) without treating profit-share compensation as lacking substance. LB&I\'s own directive requires examiners to analyze relevance and obtain executive-level approval before asserting the codified doctrine [cite-check: LB&I-4-0711-015 (July 15, 2011), as updated]; the record is silent on compliance.',
  '**Objective prong never analyzed.** Section 7701(o)(1)(A) asks whether the transaction changes the taxpayer\'s economic position in a meaningful way. The Brief\'s analysis is almost entirely about purpose (“The Fee Waiver Arrangement Lacks a Genuine Business Purpose”), followed by a conclusory sentence that nothing changed (Arg. IV.C.3). The record shows that HCP exchanged a fixed fee payable regardless of performance for an unsecured, non-interest-bearing claim subordinated to the realization of net long-term capital gains and extinguished on liquidation — and, for Fund V, actually received nothing (Issue A-3).',
  '**Purpose prong misstated.** The statute requires “a substantial purpose” apart from tax effects, not the absence of a tax purpose. The Brief repeatedly argues that tax savings were the “sole” purpose, but its citations do not support that, and the Ridgeline Opinion documents three non-tax purposes (Issue A-14). Purpose and intent are classic jury-type questions ill-suited to summary judgment.',
  '**Wrong circuit.** The Brief cites no Second Circuit economic substance authority. The opposition should address *Gilman v. Commissioner*, 933 F.2d 143 (2d Cir. 1991), and *Bank of New York Mellon Corp. v. Commissioner*, 801 F.3d 104 (2d Cir. 2015) [cite-check]. (Note: *BNY Mellon* is pro-government on its facts and emphasizes pre-tax profit potential; we should distinguish it rather than ignore it.) *Frank Lyon* in fact supports respecting the form of a transaction “imbued with tax-independent considerations” and involving genuine third-party economic stakes.'],
 'Critical',
 'Economic substance is the government\'s broadest theory and the predicate for its § 7701(o)-based penalty argument. The missing relevance and objective-prong analyses are legal deficiencies, and the purpose prong presents a fact dispute.',
 ['Structure the response in three steps: (1) the doctrine is not relevant to a choice of compensation form within a statutory regime Congress has specifically addressed; (2) even if relevant, the objective prong is satisfied as a matter of record fact (Fund V; liquidation cut-off; subordination); (3) the purpose prong presents, at minimum, a genuine dispute (Ridgeline § III.C.3; declarations of Hargrove, Sato, LP witness).',
  'Request, through discovery or a Rule 56(d) declaration if needed, any LB&I relevance analysis and approval for asserting the doctrine.']
)

issue('B-7', 'The Step Transaction Argument Collapses Steps That Never Occurred and Relies on Misattributed Authority',
 ['Arg. IV.E: the four “steps” are (1) waiver, (2) non-payment of the fee, (3) priority allocation, and (4) “the Fund distributes cash to HCP in satisfaction of the priority allocation”; “[w]hen collapsed . . . the multi-step arrangement reduces to a single transaction: the payment of ordinary management fee income.” Citing *Gregory v. Helvering* and *Klamath*, 568 F.3d at 544.'],
 ['The step transaction doctrine combines steps that actually occurred to determine their tax effect; it does not authorize the IRS to invent a step (here, payment of a management fee) that never happened. *See Grove v. Commissioner*, 490 F.2d 241, 247–48 (2d Cir. 1973); *Esmark, Inc. v. Commissioner*, 90 T.C. 171, 195–96 (1988), *aff\'d*, 886 F.2d 1318 (7th Cir. 1989) [cite-check]. Collapsing a fee *waiver* and a contingent allocation does not yield a fee payment.',
  'The record contains no evidence of step (4). Neither declaration identifies any cash distribution; Quillen describes only allocations reflected on capital account statements (¶¶ 28, 42–43). For Fund V there was neither an allocation nor a distribution.',
  '*Klamath* is a Fifth Circuit economic substance case about leveraged foreign-currency transactions; the Brief\'s quotation of the “mutual interdependence” and “end result” tests at 568 F.3d at 544 should be verified, as I do not believe *Klamath* is a step-transaction authority. *Gregory* is a substance-over-form case. The Brief cites no Second Circuit step-transaction authority [consider *Greene v. United States*, 13 F.3d 577 (2d Cir. 1994) (cite-check)].',
  'The Brief names the “binding commitment” test but never applies it, and the “end result” test turns on subjective intent — again a fact question.'],
 'Significant',
 'The step transaction theory is pleaded as “alternative and supplementary” and is unlikely to drive the outcome, but its defects reinforce the theme that the government is stacking theories without analysis.',
 ['Address briefly (one to two pages). Emphasize the absence of distribution evidence (which also matters for § 707(a)(2)(A), which requires a related “allocation *and distribution*”) and the doctrine\'s inability to create a fee payment that was never made.']
)

issue('B-8', 'The § 702(b) Argument Is Not an Independent Ground and Misplaces the “Cherry-Picking” Concern',
 ['Arg. IV.D: the priority allocations “do not properly qualify as long-term capital gains . . . under IRC § 702(b)”; “This character cherry-picking is not consistent with the principles of IRC § 702(b) when the underlying allocation is, as the government has demonstrated, a disguised payment for services.”'],
 ['The government concedes that the Funds\' gains are long-term capital gains and that § 702(b) determines the character of a distributive share at the partnership level. Its argument is expressly derivative: it applies only if the allocation is “in substance compensation for services.” It therefore adds nothing to the § 707(a)(2)(A) analysis. Whether a partnership may specially allocate a particular class of income to a partner is governed by § 704(b), and the government has not shown (apart from the misapplied transitory-allocation argument) that the allocation lacks substantial economic effect. The hypotheticals about dividends and tax-exempt interest are not this case.'],
 'Significant',
 'Low risk on its own; useful to show the Court that the government\'s “five independent theories” reduce to one or two.',
 ['Argue in a short section that § 702(b) “rises and falls” with § 707(a)(2)(A). Note the Conclusion\'s characterization that HCP “improperly invoked” § 702(b) is not an independent basis for judgment.']
)

issue('B-9', 'The Brief Misuses § 1061, Which Reflects a Congressional Choice to Preserve Capital Gain Treatment for Profits Interests Held More Than Three Years',
 ['Arg. IV.B: § 1061 “reflects a broader Congressional policy judgment that gains derived from fund management activities should not automatically receive preferential capital gains treatment.”'],
 ['In the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017, Congress considered the treatment of carried interest and chose to *retain* long-term capital gain treatment for applicable partnership interests, subject to a three-year holding period. It did not recharacterize such gains as ordinary income, and it did not legislate on fee waivers (the Brief concedes § 1061 “does not directly apply”). Treasury\'s 2015 fee-waiver proposals likewise remain unfinalized. If anything, the legislative and regulatory history shows that the policy the government asks this Court to impose has been considered and not adopted.'],
 'Significant',
 'Turns one of the government\'s policy arguments against it and supports the substantial-authority defense.',
 ['Use in the carried-interest response and the penalty section. **Caution:** do not invite a § 1061 analysis of the priority allocations themselves (Issue D-13).']
)
PYEOF
echo ok
OUTER
)"

H('V. Category (B): Legal Errors', 1)

issue('B-1', 'The Brief Inverts Rev. Proc. 93-27, Which Provides That Receipt of a Profits Interest Is Generally *Not* a Taxable Event',
 ['Arg. IV.A.4: \u201c[T]he IRS has long recognized that profits interests received in exchange for services are taxed at the time of receipt if they have a determinable value. See Rev. Proc. 93-27, 1993-2 C.B. 343.\u201d',
  'Ashford Decl. \u00b6\u00b6 50\u201355 (Opinion 3): Rev. Proc. 93-27 \u201cestablishes that profits interests received in exchange for services are taxed at the time of receipt if they have a determinable value\u201d and \u201csupports the conclusion that the profits interests received in exchange for waived fees should be taxed upon receipt.\u201d'],
 ['Rev. Proc. 93-27 \u00a7 4.01 provides that, if a person receives a profits interest for services to or for the benefit of a partnership in a partner capacity, the IRS **will not treat the receipt as a taxable event**. Section 4.02 lists three exceptions: (1) the profits interest relates to a substantially certain and predictable stream of income from partnership assets, *such as income from high-quality debt securities or a high-quality net lease*; (2) the partner disposes of the interest within two years; or (3) the interest is a limited partnership interest in a publicly traded partnership. Rev. Proc. 2001-43 supplements it. The \u201cdeterminable value\u201d language is not in the revenue procedure; it echoes the pre-1993 *Diamond*/*Campbell* case law that Rev. Proc. 93-27 was issued to address. The Ridgeline Opinion describes Rev. Proc. 93-27 correctly (\u00a7 III.D).',
  'Professor Ashford\'s reliance on the first exception is misplaced: it addresses income streams from *partnership assets* of the high-grade-debt/net-lease type, not contingent realized gains from a mid-market buyout portfolio \u2014 the paradigm of uncertain income.',
  'When Treasury proposed the \u00a7 707(a)(2)(A) regulations in 2015, the preamble announced that the IRS *intended* to issue a revenue procedure adding a new exception to Rev. Proc. 93-27 for profits interests issued in conjunction with a partner forgoing payment of a substantially fixed amount (i.e., fee waivers). 80 Fed. Reg. 43652 (July 23, 2015) [cite-check]. To my knowledge, no such revenue procedure has issued. The government\'s position therefore requires an exception the IRS itself acknowledged does not yet exist.',
  'Even on its own terms, a \u201ctaxed at receipt\u201d theory would (i) tax HCP on the fair market value of the interest at grant, not on $47,612,000 of later allocations, and (ii) place the income in the year of grant \u2014 e.g., TY 2017 for the December 2017 elections (a year not in the FPAA and outside the BBA regime), TY 2018 for the November 2018 elections, and TY 2019 for the December 2019 Fund IV election. That is irreconcilable with the FPAA\'s adjustments.'],
 'Critical',
 'This is the clearest misstatement of law in the Brief. Exposing that the government and its expert have described an authority as standing for the opposite of what it says will color the Court\'s view of every other legal proposition in the motion, and it eliminates an entire theory (Ashford Opinion 3).',
 ['Quote \u00a7\u00a7 4.01\u20134.02 of Rev. Proc. 93-27 verbatim and juxtapose them with the Brief\'s sentence. Note the 2015 preamble\'s announced (and unissued) fee-waiver exception.',
  'Point out the timing/valuation incoherence of a \u201ctaxed at receipt\u201d theory and that it is not the basis of the FPAA (Quillen Decl. \u00b6 61).',
  'Tone: measured. One clean paragraph is more effective than rhetoric.']
)

issue('B-2', 'The Brief Misstates the Treas. Reg. \u00a7 1.707-2(c) Factors, Omits Factor (4), Imports the \u00a7 704(b) \u201cTransitory Allocation\u201d Framework, and Ignores That the Regulation Is Only Proposed',
 ['Arg. IV.A.2: \u201cThe Treasury Regulations provide a six-factor test . . . . The government submits that each applicable factor weighs decisively in favor of recharacterization.\u201d The Brief then labels Factors (1), (2), (3), (5) and (6) and, in place of Factor (4), inserts a heading \u201cThe Priority Allocations Constitute Transitory Allocations Lacking Substantial Economic Effect,\u201d relying on Treas. Reg. \u00a7 1.704-1(b)(2)(iii). Arg. IV.A.5: \u201cEvery applicable factor . . . weighs in favor\u201d \u2014 listing five.'],
 ['**Status.** Section 1.707-2 is a *proposed* regulation (REG-115452-14, 80 Fed. Reg. 43652 (July 23, 2015)) that has never been finalized. By its terms it would apply to arrangements entered into or modified after final regulations are published [cite-check proposed effective date provision]. Proposed regulations are not binding and receive no deference, although they may be considered for their persuasive value. The Brief repeatedly calls them \u201cthe Treasury Regulations\u201d and \u201cthe implementing regulations.\u201d',
  '**Content.** Prop. Treas. Reg. \u00a7 1.707-2(c) makes **significant entrepreneurial risk** the most important factor ((c)(1)) and then lists five secondary factors: whether the service provider (2) holds a transitory or short-duration interest; (3) receives allocations and distributions in a time frame comparable to a non-partner service provider; (4) became a partner primarily to obtain tax benefits not otherwise available; (5) has a continuing interest in general partnership profits that is small relative to the allocation; and (6) receives different allocations for different services with significantly different entrepreneurial risk [cite-check exact text]. The government\'s Factors (2) (\u201cguaranteed payment or preferred return\u201d), (3) (\u201cconverting ordinary income to capital gain\u201d), (5) (\u201crelatively fixed in relation to the services\u201d), and (6) (\u201csubject to a ceiling\u201d) do not appear in the proposed regulation.   '**Imported framework.** The \u00a7 704(b) transitory-allocation rule (Treas. Reg. \u00a7 1.704-1(b)(2)(iii)(c)) asks whether an *allocation among partners* is likely to be offset by *subsequent allocations* so that capital accounts end where they would have been. A waived management fee is not a partnership allocation, so it cannot be an \u201coffsetting allocation.\u201d Moreover, the remedy for an allocation lacking substantial economic effect is reallocation in accordance with the partners\' interests in the partnership, not recharacterization of capital gain as ordinary income \u2014 and the FPAA made no \u00a7 704(b) adjustment (Quillen Decl. \u00b6 61). The Ridgeline Opinion specifically warned that the two frameworks are \u201cdistinct\u201d and \u201cshould not be conflated\u201d (\u00a7 III.A.4).'],
 'Critical',
 'The \u00a7 707(a)(2)(A) argument is the government\'s lead theory. A Court that sees the government has mis-described the test it asks the Court to apply, omitted the factors that favor the taxpayer, and substituted an unrelated framework is unlikely to find the issue suitable for summary judgment.',
 ['Set out the proposed regulation\'s actual text in a table and walk through each factor, with record citations. Note the regulation\'s proposed status in one sentence, but argue primarily that HCP prevails even under the IRS\'s own proposed standard (see caution below).',
  '**Caution:** the Ridgeline Opinion also cites \u201cTreasury Regulations \u00a7 1.707-2(c)\u201d as if final and uses its own, non-textual factor labels (e.g., \u201cclawback,\u201d \u201creasonably certain\u201d). The opposition should rely on the regulatory text, not on Ridgeline\'s labels, and should not overemphasize the \u201cproposed\u201d point in a way that suggests HCP\'s adviser misunderstood the law. The (c)(1) presumption list also contains facts the government may invoke in reply (see Issue D-3).']
)

issue('B-3', 'The Brief Treats Character Conversion as a \u201cDispositive\u201d Factor, Which Would Make \u00a7 707(a)(2)(A) Swallow \u00a7 702(b)',

 'Significant',
 'Undercuts the analytical core of the Brief\'s \u00a7 707(a)(2)(A) section and its \u00a7 702(b) section (Issue B-8).',
 ['Pair with the carried-interest contradiction (Issue C-2): the government concedes carried interest receives capital gain treatment, so conversion alone cannot be disqualifying.']

(Note: *BNY Mellon* is pro-government on its facts and emphasizes pre-tax profit potential; we should distinguish it rather than ignore it.) *Frank Lyon* in fact supports respecting the form of a transaction \u201cimbued with tax-independent considerations\u201d and involving genuine third-party economic stakes.'],
