issue('B-10', 'The Penalty Argument Misquotes § 7701(o)(5)(A) and Relies on a No-Fault Economic Substance Penalty the FPAA Did Not Assert',
 ['Part V.B.3: “Section 7701(o)(5)(A) provides that ‘[n]o penalty shall be imposed under [§ 6662] with respect to any portion of an underpayment which is attributable to one or more non-economic substance transactions if — (i) the relevant facts . . . are adequately disclosed . . . and (ii) there is a reasonable basis for the tax treatment.’ HCP did not adequately disclose the fee waiver arrangement on its returns.”'],
 ['Section 7701(o)(5)(A) is a *definition* (“The term ‘economic substance doctrine’ means the common law doctrine . . .”). It contains no penalty rule. The penalty for transactions lacking economic substance is in § 6662(b)(6) (20%), increased to 40% for nondisclosed transactions by § 6662(i), with the reasonable cause defense removed by § 6664(c)(2). The quoted “reasonable basis” exception does not appear in the enacted statute.',
  'The FPAA asserted the penalty only on substantial understatement and/or negligence grounds (§ 6662(b)(1)–(2)); it did not assert § 6662(b)(6) or (i) (Quillen Decl. ¶ 62; SUMF ¶ 30). The government cannot obtain summary judgment on a penalty ground not determined in the FPAA, and it would bear the burden on any such new matter.',
  'The assertion that HCP “did not adequately disclose” has no record citation.'],
 'Significant',
 'If the Court were to accept the misquoted provision, it could conclude that reasonable cause is unavailable — the most dangerous penalty outcome for HCP. Correcting it keeps the reasonable cause defense fully in play.',
 ['Quote §§ 7701(o)(5)(A), 6662(b)(6), 6662(i) and 6664(c)(2) accurately and note that none was asserted. Confirm in the FPAA itself (Ex. 14 is only workpapers; obtain the FPAA and penalty lead sheet) that no (b)(6) penalty was determined.',
  'Review the TY 2018–2020 returns for any disclosure (e.g., Form 8275, statements, K-1 footnotes) in case the government pursues the point in reply.']
)

issue('B-11', 'The Brief Ignores the Reasonable Cause and Good Faith Defense Under § 6664(c)(1)',
 ['Part V.B (entire penalty section). The Table of Authorities lists § 6664(c) (p. 42) and *United States v. Boyle* (p. 41), but neither is discussed in the text.'],
 ['No accuracy-related penalty may be imposed where the taxpayer shows reasonable cause and good faith. § 6664(c)(1); Treas. Reg. § 1.6664-4(b)–(c). Reliance on professional advice qualifies where (1) the adviser was a competent professional with sufficient expertise to justify reliance, (2) the taxpayer provided necessary and accurate information, and (3) the taxpayer actually relied in good faith. *Neonatology Assocs., P.A. v. Commissioner*, 115 T.C. 43, 99 (2000), *aff\'d*, 299 F.3d 221 (3d Cir. 2002) [cite-check].',
  'The government\'s own declarant establishes much of the defense: HCP “sought professional tax advice regarding the proposed structure before implementing it” (Quillen Decl. ¶ 67); the opinion was a written, reasoned, “more likely than not” opinion addressing §§ 707(a)(2)(A), 707(c), 7701(o), Rev. Proc. 93-27 and 702(b) (¶¶ 64–66, 69); it preceded the first election by six to seven weeks (¶ 65); and HCP asserted reasonable cause in its protest (¶ 70).',
  'Reasonable cause is determined case by case on all facts and circumstances (Treas. Reg. § 1.6664-4(b)(1)) and is ordinarily unsuitable for summary judgment, particularly against the taxpayer.'],
 'Critical',
 'The government has not carried its burden of showing the absence of a genuine dispute on the penalty. This is likely the easiest part of the motion to defeat, even if the Court were inclined toward the government on the merits.',
 ['Devote a full section to reasonable cause, supported by declarations from Hargrove and Sato (reliance, information provided) and, if strategically appropriate, Moreau. Address the vulnerabilities in Issue D-10 directly rather than leaving them for reply.',
  'Anticipate that the TOA entries signal a reasonable-cause rebuttal held back for reply (Issue C-11). Consider whether to request leave for a sur-reply if new penalty arguments appear.']
)

issue('B-12', 'The Government Has Not Shown Written Supervisory Approval of the Penalty Under § 6751(b)',
 ['Part V.B; Quillen Decl. ¶¶ 57–62 (no reference to penalty approval).'],
 ['Section 6751(b)(1) requires that the “initial determination” of a penalty be “personally approved (in writing) by the immediate supervisor of the individual making such determination.” In the Second Circuit, approval must be obtained no later than the issuance of the notice asserting the penalty. *Chai v. Commissioner*, 851 F.3d 190, 221 (2d Cir. 2017) [cite-check]. Quillen describes group-manager approval of the *expansion* of the examination (¶ 57), but says nothing about penalty approval. Note that § 7491(c) (burden of production) does not apply in partnership-level proceedings, *see Dynamo Holdings L.P. v. Commissioner*, 150 T.C. 224 (2018) [cite-check], so HCP should raise the issue affirmatively.'],
 'Significant',
 'A § 6751(b) failure would eliminate the penalty entirely regardless of the merits. At minimum, the silence of the record defeats summary judgment on the penalty.',
 ['Raise expressly in the opposition and confirm the answer pleaded it; if not, consider amendment. Serve targeted discovery (penalty approval form, lead sheet, Letter 1807/30-day letter penalty workpapers) or submit a Rule 56(d) declaration.']
)

issue('B-13', 'The Substantial Authority and Negligence Arguments Apply the Wrong Standards and Anachronistic Authority',
 ['Part V.B.3: “No reasonable taxpayer could have concluded that the conversion . . . would be sustained”; “[t]he weight of authority is overwhelmingly against the position adopted by HCP.” Part V.B.4: negligence based on “the Tax Court\'s holding in *Pinnacle Partners*” and Hargrove\'s background. Part V.B.2: understatement “vastly exceeds” the thresholds.'],
 ['Substantial authority is an objective weighing of the authorities, assessed as of the last day of the taxable year or the date the return is filed (Treas. Reg. § 1.6662-4(d)(2)–(3)); a “reasonable taxpayer could not have concluded” test is not the standard. Proposed regulations are themselves “authority” (§ 1.6662-4(d)(3)(iii)), and the 2015 proposed regulations expressly contemplate that fee waivers bearing significant entrepreneurial risk are respected. No statute, final regulation, or precedential decision held fee waivers of this type invalid.',
  'For the TY 2018 elections (December 2017) and TY 2019 elections (November 2018), *Pinnacle* (June 14, 2019) did not exist; it cannot render HCP negligent in structuring those transactions. (*Pinnacle* did exist when the TY 2018 return was filed on September 15, 2019 — see Issue D-10.)',
  'The government offers no computation of the understatement for any year, and the BBA imputed-underpayment computation (§ 6225) is not in the record. The 10%/$5,000 test it recites (§ 6662(d)(1)(A)) is the individual-taxpayer threshold; the Brief does not explain how it applies at the partnership level.'],
 'Significant',
 'These errors prevent summary judgment on the penalty even before reasonable cause is considered.',
 ['Argue substantial authority affirmatively (proposed regulation framework; Rev. Proc. 93-27; § 702(b); *Pinnacle*\'s DRO limitation) and that the penalty cannot be resolved without a computation.']
)

issue('B-14', 'The Government Ignores BBA Procedure and the Timeliness and Validity of the FPAA',
 ['Prelim. Stmt.; SUMF ¶¶ 7, 30–31 (FPAA served on Sato as “Tax Matters Partner”; TY 2018 return filed September 15, 2019, “pursuant to an extension”). Quillen Decl. ¶¶ 11, 55–63. The Brief contains no discussion of §§ 6231 or 6235.'],
 ['**Regime.** TY 2018–2020 are BBA years. The notices required are a notice of proposed partnership adjustment (NOPPA) and a notice of final partnership adjustment (FPA), mailed to the partnership and its partnership representative (§ 6231(a)). The record identifies the PR as Elliot R. Hargrove (Ex. 7), yet the FPAA was “served upon Ms. Sato in her capacity as Tax Matters Partner” (Quillen Decl. ¶ 59).',
  '**Missing NOPPA / premature FPA.** Under § 6231(b)(2)(A), an FPA may not be mailed earlier than 270 days after the NOPPA unless the partnership waives. The record describes only a “30-day letter” dated February 7, 2022, a protest on March 9, 2022, and an FPAA on June 15, 2022 — 128 days later (Quillen Decl. ¶¶ 60–61). If the February 7 letter was the NOPPA, the FPA was premature (270 days would have run on November 4, 2022); if it was not, the record shows no NOPPA at all.',
  '**Limitations.** Under § 6235(a), the period for making partnership adjustments is generally three years from the later of the return filing date or due date (with extensions keyed to the NOPPA in § 6235(a)(2)–(3)). For TY 2018 (filed September 15, 2019) the three-year period ran on **September 15, 2022**; the FPAA was within that period *if valid*. But if the FPAA is invalid for procedural defects, a new FPA for TY 2018 would now be time-barred, and TY 2019 (filed on extension, presumably September 15, 2020) likely expired September 15, 2023, absent a § 6235(b) extension or NOPPA-based extension. TY 2020 may remain open until approximately September 15, 2024. The TY 2019 and TY 2020 filing dates are not in the record.',
  '**Election out.** HCP appears to have six partners, all individuals (Quillen Decl. ¶ 10). Such a partnership may elect out of the BBA under § 6221(b) on a timely filed return. The PR designation on the TY 2018 return suggests no election out for that year, but we must confirm for each year. If HCP elected out for any year, a partnership-level FPA would be a nullity for that year.',
  '**Candor point.** HCP\'s timely petition (September 8, 2022, within 90 days of June 15, 2022, § 6234(a)) shows actual receipt, and courts are generally reluctant to invalidate a notice that the taxpayer actually received and timely contested. The strength of the argument depends on whether a NOPPA issued, whether HCP waived the 270-day period, and whether any extension was signed.'],
 'Critical',
 'Contingent on verification. If the procedural defects are established, they could eliminate the TY 2018 and TY 2019 adjustments ($31,250,000, or 65.6% of the total) regardless of the merits. Even if not ultimately dispositive, the government\'s failure to address timeliness is a gap in its summary-judgment showing if HCP has pleaded the defense.',
 ['**Immediately** pull the administrative file: all IRS letters (including any Letter 5893 NOPPA), any 270-day waiver, any extension of the § 6235 period, the FPA itself and its mailing addresses, Forms 1065 for all three years (PR designation; Schedule B-2 election out), and the Form 2848.',
  'Confirm that our answer/petition pleaded limitations and notice defects as affirmative defenses (Fed. R. Civ. P. 8(c)). If not, evaluate a prompt Rule 15(a) motion.',
  'Confirm that the § 6234(b) jurisdictional deposit for district court review was made and in what amount (see Part X).',
  'If the facts support it, consider a cross-motion for partial summary judgment on TY 2018/2019 timeliness; otherwise raise it as a genuine dispute precluding judgment.']
)

issue('B-15', 'The Brief Overstates the Presumption of Correctness and Ignores the Government\'s Burden on New Matter',
 ['Part III: “The FPAA carries a presumption of correctness, and HCP bears the burden of overcoming that presumption.” (citing *Welch v. Helvering*, which does not appear in the Table of Authorities).'],
 ['The presumption attaches to the determinations actually made in the FPAA — here, § 707(a)(2)(A) and economic substance recharacterization with § 6662(b)(1)/(b)(2) penalties (Quillen Decl. ¶¶ 61–62). The Brief and the Ashford Declaration add new theories: § 707(c) guaranteed payments, taxation at grant under Rev. Proc. 93-27, § 704(b) transitory allocations, the step transaction doctrine, and a § 7701(o)-based penalty. The government bears the burden on new matter and on theories requiring different evidence [cite-check: *Shea v. Commissioner*, 112 T.C. 183, 191 (1999); Tax Ct. R. 142(a) by analogy]. The caption also inverts the parties\' roles: HCP initiated this proceeding by petition (§ 6234), and the government\'s framing as “Plaintiff” should not be allowed to obscure the burden allocation.'],
 'Significant',
 'Even where HCP bears the ultimate burden, the government as summary-judgment movant must show no genuine dispute; the new-matter burden strengthens HCP\'s position on the alternative theories.',
 ['Include a short burden section. Do not contest the general presumption for FPAA determinations (Part VIII); target only the new theories.']
)

H('VI. Category (C): Internal Inconsistencies', 1)

issue('C-1', 'The Aggregate Tax Benefit Figure Is Arithmetically Wrong and Contradicted by the Government\'s Own Expert',
 ['Prelim. Stmt. & n.1 (“The 17% differential . . . applied to $47,612,000 yields aggregate federal tax savings of $9,530,400”); Part V.A (same); Part VI (“generating tax savings of $9,530,400”).'],
 ['$47,612,000 × 17% = **$8,094,040**. The Brief overstates its own computation by **$1,436,360 (17.7%)**. Professor Ashford\'s ¶ 18 uses the correct $8,094,040. The Brief\'s figure equals 20% of $47,652,000, which matches neither the stated base nor the stated rate. Both figures also ignore the 3.8% net investment income tax that Quillen mentions (¶ 53) and the BBA imputed-underpayment mechanics, so neither is a reliable measure of anything at issue in the FPAA.'],
 'Significant',
 'The figure is not an element of any claim, but it is the headline number of the motion, appears three times, and anchors the “windfall” theme. A demonstrable arithmetic error the government\'s own expert contradicts is a credibility problem for the government.',
 ['Point it out once, early, and factually (footnote or a sentence in the introduction): “The government\'s own expert calculates the figure at $8,094,040.” Do not dwell on it.']
)

issue('C-2', 'The Government Characterizes the Same Allocations Four Mutually Exclusive Ways',
 ['Arg. IV.A (§ 707(a)(2)(A): a transaction with HCP “acting other than in its capacity as a partner”); Arg. IV.B (“economically indistinguishable from carried interest” — a profits interest held *as a partner*); Part V.A (“guaranteed payments within the meaning of IRC § 707(c)” — payments to a partner *in its capacity as a partner*, determined without regard to income); Arg. IV.A.4 & Ashford Opinion 3 (profits interests “taxed at the time of receipt” under Rev. Proc. 93-27). Ashford Decl. ¶ 35 (“a second carried interest layer on top of HCP\'s existing promote”) vs. ¶¶ 39–46 (§ 707(c)) vs. ¶¶ 61–66 (§ 707(a)(2)(A)).'],
 ['These characterizations cannot all be true. A § 707(a) payment is made to a *non-partner*; a § 707(c) payment is made to a *partner* and is by definition independent of partnership income; carried interest is a *distributive share* determined by partnership income and, under current law, taxed as capital gain (subject to § 1061); and a Rev. Proc. 93-27 inclusion occurs at *grant*, in a different year and amount. Each leads to a different remedy, different tax year, and different correlative adjustments.',
  'The carried-interest section is especially damaging to the government: it concedes the allocations are a share of Fund profits paid to the manager as a partner, and it concedes that carried interest is taxed at capital gains rates under current law (“the current tax treatment of carried interest remains a matter of ongoing legislative debate”).'],
 'Critical',
 'A movant who cannot say which legal characterization applies has not shown entitlement to judgment as a matter of law, and the choice among characterizations depends on disputed facts (risk, partner capacity, contingency).',
 ['Make this a thematic section of the opposition (“The Government Cannot Decide What the Allocations Are”). Use a four-row table: theory, capacity in which HCP is treated, statutory predicate, and why the record defeats it. Use the government\'s carried-interest concession to support capital gain treatment under § 702(b).']
)

issue('C-3', 'The Government Says the Allocations Were Both “Payable Solely From Realized Gains” and “Determined Without Regard to the Partnership\'s Income”',
 ['SUMF ¶ 10 (“payable solely from realized long-term capital gains”); Factor (6) (“nominally limited to the amount of realized long-term capital gains”); vs. Part V.A (“They were determined without regard to the partnership\'s income”). Ashford Decl. ¶ 42 (allocations “appear to be ‘determined with regard to the income of the partnership’”) vs. ¶ 46 (they were “in substance, determined without regard to the income”).'],
 ['The record resolves the contradiction in HCP\'s favor: the Election Forms make the allocation payable only from net long-term capital gains, and Fund V shows the allocation is zero when there are none.'],
 'Significant',
 'Directly defeats the § 707(c) remedy (Issue B-5) and undermines the “guarantee” premise of the § 707(a)(2)(A) and economic substance arguments.',
 ['Quote SUMF ¶ 10 and Ashford ¶ 42 against Part V.A. Short and pointed.']
)

issue('C-4', 'The Government Concedes the 2018 and 2019 Elections Were Prospective, Then Argues Their Timing Shows Hindsight',
 ['SUMF ¶¶ 15–16 (elections executed “prior to the commencement” of each year) and n.13 (a genuine waiver “must be made before the period to which it relates”) vs. Arg. IV.C.2 (“Second”): late-November/December execution occurred “after HCP had full visibility into the Funds\' portfolio performance and could predict with substantial confidence whether sufficient realized long-term capital gains would be generated in the coming year.” Ashford Decl. ¶¶ 72–74.'],
 ['Under the government\'s own standard, a pre-year election is what a genuine waiver requires; it cannot be both the test and the evidence of abuse. The hindsight theory is also factually implausible: the TY 2018 Fund IV election was executed December 18, 2017, three months after Fund IV was formed (September 15, 2017) when, per the Ridgeline Opinion, it was “currently in its fundraising and initial investment period.” Knowledge of the prior year\'s performance does not reveal whether exits will close and produce net long-term capital gains in the coming year, and Fund V\'s 2020 outcome shows how wrong such predictions can be. There is no evidence supporting the “substantial confidence” assertion.'],
 'Significant',
 'Neutralizes the government\'s fallback timing argument once Issue A-1 eliminates the Fund IV TY 2020 point.',
 ['Juxtapose n.13 with Arg. IV.C.2. Have Dr. Chu address the unpredictability of annual realized gains for buyout funds.']
)

issue('C-5', 'The Government Argues Both That Waivers Were “Calibrated” to Available Gains and That the Carry-Forward Was Needed to Eliminate Risk',
 ['Arg. IV.C.2 (“Fourth”): HCP participated “only when the Funds had sufficient realized gains” and “calibrate[d] the waiver amounts to match available gains” vs. Factor (1), SUMF ¶¶ 12, 26 (the Carry-Forward Provision ensured eventual payment when gains were insufficient).'],
 ['If waivers were calibrated to gains already known to be available, the carry-forward would be irrelevant; if the carry-forward was the key to eliminating risk, then gains were not known in advance. Fund V — waived $6,000,000 with no gains ever realized in the year — refutes the calibration theory outright (Quillen Decl. ¶¶ 40–41).'],
 'Significant',
 'The two arguments are each central to a different theory (economic substance vs. disguised payment); exposing the contradiction weakens both.',
 ['Address in the economic substance section, using Fund V as the counterexample.']
)

issue('C-6', 'The Government Claims the Waiver Had “Zero” Net Economic Effect While Also Claiming HCP Took a Senior, “Creditor-Like” Priority Over the Limited Partners',
 ['Arg. IV.A.2 (transitory-allocation heading): “The net economic impact on the Funds and their limited partners was zero.” Ashford Decl. ¶ 30 (LPs “economically indifferent”) vs. Factor (2): HCP\'s claim “was senior to the allocations of all other partners, including limited partners” and HCP “occupied a creditor-like position in the allocation waterfall”; Ashford ¶ 35 (allocations not subject to the hurdle or clawback of the carried interest waterfall).'],
 ['A first-dollar priority on net long-term capital gains necessarily changes the LPs\' economics: in a year with gains, it reduces the LPs\' share of gain; in a year without gains (Fund V, 2020), the LPs pay neither the fee nor the allocation. The LPs\' outcome thus depends on Fund performance — which is the definition of a non-zero economic effect and of shared entrepreneurial risk.'],
 'Significant',
 'Undercuts the economic substance objective prong and the transitory-allocation argument; supports the existence of genuine third-party economic stakes.',
 ['Have Dr. Chu illustrate LP outcomes under fee vs. waiver across performance scenarios (including the actual Fund V outcome).']
)
PYEOF
echo ok
OUTER
)"

issue('B-14', 'The Government Ignores BBA Procedure and the Timeliness and Validity of the FPAA',
 ['Prelim. Stmt.; SUMF \u00b6\u00b6 7, 30\u201331 (FPAA served on Sato as \u201cTax Matters Partner\u201d; TY 2018 return filed September 15, 2019, \u201cpursuant to an extension\u201d). Quillen Decl. \u00b6\u00b6 11, 55\u201363. The Brief contains no discussion of \u00a7\u00a7 6231 or 6235.'],
 ['**Regime.** TY 2018\u20132020 are BBA years. The notices required are a notice of proposed partnership adjustment (NOPPA) and a notice of final partnership adjustment (FPA), mailed to the partnership and its partnership representative (\u00a7 6231(a)). The record identifies the PR as Elliot R. Hargrove (Ex. 7), yet the FPAA was \u201cserved upon Ms. Sato in her capacity as Tax Matters Partner\u201d (Quillen Decl. \u00b6 59).',
  '**Missing NOPPA / premature FPA.** Under \u00a7 6231(b)(2)(A), an FPA may not be mailed earlier than 270 days after the NOPPA unless the partnership waives. The record describes only a \u201c30-day letter\u201d dated February 7, 2022, a protest on March 9, 2022, and an FPAA on June 15, 2022 \u2014 128 days later (Quillen Decl. \u00b6\u00b6 60\u201361). If the February 7 letter was the NOPPA, the FPA was premature (270 days would have run on November 4, 2022); if it was not, the record shows no NOPPA at all.',
  '**Limitations.** Under \u00a7 6235(a), the period for making partnership adjustments is generally three years from the later of the return filing date or due date (with extensions keyed to the NOPPA in \u00a7 6235(a)(2)\u2013(3)). For TY 2018 (filed September 15, 2019) the three-year period ran on **September 15, 2022**; the FPAA was within that period *if valid*. But if the FPAA is invalid for procedural defects, a new FPA for TY 2018 would now be time-barred, and TY 2019 (filed on extension, presumably September 15, 2020) likely expired September 15, 2023, absent a \u00a7 6235(b) extension or NOPPA-based extension. TY 2020 may remain open until approximately September 15, 2024. The TY 2019 and TY 2020 filing dates are not in the record.',
  '**Election out.** HCP appears to have six partners, all individuals (Quillen Decl. \u00b6 10). Such a partnership may elect out of the BBA under \u00a7 6221(b) on a timely filed return. The PR designation on the TY 2018 return suggests no election out for that year, but we must confirm for each year. If HCP elected out for any year, a partnership-level FPA would be a nullity for that year.',
  '**Candor point.** HCP\'s timely petition (September 8, 2022, within 90 days of June 15, 2022, \u00a7 6234(a)) shows actual receipt, and courts are generally reluctant to invalidate a notice that the taxpayer actually received and timely contested. The strength of the argument depends on whether a NOPPA issued, whether HCP waived the 270-day period, and whether any extension was signed.'],
 'Critical',
 'Contingent on verification. If the procedural defects are established, they could eliminate the TY 2018 and TY 2019 adjustments ($31,250,000, or 65.6% of the total) regardless of the merits. Even if not ultimately dispositive, the government\'s failure to address timeliness is a gap in its summary-judgment showing if HCP has pleaded the defense.',
 ['**Immediately** pull the administrative file: all IRS letters (including any Letter 5893 NOPPA), any 270-day waiver, any extension of the \u00a7 6235 period, the FPA itself and its mailing addresses, Forms 1065 for all three years (PR designation; Schedule B-2 election out), and the Form 2848.',
  'Confirm that our answer/petition pleaded limitations and notice defects as affirmative defenses (Fed. R. Civ. P. 8(c)). If not, evaluate a prompt Rule 15(a) motion.',
  'Confirm that the \u00a7 6234(b) jurisdictional deposit for district court review was made and in what amount (see Part X).',
  'If the facts support it, consider a cross-motion for partial summary judgment on TY 2018/2019 timeliness; otherwise raise it as a genuine dispute precluding judgment.']
)

issue('B-15', 'The Brief Overstates the Presumption of Correctness and Ignores the Government\'s Burden on New Matter',
 ['Part III: \u201cThe FPAA carries a presumption of correctness, and HCP bears the burden of overcoming that presumption.\u201d (citing *Welch v. Helvering*, which does not appear in the Table of Authorities).'],
 ['The presumption attaches to the determinations actually made in the FPAA \u2014 here, \u00a7 707(a)(2)(A) and economic substance recharacterization with \u00a7 6662(b)(1)/(b)(2) penalties (Quillen Decl. \u00b6\u00b6 61\u201362). The Brief and the Ashford Declaration add new theories: \u00a7 707(c) guaranteed payments, taxation at grant under Rev. Proc. 93-27, \u00a7 704(b) transitory allocations, the step transaction doctrine, and a \u00a7 7701(o)-based penalty. The government bears the burden on new matter and on theories requiring different evidence [cite-check: *Shea v. Commissioner*, 112 T.C. 183, 191 (1999); Tax Ct. R. 142(a) by analogy]. The caption also inverts the parties\' roles: HCP initiated this proceeding by petition (\u00a7 6234), and the government\'s framing as \u201cPlaintiff\u201d should not be allowed to obscure the burden allocation.'],
 'Significant',
 'Even where HCP bears the ultimate burden, the government as summary-judgment movant must show no genuine dispute; the new-matter burden strengthens HCP\'s position on the alternative theories.',
 ['Include a short burden section. Do not contest the general presumption for FPAA determinations (Part VIII); target only the new theories.']
)

issue('C-1', 'The Aggregate Tax Benefit Figure Is Arithmetically Wrong and Contradicted by the Government\'s Own Expert',
 ['Prelim. Stmt. & n.1 (\u201cThe 17% differential . . . applied to $47,612,000 yields aggregate federal tax savings of $9,530,400\u201d); Part V.A (same); Part VI (\u201cgenerating tax savings of $9,530,400\u201d).'],
 ['$47,612,000 \u00d7 17% = **$8,094,040**. The Brief overstates its own computation by **$1,436,360 (17.7%)**. Professor Ashford\'s \u00b6 18 uses the correct $8,094,040. The Brief\'s figure equals 20% of $47,652,000, which matches neither the stated base nor the stated rate. Both figures also ignore the 3.8% net investment income tax that Quillen mentions (\u00b6 53) and the BBA imputed-underpayment mechanics, so neither is a reliable measure of anything at issue in the FPAA.'],
 'Significant',
 'The figure is not an element of any claim, but it is the headline number of the motion, appears three times, and anchors the \u201cwindfall\u201d theme. A demonstrable arithmetic error the government\'s own expert contradicts is a credibility problem for the government.',
 ['Point it out once, early, and factually (footnote or a sentence in the introduction): \u201cThe government\'s own expert calculates the figure at $8,094,040.\u201d Do not dwell on it.']
)

issue('C-2', 'The Government Characterizes the Same Allocations Four Mutually Exclusive Ways',
 ['Arg. IV.A (\u00a7 707(a)(2)(A): a transaction with HCP \u201cacting other than in its capacity as a partner\u201d); Arg. IV.B (\u201ceconomically indistinguishable from carried interest\u201d \u2014 a profits interest held *as a partner*); Part V.A (\u201cguaranteed payments within the meaning of IRC \u00a7 707(c)\u201d \u2014 payments to a partner *in its capacity as a partner*, determined without regard to income); Arg. IV.A.4 & Ashford Opinion 3 (profits interests \u201ctaxed at the time of receipt\u201d under Rev. Proc. 93-27). Ashford Decl. \u00b6 35 (\u201ca second carried interest layer on top of HCP\'s existing promote\u201d) vs. \u00b6\u00b6 39\u201346 (\u00a7 707(c)) vs. \u00b6\u00b6 61\u201366 (\u00a7 707(a)(2)(A)).'],
 ['These characterizations cannot all be true. A \u00a7 707(a) payment is made to a *non-partner*; a \u00a7 707(c) payment is made to a *partner* and is by definition independent of partnership income; carried interest is a *distributive share* determined by partnership income and, under current law, taxed as capital gain (subject to \u00a7 1061); and a Rev. Proc. 93-27 inclusion occurs at *grant*, in a different year and amount. Each leads to a different remedy, different tax year, and different correlative adjustments.',
  'The carried-interest section is especially damaging to the government: it concedes the allocations are a share of Fund profits paid to the manager as a partner, and it concedes that carried interest is taxed at capital gains rates under current law (\u201cthe current tax treatment of carried interest remains a matter of ongoing legislative debate\u201d).'],
 'Critical',
 'A movant who cannot say which legal characterization applies has not shown entitlement to judgment as a matter of law, and the choice among characterizations depends on disputed facts (risk, partner capacity, contingency).',
 ['Make this a thematic section of the opposition (\u201cThe Government Cannot Decide What the Allocations Are\u201d). Use a four-row table: theory, capacity in which HCP is treated, statutory predicate, and why the record defeats it. Use the government\'s carried-interest concession to support capital gain treatment under \u00a7 702(b).']
)

issue('C-3', 'The Government Says the Allocations Were Both \u201cPayable Solely From Realized Gains\u201d and \u201cDetermined Without Regard to the Partnership\'s Income\u201d',
 ['SUMF \u00b6 10 (\u201cpayable solely from realized long-term capital gains\u201d); Factor (6) (\u201cnominally limited to the amount of realized long-term capital gains\u201d); vs. Part V.A (\u201cThey were determined without regard to the partnership\'s income\u201d). Ashford Decl. \u00b6 42 (allocations \u201cappear to be \u2018determined with regard to the income of the partnership\u2019\u201d) vs. \u00b6 46 (they were \u201cin substance, determined without regard to the income\u201d).'],
 ['The record resolves the contradiction in HCP\'s favor: the Election Forms make the allocation payable only from net long-term capital gains, and Fund V shows the allocation is zero when there are none.'],
 'Significant',
 'Directly defeats the \u00a7 707(c) remedy (Issue B-5) and undermines the \u201cguarantee\u201d premise of the \u00a7 707(a)(2)(A) and economic substance arguments.',
 ['Quote SUMF \u00b6 10 and Ashford \u00b6 42 against Part V.A. Short and pointed.']
)

issue('C-4', 'The Government Concedes the 2018 and 2019 Elections Were Prospective, Then Argues Their Timing Shows Hindsight',
 ['SUMF \u00b6\u00b6 15\u201316 (elections executed \u201cprior to the commencement\u201d of each year) and n.13 (a genuine waiver \u201cmust be made before the period to which it relates\u201d) vs. Arg. IV.C.2 (\u201cSecond\u201d): late-November/December execution occurred \u201cafter HCP had full visibility into the Funds\' portfolio performance and could predict with substantial confidence whether sufficient realized long-term capital gains would be generated in the coming year.\u201d Ashford Decl. \u00b6\u00b6 72\u201374.'],
 ['Under the government\'s own standard, a pre-year election is what a genuine waiver requires; it cannot be both the test and the evidence of abuse. The hindsight theory is also factually implausible: the TY 2018 Fund IV election was executed December 18, 2017, three months after Fund IV was formed (September 15, 2017) when, per the Ridgeline Opinion, it was \u201ccurrently in its fundraising and initial investment period.\u201d Knowledge of the prior year\'s performance does not reveal whether exits will close and produce net long-term capital gains in the coming year, and Fund V\'s 2020 outcome shows how wrong such predictions can be. There is no evidence supporting the \u201csubstantial confidence\u201d assertion.'],
 'Significant',
 'Neutralizes the government\'s fallback timing argument once Issue A-1 eliminates the Fund IV TY 2020 point.',
 ['Juxtapose n.13 with Arg. IV.C.2. Have Dr. Chu address the unpredictability of annual realized gains for buyout funds.']
)

issue('C-5', 'The Government Argues Both That Waivers Were \u201cCalibrated\u201d to Available Gains and That the Carry-Forward Was Needed to Eliminate Risk',
 ['Arg. IV.C.2 (\u201cFourth\u201d): HCP participated \u201conly when the Funds had sufficient realized gains\u201d and \u201ccalibrate[d] the waiver amounts to match available gains\u201d vs. Factor (1), SUMF \u00b6\u00b6 12, 26 (the Carry-Forward Provision ensured eventual payment when gains were insufficient).'],
 ['If waivers were calibrated to gains already known to be available, the carry-forward would be irrelevant; if the carry-forward was the key to eliminating risk, then gains were not known in advance. Fund V \u2014 waived $6,000,000 with no gains ever realized in the year \u2014 refutes the calibration theory outright (Quillen Decl. \u00b6\u00b6 40\u201341).'],
 'Significant',
 'The two arguments are each central to a different theory (economic substance vs. disguised payment); exposing the contradiction weakens both.',
 ['Address in the economic substance section, using Fund V as the counterexample.']
)

issue('C-6', 'The Government Claims the Waiver Had \u201cZero\u201d Net Economic Effect While Also Claiming HCP Took a Senior, \u201cCreditor-Like\u201d Priority Over the Limited Partners',
 ['Arg. IV.A.2 (transitory-allocation heading): \u201cThe net economic impact on the Funds and their limited partners was zero.\u201d Ashford Decl. \u00b6 30 (LPs \u201ceconomically indifferent\u201d) vs. Factor (2): HCP\'s claim \u201cwas senior to the allocations of all other partners, including limited partners\u201d and HCP \u201coccupied a creditor-like position in the allocation waterfall\u201d; Ashford \u00b6 35 (allocations not subject to the hurdle or clawback of the carried interest waterfall).'],
 ['A first-dollar priority on net long-term capital gains necessarily changes the LPs\' economics: in a year with gains, it reduces the LPs\' share of gain; in a year without gains (Fund V, 2020), the LPs pay neither the fee nor the allocation. The LPs\' outcome thus depends on Fund performance \u2014 which is the definition of a non-zero economic effect and of shared entrepreneurial risk.'],
 'Significant',
 'Undercuts the economic substance objective prong and the transitory-allocation argument; supports the existence of genuine third-party economic stakes.',
 ['Have Dr. Chu illustrate LP outcomes under fee vs. waiver across performance scenarios (including the actual Fund V outcome).']
)

 'Significant',

issue('C-12', 'The Brief Says the Case Presents a “Pure Question of Law” but Every Theory Depends on Disputed Facts',
 ['Part III: “The sole question presented is one of legal characterization . . . . This is a question of law, not of fact.” Part VI: “No genuine dispute of material fact exists.”'],
 ['The government\'s own theories turn on facts: the degree of entrepreneurial risk (a facts-and-circumstances inquiry under Prop. Treas. Reg. § 1.707-2(c)); HCP\'s purpose and the managing partners\' intent (§ 7701(o)(1)(B); end-result test); “hindsight” at the election dates; LP involvement; the nature of the carry-forward; and, for penalties, reasonable cause and negligence. issue('D-2', 'The Ashford Declaration Is Largely Inadmissible Legal Opinion and Is Internally Contradictory',
 ['Ashford Decl. ¶¶ 9, 24–76 (Opinions 1–4: the structure “lacks economic substance,” the allocations “are, in substance, guaranteed payments,” Rev. Proc. 93-27 “supports the conclusion” they are taxable at receipt, and the structure “constitutes a disguised payment”).'],
 ['Expert testimony that tells the court what the law is or how it applies to the facts is inadmissible. *Marx & Co. v. Diners\' Club, Inc.*, 550 F.2d 505, 509–12 (2d Cir. 1977); *Hygh v. Jacobs*, 961 F.2d 359, 363–64 (2d Cir. 1992); *United States v. Bilzerian*, 926 F.2d 1285, 1294 (2d Cir. 1991) [cite-check]. Each of Ashford\'s four opinions is a legal conclusion on the ultimate issue, and Opinion 3 is premised on a misstatement of Rev. Proc. 93-27. Her Opinions 2 and 4 are mutually exclusive (§ 707(c) partner capacity vs. § 707(a) non-partner capacity), and ¶ 35 (“second carried interest layer”) contradicts both. She cites no authority for propositions such as “[a]s the Tax Court has recognized” (¶ 38) and “[c]ourts have consistently scrutinized” (¶ 26), and her “every year from 2016” premise (¶ 74) lacks foundation (Issue A-12). Her methodology is ex post (Issue D-4).',
  'Her qualifications and prior engagements (¶¶ 3–6) are a source of potential impeachment: she has testified for taxpayers on “characterization of management company allocations” (*Ridgemont Holdings*) and on economic substance of profit-sharing arrangements (*Stonebridge*), and she has published on fee waivers (46 Tax L. Rev. 289 (2014)).'],
 'Significant',
 'Eliminating or discounting Ashford removes the only “expert” support for the guaranteed-payment remedy and the Rev. Proc. 93-27 theory, and leaves the economic substance argument resting on the Brief\'s own assertions.',
 ['Object under Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(c)(2) and Fed. R. Evid. 702/704 in the opposition (targeted to legal conclusions and the misstatement of Rev. Proc. 93-27), rather than filing a stand-alone *Daubert* motion now. In a bench proceeding the Court may admit the declaration “for what it is worth,” so the opposition should also rebut it on the merits.',
  'Obtain Ashford\'s prior testimony and publications, particularly any taxpayer-side statements that a carry-forward is a “timing mechanism” consistent with entrepreneurial risk or that fee waivers can be respected.']
)

issue('D-3', 'The Brief Does Not Use the Strongest Version of the Government\'s Own Regulatory Argument — Which Is an Opportunity and a Warning',
 ['Arg. IV.A.2 (misstated factors). Compare Prop. Treas. Reg. § 1.707-2(c)(1)(ii) [cite-check text].'],
 ['The proposed regulation lists facts that create a presumption that an arrangement lacks significant entrepreneurial risk, including an allocation that is “reasonably determinable” or “designed to assure that sufficient net profits are highly likely to be available,” specifically an allocation of “net profits from specific transactions or accounting periods” that “does not depend on the long-term future success of the enterprise,” and a waiver that is non-binding or not timely communicated to the partnership and its partners. HCP\'s allocation is drawn from the net long-term capital gains of each *fiscal year* (Election Forms § 3), sits ahead of the LPs, is not subject to the carried-interest hurdle or clawback (Ashford ¶ 35), and the GP (controlled by HCP) influences the timing of exits. The government has not made this argument clearly, but a competent reply could.'],
 'Significant',
 'This is the most serious substantive risk on the merits. The government\'s failure to frame it now is a short-term advantage; we should not assume it will persist.',
 ['Prepare the response now: (i) the allocation is not “reasonably determinable” or “highly likely” (Fund V; Dr. Chu\'s ex ante analysis); (ii) unsatisfied amounts carry forward but remain dependent on long-term Fund success and expire on liquidation — i.e., they *do* depend on the long-term future success of the enterprise; (iii) elections were binding, irrevocable, and acknowledged by the GP, and changes required LPAC consent (Election Forms § 5(c)); (iv) gather evidence that LPs were notified (Issue A-13); (v) evidence on how exit timing was determined (investment committee, LP interests, market conditions) to rebut any manipulation inference.',
  'Do not invite this analysis in the opposition beyond what is needed to describe the regulation accurately; focus the presentation on the primary risk factor and the record.']
)

issue('D-4', 'Professor Ashford and the Brief Measure Risk With Hindsight',
 ['Ashford Decl. ¶¶ 33, 43–45, 69 (allocations were small relative to cumulative realized gains; “[t]he apparent risk was never a real risk”); Brief Arg. IV.B (Fund III “full compensation”).'],
 ['Entrepreneurial risk is evaluated when the arrangement is entered into, based on reasonable expectations at that time, not on how the investments ultimately performed. Ashford compares the allocations to Funds\' *cumulative, multi-year* realized gains, but each allocation was payable from *net* long-term capital gains realized *during the applicable fiscal year* (with carry-forward only to later years). The relevant question is the probability, at the election date, that the Fund would realize sufficient net long-term gains in that year or before liquidation. Fund V shows the risk was real in exactly the scenario that matters.'],
 'Significant',
 'The hindsight methodology is a legitimate ground to discount Ashford\'s opinions and to frame the issue as an ex ante factual question.',
 ['Retain Dr. Chu immediately (Issue D-7) to provide an ex ante risk analysis for each election (fund age, portfolio maturity, pipeline of exits, historical annual realization variability, comparable-fund data).']
)

 ['The Brief does not quote these documents (it miscites Ex. 10 as performance data), but the government will likely use them in reply or at trial on purpose and penalties. They are not fatal \u2014 \u00a7 7701(o)(1)(B) requires a substantial non-tax purpose, not the absence of a tax purpose \u2014 but they make the purpose prong a real contest.'],
 'Significant',
 'Risk to economic substance and negligence defenses if HCP cannot point to contemporaneous non-tax purpose evidence.',
 ['Review Exs. 10 and 11 in full now. Identify contemporaneous non-tax rationales in the same documents (LP alignment, fundraising for Fund V, LPAC discussions). Prepare Hargrove and Sato to explain the documents. Do not assert privilege over documents already produced.']
)

issue('D-6', 'Fund III and Fund IV Gains Dwarfed the Allocations, Which Gives the Government\'s Ex Post Argument Intuitive Appeal',
 ['Ashford Decl. \u00b6\u00b6 43, 45, 69 (Fund IV allocations were about 4.0% of its $742 million of realized gains; Fund III\'s $298 million was \u201cmore than twenty-five times\u201d its $11,850,000 of allocations).'],
 ['The arithmetic is correct ($29,762,000 \u00f7 $742M = 4.0%; $298M \u00f7 $11.85M = 25.1x). Although the methodology is flawed (Issue D-4), a factfinder may find it persuasive that the allocations were always very likely to be satisfied.'],
 'Significant',
 'This is the government\'s best real-world fact on risk for $41.6 million of the $47.6 million.',
 ['Counter with year-specific data (annual net long-term gains in each election year versus the allocation), the subordination and liquidation cut-off features, and Dr. Chu\'s ex ante analysis. Consider whether any year came close to a shortfall.']
)

issue('D-7', 'HCP\'s Expert Engagement Is Not Finalized, and the Opposition Is Due May 17, 2024',
 ['Assignment email (Dr. Raymond Chu of Crestview Economic Consulting expected but not yet engaged).'],
 ['Several of the most important rebuttals require expert support: ex ante risk analysis, MOIC/realization data, time value of the carry-forward, LP economics under fee vs. waiver, and industry practice. Without an expert declaration, Ashford\'s opinions on economic matters would be unrebutted.'],
 'Critical',
 'Timing risk. Three and a half weeks is tight for an expert declaration.',
 ['Finalize the Chu engagement this week (through counsel, to protect work product). Define the scope now (see Part IX). If the expert analysis or discovery we need (earlier Quillen draft, Ashford materials, penalty approval) cannot be completed, prepare a Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(d) declaration identifying the specific facts needed and why.']
)

issue('D-8', 'HCP Reported the $6,000,000 Fund V Allocation as Long-Term Capital Gain for TY 2020 Although No Allocation Was Made',
 ['Quillen Decl. \u00b6 48 (\u201cThe TY 2020 return reported the $6,000,000 priority allocation from Fund V as long-term capital gain notwithstanding that . . . Fund V had not realized any capital gains\u201d); Ashford Decl. \u00b6\u00b6 23, 48 (HCP \u201ctreated the priority allocation as a right to receive a fixed amount of compensation regardless of Fund V\'s actual performance\u201d).'],
 ['This is the most dangerous fact in the record for HCP. It allows the government to argue that HCP itself treated the allocation as a fixed entitlement, undermining the Fund V risk narrative that is otherwise HCP\'s strongest point. It may also raise questions about the accuracy of the Fund V K-1 to HCP and the TY 2020 return preparation by Ridgeline.',
  'There is a substantial counter-argument: if no allocation was made in 2020, HCP had no 2020 income from Fund V of *any* character; reporting it was an *over*-reporting error that increased HCP\'s partners\' tax. The FPAA\'s recharacterization of that $6,000,000 as ordinary income for TY 2020 is wrong regardless of the merits, because there was no allocation and distribution to recharacterize. The correct partnership adjustment for that item is its removal, not recharacterization.'],
 'Critical',
 'How we handle this will determine whether Fund V is our best fact or the government\'s. It also affects the client\'s credibility and potentially Ridgeline\'s.',
 ['Before May 17, determine from HCP and Ridgeline: what the Fund V K-1 to HCP reported; whether HCP\'s return reflected an accrual, a book entry, or an error; whether the allocation was later satisfied (in which year and amount); and whether the partners\' returns were affected. Discuss at the April 24 client call.',
  'Likely approach: acknowledge the reporting error candidly, explain it, and argue that it confirms rather than refutes the contingency (no gains, no allocation, no income). Request in the alternative that any judgment exclude the $6,000,000 from TY 2020 adjustments. Consider whether to coordinate on the treatment of the later year in which any carry-forward was satisfied (likely outside this proceeding).']
)

issue('D-9', 'The Fund V Election Is Outside the Ridgeline Opinion\'s Express Reliance Scope',
 ['Ridgeline Opinion \u00a7 IV (\u201cProspective Election Timing\u201d): \u201cThis opinion should not be relied upon for any waiver election that is not timely executed and delivered before the start of the relevant fiscal year.\u201d Election summary (\u201cNo\u201d for Election No. 6).'],
 ['The government has not yet made this argument, but it will once HCP asserts reasonable cause. For the Fund V $6,000,000, the reliance defense is weaker unless we can show that the election preceded the start of Fund V\'s first fiscal year (Issue A-2). The Opinion also addressed only Funds III and IV, extending to future funds only if the terms and facts were \u201cmaterially unchanged.\u201d'],
 'Significant',
 'Penalty exposure on the Fund V component; also a merits soft spot. The dollar amount is limited (12.6% of the adjustment), and if Issue D-8 is resolved as above, there may be no Fund V income to penalize at all.',
 ['Develop the formation-date argument and obtain any Ridgeline communications in early 2020 confirming that the Fund V election was within the Opinion. Consider a strategic concession or narrowing on Fund V if it protects credibility on the remaining $41.6 million.']
)

issue('D-10', 'The Reasonable Cause Defense Has Weaknesses the Government Has Not Yet Exploited',
 ['Quillen Decl. \u00b6\u00b6 64\u201370; Ridgeline Opinion \u00a7\u00a7 I, II.K, IV, signature block; Brief Part V.B.4 (Hargrove\'s background).'],
 ['(1) **Adviser independence.** Ridgeline designed the structure and prepared the returns (Quillen \u00b6 68). The government may argue Ridgeline was a conflicted adviser or promoter whose advice cannot support reasonable cause [cite-check: Treas. Reg. \u00a7 1.6664-4(c); *106 Ltd. v. Commissioner*, 136 T.C. 67 (2011), *aff\'d*, 684 F.3d 84 (D.C. Cir. 2012)]. Our response: the promoter line of cases concerns advisers who sell a product to multiple clients; Ridgeline was HCP\'s regular adviser and was engaged at counsel\'s request.',
  '(2) **Unverified facts.** The Opinion relies on representations by HCP and Thornfield & Locke \u201cwithout independent verification\u201d (\u00a7 II.K). The government will test whether those representations were accurate and complete (e.g., no credit support; elections before fiscal year start).',
  '(3) **Unsigned copy.** Our copy of the Opinion has a blank signature line (\u201cBy: ______\u201d). We need the executed version.',
  '(4) **No post-*Pinnacle* update.** *Pinnacle* was decided June 14, 2019, before the TY 2018 return was filed (September 15, 2019) and before the TY 2019 and TY 2020 elections and returns. Ridgeline disclaimed any duty to update (\u00a7 IV). Good faith reliance for later years is stronger if Ridgeline or counsel considered *Pinnacle* and concluded it was distinguishable (the protest and exam correspondence suggest HCP did; Quillen \u00b6\u00b6 58, 77).',
  '(5) **Taxpayer sophistication.** Mr. Hargrove\'s tax background (if accurate) is relevant under Treas. Reg. \u00a7 1.6664-4(b)(1) and cuts both ways: it supports informed reliance but invites the argument that he knew better.',
  '(6) **Waiver of privilege.** Asserting reliance on advice puts the advice at issue, and the government will seek the Moreau memorandum (Quillen \u00b6 82), Ridgeline\'s files, and possibly communications with this firm (Issue D-12).'],
 'Significant',
 'Reasonable cause remains HCP\'s strongest penalty defense on summary judgment, but each point must be prepared for trial.',
 ['Collect the executed Opinion, Ridgeline engagement letter, all Ridgeline communications regarding *Pinnacle* and Fund V, and the information HCP provided. Decide early on the scope of the reliance defense and the resulting privilege waiver (limit to Ridgeline if possible).']
)

issue('D-11', 'The Greystone Borrowing Base Disclosure Could Be Recast as Credit Support',
 ['Quillen Decl. \u00b6\u00b6 78\u201380 (borrowing base certificate dated January 15, 2020 \u201cdiscloses the resulting priority profit allocation obligations of Fund IV to HCP\u201d; arrangements \u201cintegrated into Fund IV\'s broader financial operations and were known to the fund\'s lender\u201d).'],
 ['The Ridgeline Opinion assumes no \u201cside letter, credit facility, or other arrangement that would backstop the allocation\u201d (\u00a7 III.A.2 Factor 4). A lender\'s treatment of the priority allocation as an \u201cobligation\u201d in the borrowing base might be argued to show that the allocation was viewed as a fixed liability or that facility proceeds could fund it. This is likely benign (lenders customarily require disclosure of fund-level arrangements), and third-party disclosure also helps HCP by showing the program was real and transparent.'],
 'Minor',
 'Low current risk; must be checked before we characterize the arrangement as having no credit support.',
 ['Review Ex. 13 in full: whether facility proceeds could be used to satisfy priority allocations, any covenant referencing the allocations, and how the obligation was measured. Note the date discrepancy (Oct. 1 vs. Dec. 1, 2017) (Issue C-9).']
)

issue('D-12', 'Thornfield & Locke\'s Own Involvement Creates Privilege-Waiver and Advocate-Witness Risk',
 ['Brief SUMF \u00b6 6, Arg. IV.C.2 n.14, Part V.B.4 (Hargrove was a T&L partnership tax attorney for eight years); Ridgeline Opinion \u00a7 I (engagement \u201cinitiated at the request of HCP\'s counsel, Thornfield & Locke LLP\u201d), \u00a7 II.K (facts \u201cprovided to Ridgeline by HCP and its counsel, Thornfield & Locke LLP\u201d), cc to R. Calvin Briggs; Quillen Decl. \u00b6\u00b6 56, 58\u201359 (T&L represented HCP in the examination).'],
 ['If HCP relies on the Ridgeline Opinion for reasonable cause, the government will argue that the factual representations underlying the Opinion \u2014 some of which came from this firm \u2014 and the firm\'s advice about the structure are at issue. That raises (1) a risk of at-issue waiver extending to T&L communications [cite-check: *In re County of Erie*, 546 F.3d 222, 228\u201329 (2d Cir. 2008)]; (2) the possibility that T&L lawyers could be necessary witnesses on reasonable cause and good faith (N.Y. Rules of Prof\'l Conduct 3.7); and (3) a potential conflict if the firm\'s own advice or representations are questioned (Rule 1.7). Mr. Hargrove\'s prior employment at the firm may also be relevant to the government\'s narrative and to any conflict analysis.'],
 'Critical',
 'Internal, not for the brief. If unaddressed, this could lead to a disqualification motion, a forced privilege waiver, or an awkward witness issue at trial \u2014 at a time of the government\'s choosing.',
 ['Raise with the firm\'s General Counsel this week; run an updated conflicts and witness analysis. Determine what role T&L played in 2017 (structuring advice? fact representations to Ridgeline?). Discuss with the client and document informed consent if appropriate. Consider whether the reliance defense can be confined to Ridgeline\'s independent analysis, and whether separate counsel should handle any witness issues. Prepare a privilege strategy before the opposition asserts reasonable cause.']
)

issue('D-13', 'Accepting the Carried-Interest Analogy Could Invite a \u00a7 1061 Recharacterization',
 ['Arg. IV.B (\u201cWhile \u00a7 1061 does not directly apply to fee waiver arrangements . . .\u201d).'],
 ['Section 1061 applies for tax years beginning after December 31, 2017 \u2014 all three years at issue \u2014 and treats certain gains on \u201capplicable partnership interests\u201d held in connection with services as short-term capital gain unless the holding period exceeds three years. If HCP embraces the carried-interest analogy too warmly, the government could argue in the alternative that some portion of the priority allocations is short-term capital gain under \u00a7 1061 (depending on the holding periods of the assets sold). The government has not made this argument and the FPAA did not assert it.'],
 'Minor',
 'A potential partial-loss scenario that is outside the FPAA. Worth knowing the exposure.',
 ['Use the carried-interest concession to establish partner-capacity and capital-gain character, but do not affirmatively characterize the priority allocations as \u201ccarried interest.\u201d Ask HCP for holding-period data for the assets whose gains funded each allocation to size any \u00a7 1061 exposure.']
)
PYEOF
echo ok
OUTER
)"

1:**THORNFIELD & LOCKE LLP**
5:**PRIVILEGED AND CONFIDENTIAL --- ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT --- PREPARED IN ANTICIPATION OF LITIGATION**
7:**MEMORANDUM**
10:  **TO:**                             R. Calvin Briggs, Partner
12:  **FROM:**                           Priya Anand
14:  **DATE:**                           April 22, 2024
16:  **RE:**                             United States v. Hargrove Capital Partners LLC, No. 1:22-cv-07841-LTS (S.D.N.Y.) --- Issue Memorandum: Factual Errors, Legal Errors, Internal Inconsistencies, and Strategic Vulnerabilities in the Government\'s Motion for Summary Judgment (filed April 3, 2024)
18:  **MATTER NO.:**                     HCP-2022-0093
27:**Bottom line.** The motion is vulnerable on three independent levels: (1) its core factual narrative is contradicted by the government\'s own declarant and exhibits; (2) several of its central legal propositions misstate the governing authority (most conspicuously Rev. Proc. 93-27, the Treas. Reg. § 1.707-2(c) factors, *Pinnacle Partners*, and the § 7701(o) penalty rules); and (3) it advances mutually exclusive characterizations of the same allocations, which is fundamentally incompatible with the claim that "no genuine dispute of material fact exists." We should be able to defeat summary judgment on every count, and the penalty portion of the motion is particularly weak. That said, the record also contains real problems for HCP that the government has not yet fully exploited and that our opposition must handle carefully (Part VII.B).
29:**The ten most important points for the opposition:**
31:1.  **The Fund IV TY 2020 election was executed December 10, 2019 --- before the fiscal year --- not "after the commencement of the 2020 fiscal year" as the Brief asserts** (Gov. Br. SUMF ¶ 17; Arg. IV.C.2). The government\'s own Exhibit 5-E, HCP\'s Election Form HCP-2020-IV-005, and the January 15, 2020 borrowing base certificate (Quillen Decl. ¶ 79) all confirm this. Five of six elections (\$41,612,000, or 87.4% of the adjustment) were indisputably prospective. (Issue A-1.)
33:2.  **Fund V realized zero gains in 2020, and the \$6,000,000 priority allocation went unsatisfied** --- the opposite of the Brief\'s assertion that Fund V had "substantial capital gains activity" that provided "the basis for" the allocation (SUMF ¶ 25; Arg. IV.C.2). Quillen Decl. ¶¶ 40--41, 44 and Ex. 4. This is the single best piece of evidence that HCP\'s entrepreneurial risk was real. (Issue A-3.)
35:3.  **The carry-forward provision carries no "compounding return equal to the applicable federal rate" and does expire --- on dissolution and final liquidation of the Fund.** Neither feature asserted in the Brief appears in any Election Form, in the Quillen Declaration, or in the Ashford Declaration. The "preferred return" and "creditor-like" arguments rest on this invented term. (Issue A-4.)
37:4.  **Rev. Proc. 93-27 says the opposite of what the government (and Professor Ashford) claim.** It provides that the IRS will *not* treat receipt of a profits interest for services as a taxable event, subject to three narrow exceptions. (Issue B-1.)
39:5.  **The government\'s "six-factor test" is not the test in Treas. Reg. § 1.707-2(c).** It skips Factor (4) entirely, substitutes the unrelated § 704(b) "transitory allocation" concept, invents factors that do not exist, and never acknowledges that § 1.707-2 is a 2015 *proposed* regulation that has never been finalized. (Issue B-2.)
41:6.  *Pinnacle Partners* turned on a deficit restoration obligation, and the court expressly limited its holding to that fact.\*\* The government\'s own Exhibit 12 says so; HCP\'s arrangement has no DRO, guarantee, or credit support. (Issue B-4.)
43:7.  **The tax-benefit figure is wrong.** 17% × \$47,612,000 = \$8,094,040, not \$9,530,400 (an overstatement of \$1,436,360, or 17.7%). The government\'s own expert uses \$8,094,040 (Ashford Decl. ¶ 18). The error is repeated three times. (Issue C-1.)
45:8.  **The government simultaneously characterizes the allocations as (i) payments to a non-partner under § 707(a)(2)(A), (ii) guaranteed payments to a partner under § 707(c), (iii) the economic equivalent of carried interest, and (iv) a profits interest taxable at grant under Rev. Proc. 93-27.** These are mutually exclusive and carry different remedies and different tax years. (Issue C-2.)
47:9.  **The penalty case ignores reasonable cause entirely, misquotes § 7701(o)(5)(A), relies on a no-fault economic substance penalty the FPAA never asserted, and offers no evidence of § 6751(b) supervisory approval.** The record (Quillen Decl. ¶¶ 64--70) affirmatively shows advice was obtained before implementation. (Issues B-10 to B-13.)
49:10. **The government has applied TEFRA concepts ("Tax Matters Partner," "FPAA") to BBA years and has not addressed the timeliness or procedural validity of the notice.** The FPAA was served on Ms. Sato as "Tax Matters Partner," but the TY 2018 return designates Mr. Hargrove as Partnership Representative (Ex. 7), and the record shows no notice of proposed partnership adjustment and only 128 days between the 30-day letter and the FPAA. Depending on facts we must confirm immediately, this may support a limitations defense for TY 2018 and TY 2019. (Issue B-14.)
